# Preface to the Third Edition.

The principles I have followed in this new edition of Kant’s *Philosophical Doctrine of Religion* <note>Original: "Philosophische Religionslehre," referring to Kant's 1793 work *Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason*</note> are the same as those that guided me in my editions of the *Critique of Pure Reason (O. Hendel, 1899)* and the *Critique of Judgment (Dürr, 1902)*. I may refer the reader to the more detailed prefaces found there.

The Introduction has undergone an expansion in that the sections on the origin, content, fundamental tendency, reception, and subsequent influence of the writing are now preceded by a coherent presentation of Kant’s religious development. The penultimate (V.) section of the Introduction consists this time of textual-philological remarks <note>Technical notes regarding the history and physical state of the manuscript and printed versions</note> restricted to the briefest possible scope. Finally, as "Appendices," there follow three pieces never before printed in any edition of Kant, published for the first time by *W. Dilthey* in the *Archive for the History of Philosophy (1890) Vol. III, Issue 3, p. 429 ff.*: 1) The draft of Kant’s letter to a theological faculty concerning the freedom to print his work <note>This refers to Kant's struggles with Prussian censorship under King Friedrich Wilhelm II</note>, 2) and 3) two previously unprinted drafts for the preface of our current work. — In addition to the index of persons and subjects (terminological dictionary), a list of the biblical passages cited or interpreted by Kant has been added.

The text was based on the second original edition (from 1794), but all deviations from the first (insofar as they did not concern orthography or punctuation) have been noted, as well as the variants of the other editions; our own textual changes are presented in a special list (for further details, see Section V of the Introduction).

In agreement with the publisher—the aforementioned documents, which bear a somewhat official character, and a reproduction from the *Loose Leaves from Kant’s Literary Estate* <note>Original: "Losen Blättern aus Kants Nachlaß," referring to the fragmented unpublished notes found after his death</note> in

<meta>This page continues the editor's preface, specifically addressing the orthographic choices and the updates made for the fourth edition of the work.</meta>

# Preface.

With the exception of Section IV, B of the introduction, the new spelling rules have been applied. I believe that in doing so—as I have already explained in the preface to my edition of the *Critique of Pure Reason*—I have acted in the truest spirit of Kant himself. Without wishing to offend those who think otherwise, I align myself with the words of the first editor of Kant's *Collected Works*, Rosenkranz (*Preface to Vol. I, page XVII*): "There is a servile archaism of fidelity which is concerned not so much with the subject matter and its reason as with the satisfaction of paleological precision <note>original: "paläologischer Akribie"; referring to an excessive, almost obsessive attention to ancient or outdated linguistic details</note>." Anyone who compares our text with the exceptions mentioned above will certainly notice the difference in the reading experience.

It would be the greatest reward for my labor if this edition of Kant's *Religion* <note>Referring to "Religion within the Bounds of Bare Reason," 1793</note>, appearing in a new, contemporary guise, contributed to promoting anew the study of a writing which—despite its age and certain biases inherent to its time—is still capable today, amidst the religious struggles of the present, of stimulating the most fruitful thoughts, and indeed of becoming a guiding star for many.

Solingen, August 18, 1903.
**Dr. K. Vorländer.**

### Regarding the fourth edition.

The entire introduction has been revised and has undergone numerous, sometimes quite drastic, improvements. For the text itself, the new editions published since 1903 by the Academy (edited by Wobbermin) and Cassirer (edited by A. Buchenau) have been compared. In general, in the years that have passed since my first edition of *Religion*, I have become more conservative regarding the formation of the text and have therefore deleted some of my changes from that time.

Solingen, July 1919.
**Karl Vorländer.**

# Introduction.

## **I. Kant's Religious Development.**

The following sketch, which undertakes for the first time to present Kant's religious development in a continuous context, had to rely on widely scattered material. The most reliable sources for the period starting from the beginning of his literary activity are, of course, his works, including his <term>posthumous papers (Nachlass)</term> <note>original: "Nachlass." These are the unpublished notes, sketches, and fragments found after a writer's death.</note>, his lectures, and his correspondence. Besides the oldest biographical sketches published by friends and admirers shortly after Kant's death—namely those by *Borowski, Jachmann, Wasianski, Hasse, Rink, etc. (cf. K. Vorländer, The Oldest Kant Biographies, Berlin 1918)*—see also my own work, *'Kant's Life' (Leipzig 1917)*, which will soon be followed by a more extensive biography of Kant. Furthermore, valuable individual contributions have been provided by: *E. Arnoldt, Kant's Youth and the First Five Years of his Private Lectureship. Königsberg 1882. The same author, Critical Excursions in the Field of Kant Research, now in E. Arnoldt's Collected Works, edited by O. Schöndörffer. — G. Hollmann, Prolegomena to the Genesis of Kant's Philosophy of Religion. Old Prussian Monthly XXXVI, Vol. 1 & 2. — A. Schweitzer <note>This refers to the famous theologian and physician Albert Schweitzer (1875–1965).</note>, Kant's Philosophy of Religion from the Critique of Pure Reason to Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason. Freiburg 1899. — E. Sänger, Kant's Doctrine of Faith. Leipzig 1903.*

->a) Youth.<-

**1.** *Childhood and School Days.* In his parental home, Kant enjoyed a strictly religious upbringing. His father and mother belonged to the <term>Pietist (pietistischen)</term> <note>original: "Pietismus." A movement within Lutheranism that emphasized individual piety, deep emotional religious experience, and rigorous moral living over formal dogma.</note> movement, which had moved into Königsberg since the end of the 17th century and, particularly under the influence of the preacher and professor Franz Albert Schultz (1692–1763), dominated wide circles of the population. For both parents, religion was a matter of the heart; the entire atmosphere of the simple artisan—

<keywords>Immanuel Kant, Pietism, Königsberg, religious education, Franz Albert Schultz, biography, German Enlightenment, philosophy of religion</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the biographical sketch of Immanuel Kant's youth, picking up mid-word from the previous page's description of his upbringing. It transitions from his domestic life to his formal education at the Pietist-led Collegium Fridericianum.</meta>

# Introduction.

ing. This artisan family breathed the strictest moral purity, honesty, tolerance, and genuine piety. They possessed—as their son would still praise them for in his old age—"the highest that a human being can possess: that tranquility, that cheerfulness, that inner peace which was disturbed by no passions,"¹) and they also gave their children an education that, "viewed from the moral side, could not have been better at all" (Kant to Lindblom, August 13, 1797). His mother, in particular, seems to have exerted a lasting influence on the serious and thoughtful boy; even decades later, his eyes would shine when he spoke of her. "She often led me," as he told his later biographer R. B. Jachmann, "outside the city, drew my attention to the works of God, expressed herself with a pious delight regarding His omnipotence, wisdom, and goodness, and imprinted into my heart a deep reverence toward the Creator of all things." In addition, she did not fail to have him diligently attend the <term>prayer meetings</term> <note>original: "Betstunden." These were informal devotional gatherings typical of Pietism, focused on prayer and Bible study rather than formal liturgy.</note> held by the aforementioned F. A. Schultz. As the family's pastor and advisor, Schultz arranged for the gifted son of the artisan to be admitted in his ninth year (autumn 1732) to the <term>Collegium Fridericianum</term> <note>A prestigious Latin school in Königsberg named after King Frederick I. It was a center for Pietist education.</note>, which was under his influence.

This <term>gymnasium</term> <note>A German secondary school designed to prepare students for university.</note>, directed by Schultz himself from 1733 onward, and where Immanuel spent his entire remaining school years (1732–1740), was likewise completely permeated by the spirit of <term>Pietism</term> <note>A reform movement within Lutheranism that emphasized individual piety, living a rigorous Christian life, and emotional religious experience over formal dogma.</note>. Its purpose was explicitly stated: "that, on the one hand, those under its care might be rescued from their spiritual ruin and genuine Christianity be planted in their hearts from youth onward, but on the other hand, that their temporal well-being might also be promoted." According to contemporary testimonies, religion dominated the entire curriculum from 5 o'clock in the morning until 9 o'clock in the evening. Greek, for example,

It is no wonder, then, that instruction in philosophy and mathematics suffered—subjects that Kant, "in his middle years, could not look back upon without a laugh." Moreover, even then, he could "find absolutely no taste for the ritual of piety, or rather <term>religious affectation</term> <note>original: "Frömmelei." ## 2. *University Years and the Following Period.*

Even at the university, which he entered in the autumn, a certain connection between Kant and Königsberg Pietism persisted. Although he did not enroll as a theologian—as the biographer Schubert once assumed—and likely did not enroll in any specific faculty at all, he did attend the lectures of his former director, Schultz, on <term>Dogmatics</term> <note>The systematic study and explanation of the core doctrines or "dogmas" of the church.</note>, primarily out of personal loyalty and veneration. The mathematician and philosopher Knutzen, whom Kant notoriously valued most among all his university teachers, also combined his philosophical convictions with a Pietist religious outlook. Among other works, he wrote a <note>original title: "Philosophischer Beweis von der Wahrheit der christlichen Religion, darinnen die Notwendigkeit einer geoffenbarten Religion insgemein und die Wahrheit oder Gewißheit der christlichen insbesondere aus ungezweifelten Gründen der Vernunft nach mathematischer Lehrart dargetan und behauptet wird"</note> "*Philosophical Proof of the Truth of the Christian Religion, in which the necessity of a revealed religion in general and the truth or certainty of the Christian religion in particular is demonstrated and asserted from undoubted grounds of reason according to the mathematical method*" (*Königsberg 1739 f.*). Nevertheless, it is reliably attested that it was not the religious direction that particularly attracted the young Immanuel to his teacher, but rather the fact that Knutzen stimulated independent thinking in philosophical and mathematical-physical matters.

XII
Introduction.

Instead of following the pattern of his school companion David Ruhnken and becoming a capable philologist <note>A scholar of language and literature.</note>, as his friends expected of him, he threw himself entirely into philosophy, mathematics, and "pure" natural science. That he had, in any case, completely lost sight of theology is proven by the answer he once gave his old teacher Schultz when asked about his future profession; he declared that he "wanted to become a <term>physician</term> <note>original: "Medikus." At the time, medical studies were seen as a distinct path from the theological career his family and teachers likely intended for him.</note>." The fact that in his old age (1802) he told his dinner companions that he had once drafted a sermon on Matthew 5:23 ("Be well-disposed toward your adversary" <note>original: "Sei willfährig deinem Widersacher." While the text cites verse 23, this specific phrase is found in Matthew 5:25.</note>) does not prove that he truly intended to dedicate himself to the clerical office. And, even if the remark he entered into the family book upon the death of his father in 1746¹) still seems to be kept in the same spirit that filled his home and school atmosphere, the choice of the theme of his famous first treatise (*Thoughts on the True Estimation of Living Forces*) and the manner of its development already indicate his changed intellectual direction. Furthermore, the question addressed to him with solemn earnestness in 1758 by his former teacher F. A. Schultz, before recommending him for a professorship—"Do you also fear God from your heart?"—suggests a slight doubt on the part of the said theologian regarding the young philosopher's <term>orthodoxy</term> <note>Strict adherence to established religious doctrines.</note>.

From 1755 onward, Kant's further religious development is primarily evident in his writings, from which the features most characteristic of our topic shall be presented here.

Here he still recognizes the value of the **physico-theological proof** <note>A traditional argument for the existence of God based on the evidence of design and order in the physical universe.</note>, but he believes that the "defenders of religion" and "advocates of faith"—one of whom he depicts disputing with a "free-thinker" and a "naturalist"—were "accustomed to using it in a poor manner." The theories of Democritus, Epicurus, and Lucretius, to which his own was related, by no means had to lead to the denial of God. The principle of his later <term>Criticism</term> <note>original: "Kritizismus." Kant’s later philosophical system that separates what we can know through science from what we must believe through faith.</note>—the clean separation of knowledge and faith—is already noticeable here. In the field of natural science, the strictly mechanical view is valid; beyond that, however, space remains for the religious view.

3. The concluding reflection of the small treatise on the *The Lisbon Earthquake* (1756) rejects the "blameworthy curiosity" which "always views such fates as decreed penal judgments" and "presumes to perceive the intentions of divine decrees and to interpret them according to its own insights." <note>The 1755 Lisbon earthquake was a massive disaster that sparked a European-wide debate on whether such suffering could be justified by religion.</note> On the other hand, we are "in no uncertainty, when it comes to the application, how we should use these ways of Providence in accordance with its purpose," namely "to remind us that the goods of the earth can provide no satisfaction to our drive for happiness."

4. The short treatise *On Optimism* (1759), "written down with some haste" and published as an announcement for his lectures for the winter semester of 1759/60, defends <term>Optimism</term> <note>In the 18th century, "Optimism" was the philosophical theory (popularized by Leibniz) that we live in the "best of all possible worlds" because a perfect God created it.</note> based on the thought that God cannot help but choose the best. The whole is the best, and everything is good for the sake of the whole. "Unworthy in myself and chosen for the sake of the whole, I value my existence all the more because I was chosen to take a place in the best plan. I cry out to every creature who does not make itself unworthy of being called so: Hail to us, we exist! And the Creator takes pleasure in us." In his later years, Kant wanted nothing more to do with this writing, as it stood in contradiction to his later <term>Critical views</term> <note>Kant’s later "Critical" period (starting in 1781) argued that human reason cannot prove these kinds of absolute truths about God's plan.</note>.

5. The heartfelt little consolatory writing, *Consolation of a Mother on the Death of Her Son* (F. von Funk, 1760), gives evidence of the philosopher's truly inward religiosity—that "calm cheerfulness of the soul for which no accidents are unexpected anymore," combined with a "gentle melancholy" when it "considers the worthlessness of that which is commonly regarded among us as great and important," but despite all dark fates, trusting in the guidance of a wise and kind Providence.

7. The prize essay *Inquiry Concerning the Distinctness of the Principles of Natural Theology and Morality* (1764), which already reveals its standpoint to some extent in its title, brings no essentially new motifs. The primary grounds of <term>natural theology</term> <note>The study of God based on reason and experience rather than on divine revelation.</note> are, Kant still believes here, "capable of the greatest philosophical evidence," even if not mathematical evidence; a number of problems derived from them, however, are capable of only an "approximate," that is, a moral evidence.

8. Skepticism emerges more strongly in the *Dreams of a Spirit-Seer* (1766), a work known for revealing most strongly the influence of French and English <term>empiricism</term> <note>The theory that all knowledge is derived from sense-experience.</note>. At the conclusion of this work, Kant also comes to speak of religious faith. Here, Kant wants to leave all dogmatics of the supernatural ("all noisy systems of instruction regarding such distant objects") "to speculation and the concern of idle heads." To be sure, in his opinion, "hardly an upright soul has ever lived who could have endured the thought that with death everything was at an end, and whose noble disposition had not risen to the hope of the future." But it seems to him nevertheless "to be more in keeping with human nature and the purity of morals to ground the expectation of the future world on the feelings of a well-disposed soul, rather than conversely to ground its good conduct on the hope of the other world." It is the standpoint of the "**moral faith**" appearing here for the first time, which, without engaging in subtle reasoning, leads humans "without detour to their true purposes." This concept later expands in his work *Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason* into the proposition: religion is based on morality, not morality on religion. As for the "mysteries of the—"

### c) Critical Period.

1. Regarding Kant's religious views during the decade from 1771–1781—which was entirely dedicated to the elaboration of his great critical masterpiece <note>The *Critique of Pure Reason*, published in 1781.</note>—several letters provide us with welcome insight. In them, we already see the fundamental ideas of *Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason* before us, eighteen years prior to its publication. Of particular importance are a detailed letter and a draft to Lavater (1775), as well as a letter to Chr. H. Wolke (1776).

On April 8, 1774, Lavater <note>Johann Caspar Lavater was a Swiss poet and theologian famous for his work on physiognomy and his intense religious devotion.</note> had sent a letter overflowing with reverence, asking for Kant’s judgment on his treatise on faith and prayer. In his reply on April 28, 1775, our philosopher developed his religious and historico-religious views, which differed entirely from those of the "Prophet of Zurich." In a manner reminiscent of Lessing <note>Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, a leading Enlightenment dramatist and philosopher who advocated for a religion of reason over historical dogma.</note>, he distinguishes the teachings of Christ from the reports we have about them. "In order to extract the former in its purity, I seek first of all to separate the **moral teaching** from all New Testament **statutes** <note>Referring to specific religious laws, rituals, or dogmas established by church authority rather than by universal reason.</note>. This is certainly the fundamental doctrine of the Gospel," everything else being merely "auxiliary doctrine." When we have done what is within our power, we can humbly trust that God—given the "holiness of His law and the invincible evil of our heart"—will necessarily provide some "supplement for our deficiency."

No book and no revelation occurring to me personally can impose anything on me as religion that has not already become a duty for me through the holy law within me...

3. ***Critique of Pure Reason***: Even religion must be able to endure a free and public critique if it wishes to claim "unfeigned" respect from reason (1st Preface, page 5, footnote). Immortality and freedom of the will are the cornerstones of all religion (page 773). Metaphysics cannot be the foundation of religion, but it must remain as its defensive bulwark (page 877). That which humans began with in the childhood of philosophy—namely, "first studying the knowledge of God and the hope, or perhaps even the nature, of another world"—is the point at which "we would now prefer to end" (page 880). Practical or moral faith in the existence of God and a future world is, in contrast to "doctrinal" (theoretical) faith, indeed unchangeable, but it is not knowledge (page 856). It contains not a logical, but a moral certainty; in this case, one must not say: "It is certain," but rather: "I am morally certain that there is a God," etc. (page 857). The answer to the last of the three questions in which all interests of reason unite—**What can I know? What ought I to do? What may I hope?** (page 833)—reads, according to Kant: You may hope for happiness in the same measure as you have made yourself worthy of it through your moral conduct. — The 2nd edition of the work (1787) contains no conception essentially different from the first. The much-cited sentence of the second preface: "I had to deny <note>original: "aufheben." This famous term suggests setting aside or limiting the scope of speculative knowledge to make space for moral belief.</note> **knowledge to make room for faith**," does not have the meaning, in the context of the whole book, that has often been attributed to it by both theological and radical sides.

XX
<header>Introduction.</header>

However, at a later point (p. 155), the Christian principle of morality is not counted among the theological (and "therefore" <term>heteronomous</term> <note>Heteronomous refers to laws or rules that come from an outside source, such as divine command or natural desire, rather than from one's own reason.</note>) principles, but is instead described as <term>autonomous</term> <note>Autonomous refers to the capacity of the will to be a law unto itself, independent of any outside influence.</note>; it is said to surpass even the moral concept of the **Stoics** in purity and rigor (p. 153, note). The "sanctification" of Christian religious doctrine consists of persistent "moral progress"; anyone who is conscious of having persevered in this out of genuine moral motives until the end of their life may allow themselves "the comforting hope, though not certainty, that they will continue to adhere to these principles even in an existence continued beyond this life" (p. 148, note). The existence of God is a **postulate**—that is, a necessary theoretical assumption for practical purposes—because it contains the "basis for the exact correspondence of nature (happiness) with morality" (p. 149); but belief in it is not an objective duty, but a subjective need (p. 150). Through the concept of the **highest good** as the object and final purpose of pure practical reason, the moral law leads to **religion**—that is, the recognition of all duties as divine commands (p. 155). Various passages (pp. 85, 102, 104, 145, 147) are directed against mysticism and religious fanaticism <note>original: "Schwärmerei," a term Kant used to describe irrational religious fervor or the delusion of seeing or communicating with supernatural beings.</note>: these are all thoughts that we will encounter again in *Religion* <note>Referring to Kant's later work, *Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason*.</note>.

5. The ***Critique of Judgment*** is not only the closest to *Religion* in terms of time, but also speaks more extensively about theological problems than any of the philosopher's other works; the final seven paragraphs (pp. 400–482) are dedicated exclusively to such issues. Its essence consists in the disposition <note>original: "Gesinnung," referring to the internal moral attitude or character from which actions flow.</note> (p. 477). e) Of the seven small essays from the years 1788–91 published only from Kant’s literary remains (*Philosophical Library Vol. 50*), the second (*On Miracles*) and the fifth (*On Prayer*) come into consideration for us, though they offer little that is truly distinctive. — The **miracle** is defined as “an event whose cause is not to be found in nature” (264). The incompatibility of all miracles with the natural law of <term>causality</term> <note>The principle that every effect must have a specific cause within the physical world.</note> is shown through logical conclusions; additionally, a rather <term>scholastic</term> <note>A term referring to the rigid, highly structured academic style of medieval philosophy, which Kant often found overly technical and detached from practical reality.</note> classification of miracles into external and internal, rigorous and comparative, material and formal, occasional and pre-established is given. — **Prayer** has no consequences other than natural ones. For some, it may be recommended for the sake of certain advantages (bringing about greater clarity, liveliness, or a drive toward virtue); others will not have need of it. Especially since hypocrisy is usually involved; for (we consider the following to be a fallacy!) the person praying imagines the Deity as something that can be given to the senses; he stops praying when he has made progress in goodness, and he feels ashamed if he is found praying.

Finally, the last writing that sheds light on Kant’s religious views before the publication of *Religion* is the essay: *On the Failure of All Philosophical Attempts in Theodicy*, which also appeared in the *Berlin Monthly* <note>original: "Berlinischen Monatsschrift"</note> (September 1791). As its title suggests, its content is focused on the philosophy of religion; in its line of thought, it stands extraordinarily close to the first section of *Religion*, the drafting of which occurred at nearly the same time. Its main questions: How is the existence of **evil** in the world compatible with **God's holiness**, how are the countless ills compatible with His goodness, and how is the distribution of these ills compatible with His justice? These are also found there in a different form. The answer here is that “our reason is absolutely incapable of gaining insight into the relationship in which a world—as we may ever know it through experience—stands to the highest wisdom.” Many individual thoughts of the later work are also found here: the valuation of religious sincerity, the **highest good**, and the **religion of good conduct** in contrast to the religion of “**courting favor**” <note>original: "Gunstbewerbung"; this refers to the attempt to win God's approval through rituals or flattery rather than moral living.</note> and many others. Particularly fine is the treatment of the **Book of Job** (pp. 151 to 154), which concludes with the thought that Job “did not base his morality on faith, but rather his faith on morality.” This purely moral conception of religion leads to the decisive sentence that “the concept of God that is to be suitable for religion must be a concept of Him as a **moral being**,” for “we do not need Him for the purpose of explaining nature, and thus for a speculative intent” (140 note).

## d) **Results. Other Testimonies regarding Kant’s Position on Religion.**

If we look back on the religious **history of development** of our philosopher as sketched in the preceding pages, we see before us a picture that is consistent in its essential features. Since at least the 1760s, his **overall religious view** changed so little that one can only speak of a "development" in a conditional sense. Only the method of justification changes—it progresses in connection with Kant’s overall philosophical development from the pre-critical to the critical period—whereas the **content** changes very little. This content generally coincides with the **religious rationalism** <term>rationalism: The philosophical view that reason and intellect, rather than divine revelation or tradition, are the primary sources of knowledge and truth.</term> of his time, even if the moral-practical fundamental trait is much more pronounced in Kant. The after-effects of **Pietism** <term>Pietism: A movement within the Lutheran Church that emphasized individual piety, deep emotion, and a rigorous moral life over formal dogma.</term> on Kant were more of a negative than a positive nature. He did indeed have certain things in common with genuine **Pietism**, as he encountered it, for example, through his parents or his director **Schultz**: the appreciation of inner disposition, religious sincerity, and a good way of life; even individual views, such as his sympathy for the "brave" **Spener** <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705) was the founder of Pietism.</note> and his antipathy toward **Spinoza**, may have been remnants of those youthful views. However, as a whole, he called **Pietism** a "slavish state of mind" and identified it with "**sanctimoniousness**" (*Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason*, p. 278, note), and he always most energetically warded off the accusation of holding **mystical views**. Precisely because he had to reject the latter as a result of his general philosophical and religious **worldview**, his position toward "positive" **Christianity** <term>positive Christianity: Religious beliefs and practices based on historical revelation, church tradition, and established authority rather than on reason alone.</term> remained, on the whole, much cooler than it might otherwise have been.

This personal coolness of his toward **Christianity**, insofar as it seeks to go beyond the character of a "purely moral" religion—especially when it seeks to influence **feeling**—is also attested by those who enjoyed his intimate personal company. Thus **Jachmann** <note>Reinhold Bernhard Jachmann was one of Kant's biographers and a former student.</note> relates that he just as little,

In their current form, these lectures bring nothing essentially new; rather, they present the thoughts of his printed scientific works in a more popular form, taking more account of ecclesiastical <note>Relating to the established Christian church.</note> doctrines. <term>Theology</term> is defined here as: the system of our knowledge of the Supreme Being. <term>Religion</term> is: the application of theology to morality. Reason’s interest in the knowledge of God is primarily a practical one, in that our moral disposition receives more nourishment and strength through faith in God and immortality. Natural religion is the substrate <note>The underlying layer or foundation.</note> of all religion. A detailed classification of theology into rational, empirical, etc., is provided, and speculative proofs for the existence of God are rejected here as well. The three "articles of moral faith," which are to be accepted "merely in a practical respect" rather than theoretically, are: God, the freedom of the human will, and a moral world. Evil is described here only as "the incomplete development of the seed toward the good." The concept of <term>Predestination</term> <note>The doctrine that God has ordained all that will happen, especially regarding the salvation or damnation of individual souls.</note> is immoral because it predetermines "sacrificial victims of misery." ## II. On the History of the Work's Origin.

On May 4, 1793, Kant wrote to the professor of theology C. Fr. Stäudlin <note>Carl Friedrich Stäudlin (1761–1826) was an influential German theologian and church historian at the University of Göttingen.</note> in Göttingen: ". . . My plan, established for quite some time now, for the processing of the field of pure philosophy which I see as my duty, aimed at the resolution of three tasks: 1. What can I know? (<term>Metaphysics</term> <note>The branch of philosophy that explores the fundamental nature of reality and existence.</note>), 2. What should I do? (<term>Morality</term>), 3. What may I hope? (Religion); which finally was to be followed by a fourth: What is man? (<term>Anthropology</term> . . .). — With the accompanying work: *Religion within the Boundaries* etc. <note>Kant's major work on religion is titled *Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason* (*Die Religion innerhalb der Grenzen der bloßen Vernunft*).</note> I have sought to complete the third section of my plan, in which work I have been guided by conscientiousness and true respect for the Christian religion, but also by the principle of a becoming frankness, to conceal nothing, but rather to openly set forth how I believe I see the possible union of the latter with the purest <term>practical reason</term> <note>Kant uses "practical reason" to describe how our rational minds determine moral laws and guide our actions.</note>." — The drafting of our work, therefore, rested on a well-considered plan. After Kant had provided a new foundation for science, morality, and art (the latter not being mentioned in this specific passage) in his three great critical works <note>Referring to his three "Critiques": the *Critique of Pure Reason* (science), *Critique of Practical Reason* (morality), and *Critique of Judgment* (aesthetics/art).</note>, it was only natural that he also drew the field of religion—which, as we have seen in the previous section, had been close to his heart since his youth—into the scope of his critical work. He undertook to complete and conclude the many individual explanations, which we have already seen him making in numerous earlier writings, in a comprehensive, systematic work.

<summary>This page explains Kant's motivation for writing on religion, framing it as the third major question of his philosophical career: "What may I hope?"</summary>

XXXI

# Introduction.

This systematic character seems, however, to be contradicted by the manner in which Kant first intended its publication. Initially, it was not intended to appear as a book at all, but in four individual "pieces" in the *Berlinische Monatsschrift* <note>The *Berlin Monthly*, a leading journal of the German Enlightenment.</note> edited by his friend Biester, to whom he had already entrusted so many of his smaller works (cf. p. XXI ff.). Yet only the "first piece" succeeded in this, and even then, not without difficulty. On the throne of Frederick the Great now sat King Frederick William II; in the place of the man to whom Kant had dedicated his greatest work and who had shown the philosopher his grateful respect at every opportunity <note>This refers to the previous King, Frederick the Great, who was a patron of Enlightenment thinkers.</note>, stood the obscurantist <note>A person who deliberately opposes Enlightenment and the spread of knowledge.</note> Wöllner. In April 1791, as the head of the censorship office for church and school affairs, Wöllner had installed a three-man commission—consisting of Hermes, Woltersdorf, and Hillmer—who were as narrow-minded as they were prone to persecution. <note>original: "E. Fromm, *I. Kant und die preußische Zensur* [I. Kant and the Prussian Censorship]. Lpz. 1894. E. Arnoldt, *Beiträge zu dem Material der Geschichte von Kants Leben und Schriftstellertätigkeit in bezug auf seine „Religionslehre“ und seinen Konflikt mit der preußischen Regierung* [Contributions to the Material of the History of Kant's Life and Literary Activity regarding his "Doctrine of Religion" and his Conflict with the Prussian Government]. Königsberg 1898. K. Vorländer, *Kants Leben* [Kant's Life] p. 156 ff., 176 ff."</note>

In February 1792, Kant sent his essay *Über das radikale Böse in der menschlichen Natur* (*On the Radical Evil in Human Nature*)—the first section of our current volume—to Biester, the editor of the *Berlinische Monatsschrift*, with the request that it be submitted to the Berlin censorship authorities before printing. Since the monthly journal had been printed outside of Prussia (in Jena) since the beginning of 1792, Kant actually had no reason for such caution or consideration. However, he did not want, as he said, "to have even the appearance of being willing to engage in a literary smuggling trade and of expressing so-called 'bold opinions' only by intentionally evading the strict Berlin censorship." Biester therefore submitted the article to the Senior Consistorial Councilor Hillmer, who was responsible for censoring matters of "moral content," and received it back the very next day with the <term>Imprimatur</term> <note>Latin for "let it be printed," the official license granted by a censor to publish a work.</note>.

He (Hillmer) had permitted the printing, "because, after a careful reading, he found this writing—like other Kantian works—intended for and palatable only to thinking scholars capable of investigation and discernment, but not for the general reading public." Thus, the essay appeared in the April issue of the *Monthly*, pages 323–385.

Things did not go as well for the second "piece" (titled in our edition: *On the Struggle of the Good Principle with the Evil, etc.*), which Biester received from Kant in June 1792 and immediately submitted to the censors. This time, Hillmer found that the manuscript's content "fell entirely within the realm of biblical theology." He therefore informed Biester on June 14 that, according to his instructions, he had read it together with his theological colleague Hermes; since the latter refused his *permission to print* <note>original: "Imprimatur" — the official license granted by a censor to publish a book.</note>, Hillmer concurred with him. Following a further letter from Biester to Hermes, the latter simply cited the (Wöllner) Edict on Religion <note>The Religious Edict of 1788 was a decree by the Prussian King intended to curb the influence of Enlightenment thinking on the clergy and maintain orthodox Christian doctrines.</note> as his guiding principle; "he could not provide any further explanation." With good reason, Biester added these words to his report in a letter to Kant on June 18: "It must surely outrage everyone that the likes of Hillmer and Hermes want to presume to dictate to the world whether it should read a Kant or not." Biester himself, however, despite being a royal official (a librarian), did not hesitate to stand up for his famous collaborator by sending a detailed *direct petition* <note>original: "Immediat-Gesuch" — a formal request sent directly to the monarch, bypassing the usual bureaucratic hierarchy.</note> to the King as early as June 20.

However, it was an unfavorable time for such petitions. The State Ministry, which Biester had asked to review his complaint, had already been on the receiving end of a harsh royal *cabinet order* <note>original: "Kabinetsordre" — a decree issued directly from the King's private office.</note> on February 21. This occurred after the ministry had dared to express various concerns regarding the strict enforcement of censorship—a measure recommended by the Emperor in light of the French Revolution. The King had reproached his ministers, stating that it seemed as though they were speaking on behalf of the Enlightenment thinkers <note>original: "Aufklärer"</note> and treating the "falsifications of the pure Christian religion so boldly undertaken by so many clergy and other Enlightenment figures" as "inessential"...

XXX); and finally, as shown by his printed and two (until recently) unprinted (see below) prefaces to his *Religion*, he also wanted to bring the philosopher's right to free religious research within the boundaries of his science to a fundamental decision through his actions. He therefore combined the four related treatises into one book, today's *Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason*, and decided to submit this to a "domestic"—that is, a Prussian—theological faculty for an evaluation as to whether they "laid claim to its censorship as encroaching upon biblical theology, or rather rejected it as belonging to philosophical theology" (to Stäudlin, in the place cited <note>original: "a. a. O." (am angeführten Orte) — a citation shorthand equivalent to "loc. cit."</note> p. 415).¹)

XXXIV

# Introduction.

Out of a delicate sense of consideration for his colleagues in Königsberg, whom he was reluctant to "set at odds with the Spiritual Higher Examination Commission," <note>The *Geistliche Oberexaminationskommission* was the Prussian state body established by King Frederick William II to enforce religious orthodoxy and censor Enlightenment ideas.</note> Kant initially thought of having his book submitted for examination by the theological faculty in Göttingen (through Stäudlin); he then considered Halle, but moved away from that plan because the dean of the faculty there had shortly before refused the permit to print <term>Imprimatur|The official license or "let it be printed" permission required from a recognized authority before a book could be published.</term> to Fichte’s *Critique of All Revelation*. However, since the Königsberg theological faculty itself did not fear any trouble from the situation, he requested their decision. They ruled in his favor, assigning the right of censorship <note>In the university system of the time, "censorship" was often a routine internal review by a faculty rather than a hostile state action.</note> to the philosophical faculty. It was by such a faculty—not the theological one in Königsberg, as was mostly assumed until now following the account by Borowski, and also not the philosophical faculty in Königsberg, as **Dilthey** and **Fromm** still believed—but by the one in Jena that the permit to print was granted.

**Arnoldt**, in fact, discovered the censorship mark on several sheets of the Kantian manuscript in R. Reicke’s possession: "**I have seen this. J. C. Hennings, dean at this time**" <note>original: "Vidi J. C. Hennings, h. t. Decanus"</note>. Justus Christian Hennings was *h. t.*, that is, "at this time" (winter semester 1792/93), a professor of philosophy and dean of the philosophical faculty in Jena. Why was Jena chosen in particular? Likely because Kant was reluctant to have the printing permission granted to him by his own student, **Chr. J. Kraus**, who was serving as dean of the Königsberg faculty during that winter semester; but also because the book, like the first essay published in the *Berlin Monthly*, was being printed in Jena (by Göpfert). By February 28, 1793, it was half-printed, as **Schiller**—who read the completed galley proofs with enthusiasm—reported to his friend **Körner**.

The history of the origin of a literary or scientific work is usually accompanied by a discussion of the sources from which the writer in question has drawn. However, with hardly any author is such a discussion so little appropriate as with **Kant**. For, as great a reader as he was, and as much knowledge as he possessed in the most diverse fields of human knowledge, they provided him at best only with the raw material, which he processed entirely independently; and, being completely occupied by his systematic task, he involved himself only slightly—at least in his critical period—with the historical-literary side of the problems he treated. Thus, our **Index of People for the *Religion*** <note>Referring to Kant’s work *Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason*.</note> is very short and contains, besides a few names of poets and authors of travelogues (of whom **Kant** was famously a particular friend), only a few names of philosophers and theologians. Nevertheless, let the little that we know of **Kant’s** theological studies be reported here.

**Jachmann** asserts (in the work cited, p. 30) that **Kant** possessed “an exact knowledge of the religious documents of the Christians, Jews, and other peoples and much theological scholarship,” but soon thereafter limits this very general statement with the words: “He also occasionally read theological writings.” **Borowski** expresses himself more specifically and therefore probably more reliably to the effect that **Kant** never touched “theological investigations of any kind, especially those concerning <term>Exegesis|The critical explanation or interpretation of a text, especially of scripture.</term> and <term>Dogmatics|The systematic study of the fundamental doctrines of a religion.</term>” (p. 252); that he found no taste for **Ernesti’s** theological works and “knew very little of the further research of **Semler**, **Teller**, and others, as well as the results thereof . . . . Indeed, his knowledge reached into the—” <note>Johann August Ernesti, Johann Salomo Semler, and Wilhelm Abraham Teller were leading Enlightenment theologians who sought to interpret the Bible through reason rather than tradition.</note>

### III. Basic Tendency and Content of the Work.

Kant's writing is, in its basic tendency, an
attempt at reconciliation between faith and
knowledge, biblical Christianity and reason. ¹)
He proceeds aggressively only against orthodoxy:
otherwise, he maintains a certain middle
ground. He rejects freethinking <note>original: "Freigeisterei"</note> and naturalism just as
clearly as he does mysticism and pietism <note>A movement within Lutheranism that emphasized individual piety and living a "vigorous" Christian life.</note>. Revealed
religion and rational religion are for him—this is, according to
the second preface, p. XXII, the meaning of the title of his
work—not two separate (eccentric) circles, but
concentric circles; that is, within the
Christian doctrine of revelation, the "pure system of
rational religion," which is his aim, is
contained. It only needs to be "peeled out," the "historical"
system only "fragmentarily held to moral concepts,"
and then, "after the omission of everything empirical," the
"actual," pure, or moral religion of reason will remain.
Also in the preface to the *Conflict of the Faculties* (1798), he
expressly declares that he chose the title *Religion within the
Boundaries of Mere Reason* intentionally,
so that it would not look as if he wanted to "dishonor

...right, that it <note>The "it" likely refers to the Berlin censorship or the faculty mentioned on the previous page.</note> regarded the first essay as belonging to the field of moral philosophy. For this treats problems that predominantly belong to the latter field, such as: Does the world progress toward the better or not? What does "evil" mean? Is man by nature good or evil or indifferent? How do the three predispositions of man—toward animality, humanity, and personality—relate to one another? It is only through the free choice of human beings, Kant argues, that they become evil. In this respect, one can claim: Man is "by nature" evil, and indeed "radically" so, because the perversion of moral incentives within him corrupts the motive of all principles. This "origin" of evil in man is, however, to be understood as a rational origin <note>term: "Rational origin" (Latin: *origo rationalis*). Kant distinguishes between a "temporal origin" (a historical start) and a "rational origin" (the logical reason why a free will chooses evil), arguing we cannot blame our ancestors for our own moral failings.</note>, not as a temporal origin; in any case, it is not inherited. Therefore, the Old Testament story of the Fall of Man is to be reinterpreted morally, for whatever "contributes nothing to becoming a better person" is "only an unfruitful increase of our historical knowledge" (p. 47 note). How can a man who is evil by nature then make himself into a good man? Only through a **revolution of his way of thinking** <note>term: "Revolution of the way of thinking" (German: *Revolution der Denkungsart*). Kant argues that while behavior can be improved gradually (reform), becoming a truly moral person requires a single, fundamental decision to change one's core principles.</note>, which is possible for us as a result of our original moral predisposition. Only at the very end of the "first piece" does a thought appear that is no longer moral-philosophical but religious-philosophical, namely: When man has completed this revolution of the way of thinking within himself and strives with all his might to become better, he can hope that what is still lacking in him will be supplemented through "higher cooperation." (p. 62 in the "General Note" regarding "effects of grace.")

a) The required holiness of disposition is never attainable for human beings;

b) One who is on the path of improvement may trust that it will endure;

4. The third section <note>original: *Stück*. Kant’s work is famously divided into four "pieces" or parts. This section deals with the "Ethical Commonwealth."</note> leads from the individual to the community. Most, if not all, human passions arise from living together with others (in modern language: from social conditions). Therefore, to counteract evil in a lasting way, a “society according to laws of virtue” or a “Kingdom of God on Earth” must be established. Similar to the legal-political commonwealth, the ethical commonwealth also emerges from a kind of state of nature, in which people consciously unite into a “people of God”; for it is not the people themselves, but only God who can be the legislator in this ethical state, where the focus is on morality <note>term: Morality (German: *Moralität*). The churches that actually exist always start from a historical (revelatory) faith or an “ecclesiastical faith,” which is best founded on a Holy Scripture, but which can never replace pure religious faith. There may well be many kinds of faith, but only one (true) religion. Ecclesiastical faith has as its highest interpreter the purely moral religion of reason; therefore, the scriptural text—as Kant quite openly states here—is to be interpreted morally, even if such an interpretation might often “seem forced,” or indeed “often really be so” (158). <page-num>XLVIII</page-num>
<header>Introduction.</header>

We now return to the fundamental philosophical question posed at the beginning of this section (p. XLI): Did Kant succeed in his “philosophical doctrine of religion” in truly creating a lasting and definitive systematic foundation for religion, in the same way he did in his other major works for science, ethics, and art? Our opinion is: No. For, no matter how much religion may be connected with knowledge and the will, and no matter how true it may be (as we unreservedly admit) that true religion can only be built upon the foundation of scientific knowledge and pure ethics: in the final analysis, it rests—both historically and according to its actual presence in human souls—on a particular direction of consciousness: **feeling**. We are of the opinion that at this point, Schleiermacher <note>Friedrich Schleiermacher (1768–1834) was a theologian and philosopher who argued that religion is not primarily about knowledge or morality, but about a "feeling of absolute dependence" on the divine.</note> most successfully complemented the critical system. Psychologically, Kant's position can be very well understood. He, who systematically<gloss>¹)</gloss> as well as personally was no friend of strong emphasis on the emotional life, also saw only mysticism, pietism <note>term: Pietism. A reform movement within Lutheranism that emphasized individual piety and the "living" religious experience of the heart over formal dogma.</note>, and all sorts of fanaticism <note>original: *Schwärmerei*. A derogatory term Kant used for "religious enthusiasm" or "fanaticism" that he felt bypassed reason.</note> and sectarianism associated with it in the religious field. He therefore conceived of religion, as is evident from his frequently repeated definition of the concept, partly intellectually (“knowledge”), and even more so morally (“viewing all our duties as divine commands”). It is “to be founded on principles” (269), though admittedly not as knowledge, but only as problematic acceptance (230 note) or free faith. His philosophy of religion is, at its core, nothing other than an appendix to his morality; in other words: **applied ethics**. This emerges most strongly, as we have already seen, in the “first part”; but the remaining parts, though they deal with the Kingdom of God, the church, sacraments, divine service, and the like, treat all of these as purely moral institutions without doing justice to the side of feeling.

<page-num>XLIX</page-num>
<header>Introduction.</header>

Even in its external form—this may be due to its origin: the merging of four separate essays—the intended systematic character of the work does not seem to us to have been achieved. At least not in relation to “**Religion**,” which is supposed to be the book's theme, while its definition is only provided at the beginning of the final chapter. Kant seems to have observed external systematics more closely in his lectures on **natural theology** <note>original: *natürliche Theologie*. This refers to the study of God based on reason and experience rather than revelation.</note> (see above p. XXIX f.). In contrast, the four chapters of our current text stand in a rather loose connection to one another: the “indwelling” of the evil principle alongside the good, the struggle of both for dominion, the victory of the good, and service and <term>pseudo-service</term> <note>original: *Afterdienst*. A term Kant used for "spurious worship" or religious practices that mistakenly substitute ritual for moral conduct.</note> under its dominion—and, moreover, in a connection that essentially relates only to **morality**.

It is, therefore, religiously applied **morality** that we receive, or conversely: religion, specifically Christian, New Testament religion, insofar as it contains moral content. Does this not perhaps impair the purity of morality itself in a certain sense? We believe that if morality in itself does not require the **idea of God** (p. III), then it must not “unavoidably” lead to religion either (IX). For all people “it is enough that they do their duty; even if everything were to end with this earthly life and if, in this life, happiness and worthiness should never even coincide” (p. XI f. Note). Already in the *Critique of Practical Reason*, the addition of the “highest good” and the “postulates” <note>In Kantian philosophy, "postulates" are assumptions—like the existence of God or the immortality of the soul—that are necessary to make sense of moral requirements, even if they cannot be proven by pure reason.</note> contained a deviation from the strict standard of pure, self-sufficient **ethics**. This "highest good" emerges even more strongly as the final end in the (1st) Preface to our text. This final end, however, despite all the legalistic phrasing, is no longer a purely moral one, for it is based on a “**natural property**” (XII A.) and a “**need**” of the human being—just as the belief in a future life is based on the “universal moral disposition in human nature” (188)—even though, on the other hand, “**human power**” <note>original: *Menschenvermögen*.</note> is not sufficient to bring it about—

is sufficient (XIII A.). Thus, God appears—in a way that will not satisfy a truly religious person—primarily as the distributor of a happiness that corresponds to one's **worthiness of being happy**.

While our philosopher approaches biblical Christianity by recognizing the **radical evil** in humans—so much so that he repelled our two great classical poets <note>This refers to Johann Wolfgang von Goethe and Friedrich Schiller, who were famously unsettled by Kant's "Radical Evil" theory, as they held more optimistic views of human nature.</note> for this very reason (see below)—he steers back toward the path of the **religious Enlightenment** with his subsequent assumption: that God will regard the sincerity of one's disposition as a supplement to the lack of successful action. Thus, the historical Jesus gains no central religious significance; he remains partly a "symbol" and partly a moral example, a "personified idea of the good principle." The historical perspective recedes entirely; the Bible is, as we have already seen, deliberately interpreted in a moral sense.

If we have emphasized the weaknesses of Kant's writing more than its virtues in the preceding sections, we do not fear being misunderstood. To specifically point out the virtues of a thinker like Kant seems, in truth, hardly necessary. Yet this very work possesses such a treasure of moral majesty, intellectual refinement, and religious broad-mindedness; it casts so many moral, theological, and historical-philosophical problems into a new and bright light. Furthermore, it distinguishes itself from the philosopher's other major works by its popular language, so much so that it not only exerted a powerful effect on his immediate contemporaries but also significantly influenced the theological development and religious-ecclesiastical life of the following decades, and is still valued by the most prominent theologians of the present day.

<header>Introduction.</header>

## IV. Impact of the Work.

### a) Reception Among Contemporaries.

Kant’s writing naturally caused a great stir immediately upon its appearance. As he himself modestly noted on one of his "Loose Leaves"—that is, his personal notepads—it gave "much cause for talk." A second edition was already necessary after just one year. Among the voices of unconditional and conditional supporters, there were, of course, also those of more or less fierce opponents. Let us speak of these first.

### 1. Opponents.

Corresponding to Kant’s middle-ground position (see page XL), opposition came from two sides: the <term>Naturalism (the philosophical view that everything arises from natural properties and causes, and supernatural or spiritual explanations are excluded or discounted)</term> of the Enlightenment on one hand, and the <term>Supranaturalism (the belief in a divine power that operates above or beyond the laws of nature)</term> of <term>Pietism (a movement within Lutheranism that stressed personal piety and the emotional devotion of the individual)</term> and ecclesiastical Orthodoxy on the other.

1) *Enlightenment* and *Humanism* (*Goethe*). The representatives of the "vulgar" <note>In this historical context, "vulgar" refers to the "Popular Enlightenment," a movement that sought to simplify complex philosophy into "common sense" for the masses, often losing intellectual depth in the process.</note> Enlightenment, of whom the well-known Nicolai <note>Friedrich Nicolai (1733–1811) was a famous writer and bookseller in Berlin and a leading figure of the German Enlightenment who often sparred with Kant and the Romantics.</note> is the primary representative, had already had plenty of reason to be angry with the philosopher who initially seemed to be one of their own. His *Critique of Pure Reason* had destroyed their "beautiful proofs" for the existence of God; his *Critique of Practical Reason* had victoriously overcome their ethics of happiness and utility; and his *Critique of Judgment* had put an end to their shallow theories of art. Now they were dissatisfied once more that the critical philosopher had not, like them, cleared away everything in Christianity and the Bible that exceeded the standard of their "common human understanding." Thus, the *New General German Library* <note>original: "Neue Allgemeine Deutsche Bibliothek," a major review journal of the Enlightenment era.</note> wrote in a review of the second edition of *Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason*:

> "It seems then, in Kant’s opinion, that in matters of church faith, everything should remain quite nicely as it was before; the pillars of religious superstition cannot be abolished, but must always be retained as the indispensable foundations of a moral religion." A

<page-num>LII</page-num>

No judgment from a radical-freethinking, naturalistic, or materialistic perspective is known to us.

Through his doctrine of <term>radical evil (Kant’s theory that human nature possesses an inherent tendency to deviate from the moral law)</term>, our philosopher had, incidentally, also spoiled his relationship with the Goethe circle. Goethe, who during those years following his Italian journey had become thoroughly saturated with the beauty-loving, harmonious worldview of Antiquity and professed a "decided paganism,"¹⁾ wrote to Herder from the camp near Mainz on June 7, 1793, that Kant—after using a long human life to cleanse his philosophical mantle of various dirty prejudices—had "wickedly smeared it with the shameful stain of radical evil, so that Christians too might be lured to come and kiss its hem"; he wrote similarly to Jacobi a month later. Schiller also found this same proposition of radical evil "revolting" to his "feelings," but he believed that "nothing can be objected" against Kant's proofs, "as much as one might wish to,"²⁾ and otherwise adopted, as we shall yet see, a completely different general position toward the philosopher he so highly revered.

2) *Pietism and Orthodoxy.* That the philosopher's outreach toward the Church did not go very far—and that he, as Schiller writes in the same letter, had "earned little thanks from the theologians" by abolishing "all inherent authority of ecclesiastical faith"—was demonstrated by the sometimes violent attacks from that side. To be sure, as early as 1788, the Kantian Abicht had published a work bearing the title: *Convincing Proof that Kantian Philosophy is not Detrimental to Orthodoxy, but Rather Useful to it, since Theoretical Reason Explains that it is Able to Say Nothing about the Realm of the Supersensible.* Indeed, there were eccentric minds (such as Schad) who interpreted the bread and wine of the <term>Lord's Supper (the Eucharist or Communion)</term> as <term>phenomena (objects as they appear to our senses, rather than as they are in themselves)</term>, the body—

3) But the representatives of Protestant theology at the universities also felt threatened, in part, in their old, long-established views. F. Ammon**, writes from **Erlangen** on March 8, 1794, it was countered "with great zeal" against **Kant’s** moral interpretation of scripture that "with this kind of <term>exegesis</term> <note>The critical explanation or interpretation of a text, especially of scripture</note>"—which, by the way, was only the "long-ridiculed allegorical [interpretation] of the Church Fathers, especially of **Origen**" <note>original: "Origenis"; an early Christian scholar known for interpreting the Bible symbolically rather than literally</note>—"all dogmatic certainty would be lost . . . and that a new barbarism would be the conclusion of this interpretation." **Ammon**, who spoke up for **Kant’s** principles, was rewarded for his efforts with the accusation of "blind <term>Kantiolatry</term>" <note>original: "Kantiolatrie"; a derogatory term for the idol-like worship of Kant's philosophy</note>.

<page-num>LV</page-num>
<header>Introduction.</header>

The theologians of the older **Tübingen School** <note>A circle of influential Protestant theologians at the University of Tübingen who attempted to reconcile traditional biblical supernaturalism with the new "Critical Philosophy" of Kant</note> expressed their concerns more moderately: for example, **G. Chr. Storr** (1746–1805), whose *Some Theological Annotations, etc.* <note>original: "Annotationes quaedam theologicae etc."</note> (Tübingen 1793, translated into German by **Süßmilch** in 1794) **Kant** mentions with great respect in his second preface (p. XXIV). **Storr** argued that biblical doctrines should only be contested if they violated irreproachable moral principles; otherwise, one should only examine their historical credibility. Even more noteworthy objections were raised by the Tübingen scholar **Joh. Fr. Flatt** (1759–1821), who had already appeared as a critic of **Kant** in several previous writings:¹) He argued that a practical purpose alone was not sufficient to prove the truth of a proposition; that happiness within **Kant**'s concept of the <term>highest good</term> <note>The 'summum bonum,' or the ideal state where moral virtue and happiness are perfectly joined</note> was an inconsistency on the philosopher's part; that the harmony of virtue and happiness was conceivable even without the existence of God, who in **Kant**'s work did not emerge at all as the almighty, omniscient Creator of the world; and that the relationship between freedom (and the moral improvement based upon it) and <term>natural necessity</term> <note>The laws of cause and effect that govern the physical world</note> was not clear in **Kant**'s system, among other points.²)

## 2. Followers.

The number of followers was hardly less significant. To those who had sat at the master’s feet in **Königsberg** and, to use **Jachmann**’s words, "departed as apostles and taught the gospel of the kingdom of reason," the written word now recruited new adherents. "Already," **Ammon** wrote on April 28, 1795 (*Correspondence III, 17 f.*), "your principles, great teacher, are too common among our better theologians for a sudden standstill to be feared; they will flourish as a blessing for humanity and bear fruit for eternity."

1) Naturally, the earliest to express their enthusiasm were those in his inner circle of friends. For instance, **Kiesewetter** wrote on June 15, 1793: “Your writing has delighted me, partly because of the new insights I gained from it, and partly because of the extremely fortunate interpretation of several biblical passages. Correctly understood, it can bring infinite benefit; at the very least, it can put an end to the wretched strife between religious parties and <term>heresy-hunting</term> <note>original: "Ketzermacherei"—the practice of denouncing others as heretics to suppress intellectual dissent</note>.” The young physician **Erhard** from Nuremberg, who also reviewed the book in the *Jena General Literary Gazette* <note>original: "Jenaer Allgemeine Literaturzeitung"</note>, wrote to **Reinhold** on July 4, 1793: “**Kant's** work on religion has completely satisfied me.” And the latter replied on August 12: “**Kant's** *Religion within etc.* <note>Referring to the full title: "Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason"</note> has granted me the indescribable comfort of being able to call myself a Christian out loud and publicly with a clear conscience.” Similarly, **Biester** wrote on July 13: “Such a work is always a great merit and a true blessing for the human race, but especially in these present times.” **Hippel** wrote on December 5: “During my illness, I had *Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason* read aloud to me and wished a thousand times that this book—which here in Danzig goes by the name ‘**Kant's** Religion’—could be read in France right now <note>A reference to the religious and political upheaval following the French Revolution</note>. The immortal name **Immanuel Kant** truly need not hesitate to be placed before this writing, which can and will do a great deal of good.” **Maria von Herbert**, who is well known to those familiar with **Kant’s** correspondence <note>A student and correspondent of Kant known for her philosophical intensity and tragic life</note>, thanks the “highly honored and most dearly beloved man” for his new gift “most warmly in the name of all those who have torn themselves away from those so many-tangled fetters of darkness” (*Correspondence II 466*). **Fichte**, on the other hand, speaks only briefly of the “joy” with which he read **Kant's** new work (*ibid. 435*).

...letters written in *Kant’s* spirit: that theology could only achieve a secure standing through a moral foundation; that <term>moral theology</term> <note>A branch of theology that focuses on ethical behavior and the "moral law" rather than traditional dogma or ritual.</note> is "the only true, pure, and living" theology, and is simultaneously the theology of Jesus and his pupils, and so forth.<sup>1)</sup> In Göttingen, the theologian *Stäudlin* (1761–1826), whom we have already encountered, worked in the same spirit. He "promoted the spirit of <term>Criticism</term> <note>Refers to Kant’s "Critical Philosophy," which examines the limits of human reason.</note> in every direction—systematically, exegetically, in historical monographs, and in various journals" and "made it his particular concern to show how the process of intellectual processing of religious beliefs had to gradually ripen toward the standpoint of moral interpretation" (*Rosenkranz*, in the work cited, p. 325 *f.*). A few years later, *Kant* dedicated his work *The Conflict of the Faculties* <note>original: "Streit der Fakultäten"—a book in which Kant argues that the philosophy faculty should be free to evaluate the teachings of the "higher" faculties of theology, law, and medicine.</note> to him. A great many of the actual *School-Kantians* <note>Those who strictly followed and taught Kant's philosophical system.</note> were also theologians: such as the court chaplain *J. Schulze* in Königsberg; *Rink*, the editor of *Kant’s Pedagogy*, also in Königsberg; *Mellin*, the author of the great dictionary of critical philosophy, in Magdeburg; and *K. Chr. F. Schmid* in Jena (perhaps the same "*Kantian theologian*" who performed the marriage ceremony for the poet *Schiller* on February 22, 1790).

Everywhere, "moral exegesis" began to emerge; people sought to give a moral meaning to all possible—even the most incomprehensible—passages of the Bible, and to give all dogmas a moral turn. Even in theological examinations, the examiners were frequently embarrassed by the overly bold attempts at interpretation made by the candidates. Church history, following *Kant’s* lead, was perceived as a struggle between <term>ritualistic religion</term> <note>original: "gottesdienstlichen"—referring to religion based on worship services, rites, and external ceremonies.</note> and purely moral religion. In the field of ethics, it was claimed that Christian moral commandments were in agreement with the demands of Reason (that is, *Kant’s* practical philosophy), or it was even asserted that the former (with their promises of reward and punishment) were inferior to the latter. Even sermons "according to Kantian principles" were delivered. And it is unlikely...

<page-num>LVIII</page-num>

...who were little moved by the warnings and prohibitions of the royal <term>rescript</term> <note>A formal decree or edict issued by a monarch; in this case, the 1794 decree aimed at curbing the spread of Kantian rationalism in theology.</note> of 1794, which was issued to the theological faculty in Halle specifically to counter these tendencies.

Among the younger philosophers who followed Kant, *Heidenreich* (born 1764) wrote a "Pocketbook for Thinking Divines" in several volumes in Leipzig, as well as letters against atheism. *Niethammer* (born 1766) in Jena wrote *On Religion as Science* (1795), and *Krug* (born 1770, later Kant’s successor in Königsberg) wrote: *Letters on the Perfectibility of Revealed Religion* as "*Prolegomena to any positive doctrine of religion which in the future will be able to follow the secure path of a firmly established science*," Jena and Leipzig 1795. Krug resolved the "conflict of reason with itself and the doctrine of atonement" exactly as Kant did, through the thought: that every person should strive toward the moral ideal and, if he "cannot do everything," he could trust firmly in God's grace.

Indeed, Kant's religious views even penetrated enlightened Catholic circles. We have already heard of *Maternus Reuß* in Würzburg on page XLI, note 1. Professor *Koller* in Heidelberg, a <term>Lazarist</term> <note>A member of the Catholic "Congregation of the Mission," often involved in teaching and missionary work.</note>, introduced his students to Kant's writings and principles and finally put forward the proposition that one cannot prove the existence of God through mere speculative reason. When called to account by his superiors, he explained that this did no harm to religion; rather, religion gained infinitely by it. He appealed to the academies in Mainz and Würzburg, where <term>Criticism</term> <note>The "Critical Philosophy" of Kant.</note> was taught with great acclaim. But it was in vain. He was condemned to recant and to provide a public refutation (!) of his own proposition; when he refused to do so, he was summarily dismissed from his office.

However, more than all the aforementioned scholars—who for the most part have become mere names to us today—most of our readers will be interested in the reception that Kant’s book received from his great...

### b) Kant and Schiller.

*Cf. K. Vorländer, Kant-Schiller-Goethe, Chapter 1, where the individual passages from the letters are also cited.*

Schiller, who by then had already been an ardent <term>Kantian</term> <note>A follower of the philosophy of Immanuel Kant, particularly his ideas on ethics, aesthetics, and reason.</note> for two years, read Kant’s *Religion* <note>Referring to Kant's 1793 work, *Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason*.</note> while it was being printed in Jena, as we saw above (p. XXXIV f.). As he wrote to his friend Gottfried Körner on February 28, 1793, he felt "enthralled" by the first half he had read so far and could "hardly wait for the remaining sheets." He described the content as the "most ingenious <term>Exegesis</term> <note>The critical interpretation or explanation of a text, especially a religious one.</note> of the Christian concept of religion based on philosophical grounds." Regarding Kant’s tendency and method, he then judged: "Kant, as you have already been able to notice in him several times, is very fond of giving scriptural passages a philosophical meaning. It is, as one soon sees, not so much a matter for him of supporting the authority of Scripture thereby, but rather of linking the results of philosophical thinking to the <term>children's reason</term> <note>Schiller uses this term to describe the simple, undeveloped reasoning capacity of the general public, suggesting Kant is trying to make complex ideas accessible to those who still rely on traditional religious imagery.</note> and, as it were, popularizing them. He seems to me to be guided by a principle in this that you love very much, namely this: not to throw away what already exists as long as some reality is still to be expected from it, but rather to ennoble it. I respect this principle very much, and you will see that Kant does it honor." To be sure, he harbors strong doubts whether the philosopher "has done well to support the Christian religion through philosophical reasons. All that can be expected from the known nature of the defenders of religion is that they will accept the support but throw away the philosophical reasons, and thus Kant has done nothing more than patch the crumbling building of stupidity." There follow the thoughts we have already reproduced on page LII, and finally the closing passage: (He) "also gives it very clearly to be understood that the <term>ecclesiastical faith</term> <note>Original: "Kirchenglaube." This refers to religious faith based on historical tradition, dogma, and church authority, which Kant contrasted with "rational faith" based on morality.</note>

is merely of subjective validity and it would be better if it could be dispensed with. But, because he is convinced that it is not dispensable, nor will it be so anytime soon, he makes it a duty of conscience to respect it. The <term>Logos</term> <note>From the Greek for "word" or "reason"; in this context, the divine reason or the person of Christ as a philosophical concept.</note>, redemption (as a philosophical myth), the conception of heaven and hell, the Kingdom of God, and all these conceptions are explained most successfully." — Not as extensively, but in a similar spirit, he wrote on March 20 to Fischenich, after he had in the meantime read the entire work: The content of the "new and extremely important writing by Kant" was "nothing less than a deduction of the necessity of a <term>positive religion</term> <note>A religion based on specific historical revelations and established institutions rather than universal reason alone.</note> and a church from philosophical grounds, and a—admittedly more Platonic than <term>exegetical</term> <note>Based on the critical interpretation of religious texts.</note>—explanation of Christianity . . . ### Thalia <note>The title of the literary journal edited by Friedrich Schiller where his essay "On Grace and Dignity" was first published in 1793.</note>

The question is whether grace <note>original: *Anmuth*</note> must precede dignity <note>original: *Würde*</note> or the latter before the former (as logically prior <note>original: *ratione prius*</note>), for they cannot be fused into one in the concept of duty if they are heterogeneous <note>Meaning they are composed of different, perhaps incompatible, elements—in this case, reason versus sensory feeling.</note>. Respect for the law in a being that is fallible—that is, tempted to transgress it—is fear of transgression (fear of God) but at the same time free submission under the command; yet simultaneously free submission under a law that the subject’s reason prescribes to itself. Submission proves respect; the freedom of that submission—the greater it is, the more grace is present. Both together constitute dignity (just self-esteem <note>original Latin: *iustum sui aestemium*</note>). Not a saint or a beast, but in humility in comparison with the law. On the grace of legislation. Duty contains no grace in its representation, nor does it allow grace to be added to it to determine action, for that is a flattery of the legislator and contrary to his authority. — The belt of Venus Dione <note>In mythology, Dione was sometimes identified as the mother of Venus; the "belt" or *cestus* conferred the power of grace and attraction. Human actions are divided into business (which stands under the law of duty) and play. It would be a misfortune if the latter were forbidden to him; he would not become happy in life. But these must still be restricted to the condition of the former. The Graces belong to play insofar as they can provide good cheer and strength to promote the former.

People who are most in agreement with one another in spirit often fall into conflict because they are not understandable to each other in words. — To make the concept of duty, separated from all grace that may accompany its fulfillment, the primary ground of morality <note>original: *Moralität*</note> should not mean the same as tearing it away from all accompanying grace.

> I have always insisted on cultivating and maintaining virtue and even religion in a cheerful state of mind.
