Sensory nature must not be considered a collaborator; instead, under the despotism of the categorical imperative <note>Kant’s core moral rule: one should act only according to principles that could be made into universal laws for everyone.</note>, it must be reined in to resist the anarchy of natural inclinations, the abolition of which alone promotes their thorough harmony with one another.

If all people were to follow the moral law gladly and willingly, just as reason contains it as the rule, there would be no duty at all—just as one cannot think of this law, which determines the Divine Will, as obligating Him. Thus, if there are duties, if the moral principle in us is a command for us (the categorical imperative), then we must be seen as being compelled to it even without pleasure and against our inclination. To do something out of duty gladly and out of inclination is a contradiction.

### c) Further After-effects.

### 1. Theological Rationalism in the first half of the 19th century.

From the spread of Kant’s philosophy of religion, the primary document of which—though not the only one—was indeed *Religion within etc.* <note>Referring to Kant’s 1793 work, *Religion within the Bounds of Bare Reason*.</note>, a specific theological-religious movement gradually emerged: <term>Rationalism</term> <note>A theological movement that argues religious beliefs should be consistent with human reason rather than based solely on tradition or divine revelation.</note>, which remained the dominant tendency in theological science as well as in the religious and church life of the Protestant congregations for nearly half a century. Entirely in the spirit of Kant, who had after all confessed himself to be a “pure rationalist” (cf. our index), this movement also elevated reason to the highest principle of knowledge in religious matters. It turned away from dogma and speculation toward morality; while it did not reject the Bible and revelation...

<summary>This page describes Friedrich Schiller's transition from philosophy back to poetry, influenced by Kantian themes, and introduces the rise of Theological Rationalism as a major historical consequence of Kant's religious writings.</summary>
<keywords>Friedrich Schiller, Immanuel Kant, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Hercules Musagetes, Ideal and Life, radical evil, Theological Rationalism, 19th-century theology</keywords>

--- Page 73 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of how Kantian philosophy transitioned into the field of theology, specifically looking at the rise of "Theological Rationalism" and the thinkers who attempted to reconcile Christian doctrine with human reason.</meta>

<page-num>LXIX</page-num>
<header>Introduction.</header>

...absolutely, but removed everything from it that went beyond pure <term>rational faith</term> <note>Vernunftglauben: a belief system based solely on what can be proven or supported by human reason, rather than divine revelation.</note>, explained miracles in a natural way, etc., whereby the critical standpoint admittedly often flattened out into the old dogmatic one of the <term>Enlightenment</term> <note>Aufklärung: the intellectual movement of the 17th and 18th centuries that emphasized reason and individualism over tradition.</note>.

The actual transition from philosophy to theology was made by Tieftrunk in Halle (1759 to 1837), who declared the consciousness of our absolute freedom and autonomy to be the foundation of all religion, and the <term>categorical imperative</term> <note>Kant’s fundamental moral law: "Act only according to that maxim whereby you can, at the same time, will that it should become a universal law."</note> to be the fundamental law of Christianity. Our personal value lies within our own power; happiness, on the other hand, must be bestowed by God. The core of even "revealed" religion is natural religion; revelation accompanied by miracles was necessary only because of the moral low point of the era in which it occurred.

A closer connection with historical theology was sought and gained by the Rationalists Ammon, Bretschneider, Wegscheider, Röhr, and Paulus, who thereby exerted a stronger influence on its development. — Ammon (1766–1850), whom we have already encountered above, pointed out how natural religion experiences confirmation and enrichment through divine revelation as proclaimed in specific persons and facts. He sought to further develop Christianity into a “world religion” by purifying it of the dross of its time of origin. — More radical than Bretschneider—who believed it necessary to assume a "special" revelation suited to our need for education alongside the general revelation of God in nature and the world—Wegscheider (1771–1849) and Röhr (1777–1848) completely denied supernatural revelation. In lively polemic with Schleiermacher, Marheineke, Hase, and others, they declared human reason to be the sole sufficient source of knowledge, and viewed the theories of atonement and redemption as mere symbols. Similar to the Enlightenment thinkers of the 18th century (whom many of these “Rationalists” resemble to the point of being indistinguishable), and in contrast to Kant, they consider human nature to be essentially good. They therefore do not demand a complete “rebirth,” but rather a gradual improvement...

Wegscheider, a professor in Halle for decades, exerted his influence primarily through his textbook, *Instructions in Christian Dogmatic Theology* <note>original: *Institutiones theologiae christianae dogmaticae*</note> (1st ed. 1815, 8th ed. 1844); though the work was lacking in original thoughts, it was widely distributed. Röhr, the General Superintendent in Weimar, was influential as a pulpit orator and writer (*Letters on Rationalism* <note>original: *Briefe über den Rationalismus*</note>, 1813); he had the courage, in his *Fundamental Principles and Articles of Faith of the Evangelical-Protestant Church*, to demand the establishment of new <term>creeds</term> <note>Glaubenssymbole: formal statements of religious belief. Röhr argued that the traditional 16th-century confessions no longer reflected modern reason.</note> for his church.

Paulus (1761—1851, first in Jena, then in Heidelberg) earned a reputation above all in the field of <term>exegesis</term> <note>The critical explanation or interpretation of religious texts.</note> through his "natural" explanations of biblical miracles. <note>Paulus was famous for suggesting that miracles were actually natural events misinterpreted by observers—for example, suggesting Jesus was walking on the shore rather than on top of the water.</note> — Similar views were held by the church historian H. Henke (1752 to 1809), the Old Testament scholar Gesenius (1785—1842), and many others. Meanwhile, De Wette (1780—1849) occupied a middle ground between <term>Kantian Rationalism</term> and Jacobi’s <term>philosophy of feeling</term>, leaning primarily on the philosopher Fries. — Finally, the Catholic theology professor Hermes (1775—1831, in Bonn) was also influenced to a certain degree by Kantianism. He sought to bring Catholic <term>dogmatics</term> into agreement with reason without directly attacking any of its tenets, thus representing a kind of "rational <term>supranaturalism</term>" <note>A viewpoint attempting to harmonize the belief in supernatural revelation with the requirements of human reason.</note>; this, however, went too far for his Church and was subsequently expressly condemned.

We conclude with the judgment of Eduard Zeller:

But despite these deficiencies, they have earned the greatest merit regarding theological science, the moral education, and the religious enlightenment of our people; and the Kantian philosophy

## 2. Judgments of Modern Theologians on Kant’s Philosophy of Religion.

Around the end of the 1830s, <term>Rationalism</term> <note>A theological movement that held that religious beliefs should be based on reason rather than revelation.</note> within Protestant theology receded more and more behind other schools of thought. On one hand, <term>Orthodoxy</term> <note>Conservative adherence to traditional church creeds and doctrines.</note> began to raise its head again, with which the regressive tendencies of the <term>Old Hegelians</term> <note>Followers of G.W.F. Hegel who interpreted his philosophy in a way that supported traditional religious and political structures.</note> and the school of Schelling were generally allied. On the other hand, we see the most diverse viewpoints represented, from the radicalism of the <term>Young Hegelians</term> <note>The "Left Hegelians" who used Hegel’s ideas to critique religion and the state, including figures like David Strauss and Ludwig Feuerbach.</note> to the historical gospel criticism of the <term>Tübingen School</term> <note>A group of scholars at the University of Tübingen famous for applying rigorous historical-critical methods to the New Testament.</note>, through to the <term>mediating theology</term> <note>Vermittelnde Theologie: A school of thought that sought to bridge the gap between traditional faith and modern scientific/philosophical inquiry.</note> of Schleiermacher’s followers. The influence of <term>Criticism</term> <note>Kritizismus: The philosophical system of Immanuel Kant, based on the "critique" of the faculties of reason.</note> was hardly felt in theology (as in philosophy) during the two decades from 1840 to 1860. 

In contrast, shortly after the revival of Criticism in philosophy at the beginning of the 1860s (<term>Neo-Kantianism</term>), a lively impact on theology can also be observed, particularly on A. Ritschl and R. A. Lipsius along with their followers. However, this Neo-Kantian movement within theology—notably in the Ritschlian school—linked less to Kant’s specific philosophy of religion than to his general critical-epistemological foundation, by demanding a clean separation between science and faith, ethics and religion, the knowledge of nature and value judgments. Thus, one can hardly speak of an influence of *Religion within the Bounds of Bare Reason* <note>original: *Religion innerhalb der Grenzen der bloßen Vernunft*</note> appearing directly upon the theology of the present day. On the other hand, not only the historical achievement but also the objective significance of Kantian philosophy of religion even for...

He only appears at first glance to be a rationalist <term>Enlightener</term> <note>A follower of the Aufklärung (Enlightenment), emphasizing human reason over divine revelation.</note> (408). In truth, he represents the "practical restoration of Protestantism" (410); for he has "established its prerequisites—the concepts of moral freedom and moral guilt—in a critical, i.e., scientifically necessary manner" (408) and "through his concept of the absolute binding nature of the <term>moral law</term> <note>Sittengesetz: The inner ethical imperative that Kant believed was universal to all rational beings.</note>, he has more securely grounded the corresponding subjective consciousness of possible guilt against the law than was done by the old Protestant doctrine of original sin" (409). He has thus become the "renovator of the moral worldview of the Reformation" (411), which "ethically asserts the absoluteness of the public law" and "religiously founds itself upon the absoluteness of God’s grace" (410). Admittedly, Kant’s connection of the doctrine of the <term>highest good</term> <note>Summum Bonum: The supreme end of human existence, combining perfect virtue and perfect happiness.</note> with the "critical principles of morality" is an "incongruity" (420; this is also our opinion, see above), and thus for him, religion becomes a "kind of appendage" (422 f.) and indeed an "accidental" (425) appendage to religion.

Similarly to Ritschl, **J. "Kant has restored the practical faith of Christianity to itself, after it had lost its unique character through and within theology from the 2nd century onwards;" he broke the rule of the "school dogmatists" <note>Schuldogmatiker: Scholastic theologians who used formal, rigid systems of logic to define church doctrine.</note> (Thomas Aquinas), according to whom man "must seek his highest good on the path of cognition and knowledge" (212). Even more strongly than his teacher Ritschl, **W. Herrmann** <note>Wilhelm Herrmann (1846–1922), a leading Ritschlian theologian who emphasized the importance of the individual's inner experience of Jesus's moral character.</note> (*Religion in Relation to World-Cognition and Morality*, 1879) aligns himself with Kant in the <term>epistemological</term> <note>Epistemology: The branch of philosophy concerned with the nature and limits of human knowledge.</note> foundation of religion. In Kant’s "separation of theoretical knowledge from conviction conditioned by morality," he sees nothing less than a "charter of freedom for theology, liberated from the shackles of philosophical worldviews" (pp. II, IX); only Kant had "released theology into the freedom toward which it had looked out during the Reformation era" (17). Nevertheless, he harbors significant reservations regarding the specific Kantian philosophy of religion as it appears in *Religion within* <note>Referring to Kant’s 1793 work, *Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason*.</note>. To be sure, he acknowledges along with the critical philosopher that "the autonomy of the moral will is at home in Christianity" (282), and praises him for having "demonstrated the true universal validity of religion in the practice of Christian life" (296) and for correctly recognizing the "specific advantage of Christian self-judgment over the Stoic one" (283); however, he argues that Kant did not manage to "understand the essence and value of historical, positive religion" (ibid.), because he committed the "error" of "substituting the moral ideal for the religious worldview" (288). ...to mutilate personality," to establish a "thoroughly Catholic" concept of grace <note>In this context, the author likely means a "legalistic" or merit-based view of grace, which Protestant theologians often contrasted with their own view of grace as a free gift.</note>, and more (287). Kant is seen as a rationalist in that he takes the measure of religion not from religion itself, but from the outside (288 f.), viewing religious faith as a "natural function" of reason (293). **O. This principle, he argues, prevents Kant from doing justice to feeling and imagination—the "birthplace and permanent domain of religious life." Meanwhile, Pfleiderer claims that Kant, "the theoretical skeptic and moral rigorist," has on the other hand "reached out for peace with popular thinking" through his "utilitarian-based theological <term>postulates</term> <note>Postulates: In Kant's system, these are beliefs (like the existence of God) that we cannot prove through logic but must assume to be true to make sense of our moral duties.</note>" and has "offered a welcome point of connection for both the old-believing <term>supranaturalists</term> <note>Supranaturalism: The belief that religious truths are revealed by God and exist above or beyond human reason.</note> and the <term>neologians</term> <note>Neology: An 18th-century movement that tried to explain Christian doctrines using Enlightenment reason, often discarding traditional miracles.</note> of the Wolffian Enlightenment" (*Development etc. p. 85*).²)

# V. Textual Philology. <note>The study of the history, physical transmission, and variations of a text.</note>

## A) The Previous Editions.

1. *Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason. Presented by Immanuel Kant. Königsberg, published by Friedrich Nicolovius. 1793. XX and 296 pages.*

2. *The same. Second expanded edition. 1794. XXVI and 314 pages. Added to the second edition is a larger number of notes, some of which are significant in content, or additions to existing notes; these are designated as such in our edition. Other textual changes concern only the style and are almost all of an insignificant nature.*

3. *Reprints of the first edition appeared as early as 1793 in Frankfurt/Leipzig and in Neuwied; a reprint of the second edition appeared in 1794 in Frankfurt/Leipzig. An excerpt under the title "Kant’s Theory of Purely Moral Religion with Regard to Pure Christianity. Briefly Presented." Riga, Hartknoch 1796. 190 pages. (The author is said to have been a certain G. L. Remer.)*¹)

5. *In the 6th volume of the complete edition by G. Hartenstein, Leipzig 1839 as No. V, XVI pages and pages 159 to 389.*

6. *In the 6th volume of G. Hartenstein’s complete edition in chronological order, Leipzig 1867, as No. IV, XII pages and 195—301.*

## VI. Appendices.

**1. Draft of a letter from Kant to a theological faculty—**
**likely that of Königsberg—concerning the freedom to**
**publish his work: Religion within the Boundaries of**
**Mere Reason.¹)**

I have the honor of presenting to Your Reverences <note>original: "Ew: Hochehrwürden"; a formal honorific for members of a university faculty or clergy.</note> three philosophical essays which, together with the one already in the *Berlin Monthly Journal*, <note>The *Berlinische Monatsschrift* was the premier journal of the German Enlightenment.</note> are intended to form a whole. I submit them not so much for censorship as for an assessment of whether the theological faculty should even claim the right to censor them. My aim is that the philosophical faculty may exercise its own jurisdiction over this work without hesitation, in accordance with the title it bears. — For since pure philosophical theology is presented here also in relation to biblical theology—specifically, how far the former might dare to approach the latter through its own attempts at scriptural interpretation, and where, conversely, reason does not suffice or cannot follow the accepted interpretation of the Church—this is an indisputable right of the philosophical faculty. In doing so, philosophy remains within its own boundaries and does not interfere with biblical theology, no more than the latter is accused of interfering in the rights of another science when it utilizes as many philosophical ideas as it deems fit for its own purposes of confirmation or illustration. — Even in those instances where philosophical theology seems to adopt principles opposite to those of biblical theology—for example, regarding the doctrine of miracles—it admits and proves that these principles must be understood not as objective truths, but only as subjective ones; that is, as **maxims** <term>maxims: subjective rules of conduct or interpretation that guide how an individual uses their reason.</term> to be followed if we wish to consult merely our own (human) reason in theological judgments. By this means, the miracles themselves are not denied, but are left unhindered to the biblical theologian, provided he wishes to judge solely as a theologian and scorns any union with philosophy.

<header>Introduction.</header>

Since the interests of biblical theologians, in their capacity as such, have for some time now become a matter of state concern—and since the advancement of the sciences is likewise a matter of state concern, which these same theologians are bound and entitled to uphold as university scholars (not merely as clergymen), and not to restrict one faculty, such as the philosophical, for the supposed benefit of another, but rather to expand each—it is therefore evident that if it is established that a writing belongs to biblical theology, the commission authorized for its censorship should have jurisdiction over it. However, if this is not yet established but remains subject to doubt, only that university faculty responsible for the biblical field <note>The theological faculty.</note> has the right to judge whether a writing encroaches upon its entrusted business or not. (A university bears its name precisely because it must ensure that one science does not expand its territory to the detriment of another). If that faculty finds no grounds to claim the work, the censorship of it must then fall to the faculty under which the work has announced itself <note>In this case, the philosophical faculty.</note>.

However, the question then arises (and is resolved in the final preface) as to which court should decide if a writing interferes with statutory church faith, and what criteria that court should use. From this, the right of a religious work to employ a moral interpretation of the Bible is derived. The energy of this second draft is softened in the printed preface, and the ambitious plan for a scientific magistracy, which it contained, is no longer mentioned. Following a majestic opening that rightly begins with the most general and profound reflections, the printed preface proceeds to treat the question of the right of interpretation in a simpler, yet also more reserved, manner.

We now present the two drafts in their original spelling. A few clerical errors have been corrected according to Dilthey <note>Wilhelm Dilthey (1833–1911), a renowned German philosopher and historian of ideas who edited these volumes of Kant's work.</note>.

But how can one recognize with certainty whether a piece of writing or a public religious lecture encroaches upon biblical theology or stays within the bounds of mere philosophy? — However much the philosopher may refrain from dealing with the specific tenets of <term>revealed faith</term> <note>Belief based on divine communication or sacred scripture rather than logic alone.</note> and limit himself solely to the principles of pure reason, he must still consider the possibility of carrying out his ideas in experience. Such a method could never provide a valid example for explaining how a revealed faith might actually function among human beings. Therefore, some existing history of faith—whether contained in the <term>Zend-Avesta</term> <note>The sacred texts of Zoroastrianism.</note>, the <term>Vedas</term> <note>The oldest scriptures of Hinduism.</note>, the <term>Quran</term>, or the book preeminently called the **Bible**—must provide him with the only suitable material for this purpose.

It must therefore ensure that no faculty takes for itself exclusive rights to the detriment of others. ...as a scholar who measures himself against the philosopher, [the theologian] stands under the judgment of the faculty to which his science belongs—namely, the biblical-theological faculty. This faculty, as a department of the university, must care not only for the "salvation of souls" (by training students for the ministry) but also for the "salvation of the sciences." It often finds it necessary to utilize the research into reason, language, and history conducted by the philosophical faculty. Consequently, the theological faculty can impose absolutely no restrictions on how far philosophy may spread its influence, because the very nature of philosophy is to extend its inquiry over everything.

— Should the latter, in its philosophical capacity, presume to establish congregations through its own interpretations of reason and scripture, or to train clergy to be public teachers of the church, this could be called an infringement upon biblical theology (and the rights of the faculty designated for it), as that faculty alone is <term>privileged</term> <note>Granted a specific legal monopoly or right by the state to perform a public function.</note> to do so. However, if the philosophical faculty merely offers for consideration what reason and historical science have to say for or against the interpretations of scripture currently in vogue, it does so according to the right held by all sciences. For a biblical theologian to refuse to acknowledge this right, and to instead appeal to a legal privilege, would be to descend from the rank of a scholar to that of a <term>shopkeeper</term> <note>Original: "Krämer." A derogatory comparison suggesting the theologian is more interested in protecting a commercial monopoly than seeking truth.</note>.

If we depart from this principle—and if we grant the clerical community the right to judge for itself whether a matter falls under its jurisdiction, thereby allowing them to judge their own competence—then everything is lost for the sciences. We would soon reach a point where, as in the time of the <term>Scholastics</term> <note>Medieval academics who attempted to reconcile Christian dogma with philosophy, often subordinating logic to church doctrine.</note>, we would have no philosophy except that which has been modeled after the accepted dogmas of the church; or, as in the time of <term>Galileo</term>, no astronomy except that which the biblical theologian, who understands nothing of it, has permitted. ### Second Draft.

Although the only true religion—because it binds everyone—must also be allowed to be publicly examined by everyone in every conceivable way (so as to use the judgments of others as a touchstone for one's own), especially since no one but I myself shall answer for my wandering from it: yet it can well happen that in a state, perhaps because it is believed that the state must also care for the **salvation** <note>Refers to the eternal well-being of the soul, as opposed to worldly comfort.</note> (not merely the **earthly happiness**) of the subjects, or perhaps to support itself by means of the church, regulations are made which place the once-accepted public religious faith under a sort of **interdict** <note>original: "Interdict." A legal or ecclesiastical prohibition; here, a ban on any changes to established doctrine.</note> against all innovations and changes (which could stir up suspicion of its uncertainty) and <term>privilege</term> <note>Grant exclusive legal rights or a monopoly.</note> certain persons as keepers, guardians, and sole interpreters of its documents. — In this case, for the faithful and quiet **subject** (who, under these circumstances, is certainly not considered an active, voting **citizen**), there is nothing to do but obey. 

Only one thing still causes **concern**: namely, since in every revelation-based faith founded on **facts** <note>original: "Facta." Historical events or miracles that serve as the basis for a specific religion, such as the life of Jesus or the giving of the Torah.</note> there must always be contained universal religious concepts and principles—and therefore that which relates to a **pure rational faith**—it depends, in the **concurrence** of the latter (which must never be forbidden) with the former, on who has the authority to decide on the **forum** <note>original: "Forum." A court or tribunal with the jurisdiction to hear a specific type of case.</note> before which an opinion or a writing must be brought, if it seems to have infringed upon the legally protected revelation-based faith through merely philosophical assertions, or conversely, if the revelation-based faith seems to have done damage to the pure rational faith. This question, which actually concerns only the **competence of the tribunal**, thus asks to know who [should judge] when a writing is accused of, for example, interfering in biblical theology with merely philosophical assertions, or conversely, that the latter [theology] [forces] its doctrines of revelation upon the philosophical...

...theology, who, I say, is entitled to speak about this alone, without yet looking at whether this interference of one into the other is advantageous or disadvantageous.

Before we answer the question of who has the authority to speak on this, we first wish to examine how that person (whoever they may be) can recognize that such an interference—such an encroachment into foreign affairs—has actually occurred.

When the philosopher cites biblical verses to prove the truth of his supposedly <term>pure rational theology</term> <note>original: "reinen Vernunfttheologie." A religious system based entirely on human reason rather than divine revelation.</note>, and thereby brings the <note>original: "Offenbarungsbuch," or book of revelation (the Bible).</note> under suspicion of having intended to present nothing but rational doctrine, his interpretation of the scriptural passages was an encroachment on the rights of the biblical theologian. It is the theologian's proper business to determine the meaning of these passages as a revelation, which may perhaps contain something that no philosophy can ever perceive—a type of teaching toward which the theologian has mainly directed his primary duties. The philosopher thus interferes here if he conducts himself as a definitive <note>original: "bestimmender," meaning one who has the final say in the legal or dogmatic sense.</note> interpreter of scripture, which is not his business at all; for that requires <term>scriptural scholarship</term> <note>original: "Schriftgelehrsamkeit." The technical, linguistic, and historical expertise required to interpret holy texts.</note> or, as some prefer, even "inner enlightenment," the possession of which he, as a pure researcher of reason, must renounce.

However, it cannot be counted against the philosopher as an interference in this theology if he draws upon passages from the doctrine of revelation merely for illustration, or perhaps even for the confirmation of his own propositions (according to his own way of understanding and interpreting them). This is no more an encroachment than it is for a teacher of <term>natural law</term> <note>Legal principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason, independent of specific state laws.</note> to use expressions and formulas from the Roman code of laws (even if he draws entirely different conclusions from them than the legal scholars of the latter). As long as he does not intend to diminish their authority as <term>state laws</term> <note>original: "Landesgesetze."</note> through his use of them, he remains within his rights. In such a case, philosophical theology seeks only to clarify its own concepts and give them a certain life and an <term>unction</term> <note>original: "Salbung." In this context, it refers to a quality of religious earnestness or spiritual "flavor" that makes a rational argument more persuasive or moving.</note>, but by no means—

...sees the preservation of its organization, which sets boundaries for each individual <note>Referring to the branches of science or academic disciplines.</note> insofar as it might take away the space for another’s expansion. That is to say, it must judge whether a writing encroaches upon **biblical theology**—according to the principles publicly granted to it by the state with exclusive freedom—in order to put **principles of reason** <note>original: "Vernunftprincipien." Concepts derived from human logic and ethics rather than divine revelation.</note> in their place, or whether it merely treats theology as one of the various sciences of reason (which do not take historical facts as their basis) in order to present its contents as a system. In the latter case, the work remains within its own boundaries—specifically, those of **mere philosophy**—and leaves it to biblical theology to bring the two into harmony, unless theology considers it beneath its dignity and holiness to bother with the matter and allows the philosophers to <term>rationalize</term> <note>original: "vernünfteln." To engage in philosophical speculation; often used in this period to describe human reasoning on matters of faith.</note> as much as they wish, while it calmly follows its own path, unconcerned.

For since the progress of **culture** <note>original: "Cultur." The historical development of human civilization and rational capacity.</note> has brought humanity to the point where even **wisdom** cannot properly spread its influence, let alone secure it, except by means of a science: it follows that even when we speak of the "salvation of souls," we are simultaneously concerned with the "salvation of science" itself. This science contains its teachings in a complete, convincing, and purified presentation; and such a science, in turn, is concerned that it can coexist with others and their growth, and

<summary>Kant explains that the theological faculty must oversee the boundary between state-sanctioned biblical doctrine and philosophical inquiry. He argues that in a modern, cultured society, even spiritual wisdom requires the structure of a "science" to be influential and secure.</summary>

<page-num>XC</page-num>
<header>Introduction.</header>

...does not, as it were, claim a monopoly to the detriment of the others; for such a monopoly, because of the connection that all sciences have with one another, must ultimately fall back upon it as a disadvantage. — Thus, if the claims of **biblical theology** were unconditionally granted (without regard for other sciences and their legal rights), there would soon be no **natural ethics** <note>Also known as "moral philosophy," this refers to ethics derived from human reason rather than divine revelation.</note>, much less a **natural religion**; indeed, there would not even be a **rational astronomy** anymore, as the fate of **Galileo** proves. <note>Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) was famously condemned by the Church for supporting the Copernican view that the Earth revolves around the sun, which was seen as contradicting certain biblical passages.</note> — Even a privileged person in civil affairs does not have the authority to seize the property of others, which he might consider contrary to his monopoly, at his own discretion. Instead, it still depends on the claim of those whose duty it is to look after the rights of the citizens as a whole, to determine whether what he presumes to claim is truly a "seized good" subject to compulsion or a "free good."

It would therefore certainly be better if **biblical theology** allowed itself to be placed in the same line as other sciences and contented itself with the influence it can obtain through its own dignity. This is especially true since **philosophy**, which as an opponent is the most dangerous of all to it, offers itself as a companion and friend. (For it is no longer to be thought of that philosophy should serve as a <term>handmaid</term> <note>original: "Nachtreterin." This refers to the medieval scholastic concept of *ancilla theologiae*, the idea that philosophy must be subordinate to theology.</note> to theology, as was previously said.) If, however, a <term>curb</term> <note>original: "Kapzaum." A bridle or restraint used for horses.</note> must absolutely be placed upon humans because of their "hardness of heart" <note>A biblical idiom (Matthew 19:8) referring to human stubbornness or moral frailty.</note>, this must at least not be done by those who are extraordinarily favored by a monopoly. For them, the convenience that arises from the fact that they need not bother themselves with other sciences might be a strong temptation to suppress them all.

So much for the **governance** <note>original: "Policey." In the 18th century, this term referred broadly to the administration and regulation of a community to maintain order and public welfare.</note> regarding public **religious doctrines** and the limits within which it must be held—as an arrangement belonging to the learned commonwealth—in order not to eradicate general **civil liberty** for the sake of an imagined security.

<page-num>XCI</page-num>
<header>Introduction.</header>

In the present work, the whole of a religion in general, insofar as it can be developed solely from reason guided by moral ideas, is presented. I cannot deny that in this treatment, the Christian **doctrine of faith** <term>Glaubenslehre</term> <note>This refers to the formal system of teachings or dogmas within a specific religion, in this case, Christianity.</note> has been constantly kept in view. This was done not to explain it according to the sense of its Scripture (other than merely conjecturally), nor to limit its inner content to the sum of those rational doctrines. Rather, it was done because philosophy would hardly succeed in assuring itself that it had not only encompassed a whole of religion in general but also executed it in its particular determinations (in detail), if there were not already a work aiming at religion, worked upon through many centuries, sometimes perhaps provided with useless additions, yet referring to all conceivable determinations of the same (a holy scripture with its interpretations), which can lead reason to investigations that it would not have hit upon by itself.

Just as little can I conceal that—given that so many of its doctrines evidently agree with reason to such an extent as if they had been dictated by reason itself—a certain inclination has played a part in this treatise to derive the remaining doctrines from the same source. Thus, I treat that which may perhaps for a large part be **revealed theology** <note>Theology based on divine revelation, such as the Bible, rather than human logic alone.</note> as **pure rational theology** here. This is not done with the speculative intent of expanding the latter toward the knowledge of the unsearchable (for the rote repetition of words not understood is no knowledge), but rather, insofar as its ideas are practical, to use them for religion as a **moral disposition** <term>moralische Gesinnung</term> <note>In Kantian ethics, this refers to the internal "spirit" or intention behind an action, which determines its moral worth.</note>.

Although through this preference the sense of many cited scriptural passages may in itself be missed, the mere possibility that they can admit such a sense is very advantageous for the expansion and confirmation of this doctrine; for it allows the rationalizing part of humanity (which, however, with increasing culture,

<summary>Kant explains that while his work seeks to establish a religion based purely on reason, he uses Christian scripture as a historical guide to help structure his investigations. no matter how much one might suppress it, [reason] gradually makes [one] very much inclined toward accepting it

Philosophy, in the progress of the moral work belonging to its pure **business of reason** <term>Vernunftgeschäft</term>, inevitably encounters ideas of a religion in general and cannot avoid them; it can, however, bypass the specific arrangements that humans might make to establish a religious state among themselves. In this respect, the present treatises might seem not to contain pure philosophy (unmixed with empirical experience) and to exceed their **boundaries** <term>Gräntze</term>. Yet, the transition from the realm of pure practical ideas to the ground upon which they are to be put into practice—where philosophy must still necessarily stand with one foot on the former—nevertheless still belongs to the field of pure philosophy. One cannot say, therefore, that philosophy has overstepped its limits when it incorporates the consideration and judgment of a **positive religion** <term>positive Religion</term> <note>A "positive" religion is one based on historical facts, specific laws, and institutional authority, as opposed to a "natural" religion based solely on reason.</note> into its business, especially since it believes it can best demonstrate the conditions under which alone the idea of a religion can be realized. Therefore, the present treatises can absolutely be judged as nothing other than reflections belonging solely to philosophy.

# Preface to the First Edition.

<margin>X</margin> ...that which is the final end (of the creation of the world) is that which can and should simultaneously be the final end of man.

---

<margin>XI</margin> When morality recognizes in the holiness of its law an object of the greatest respect, it presents, at the level of religion, the highest cause that carries out those laws as an object of **adoration** <term>Anbetung</term> <note>Kant distinguishes between "respect" for the law and "adoration" for the Lawgiver (God).</note>.

<margin>XI XII</margin> The resolution of this problem, as far as I believe I can see into it, I can only indicate here without carrying it out in detail.
    A "purpose" is always the object of an inclination—that is, an immediate desire to possess a thing by means of one’s <sup>a</sup>) action; just as the **law** (which commands practically) is an object of **respect**. An objective purpose (i.e., the one we *ought* to have) is that which is assigned to us by mere reason as such. The purpose which contains the unavoidable and, at the same time, sufficient condition of all others is the **final end** <term>Endzweck</term>. One’s own **happiness** <term>Glückseligkeit</term> <note>This refers to the state of a rational being in the world for whom everything goes according to their wish and will throughout their life.</note> is the subjective final end of rational worldly beings (which each has by virtue of its nature, which is dependent on objects of the senses, and about which it would be absurd to say that one *ought* to have it), and all practical propositions that have this final end as their basis are synthetic, yet also empirical. But that everyone should make the highest possible good in the world their final end is a synthetic practical proposition *a priori* <note>original: "a priori"; this describes knowledge or principles that come from pure reason rather than from sensory experience.</note>, and indeed an objectively practical one, assigned by pure reason. This is because it is a proposition that goes beyond the concept of duties in the world and adds a consequence (an effect) that is not contained in moral laws and thus cannot be developed analytically <note>An "analytical" development would mean the idea was already hidden inside the definition of duty. Kant argues the "final end" is a new, additional idea.</note> from them. For these laws command absolutely, regardless of what the outcome may be; indeed, they even compel us to abstract from the outcome entirely when it comes to a specific action. In doing so, they make duty the object of the greatest respect, without presenting or assigning us a purpose (or final end) that would have to serve as a recommendation for them or as the incentive to fulfill our duty. All humans could have enough here if they (as they should) simply held to the instruction of pure reason in the law. What need do they have to know the outcome of their moral conduct that the course of the world will bring about? For them, it is enough that they do their duty; even if everything were to end with this earthly life, and perhaps even...

in this world, **happiness** <term>Glückseligkeit</term> and **worthiness** <term>Würdigkeit</term> <note>For Kant, "worthiness to be happy" depends on a person's moral conduct, whereas "happiness" is the fulfillment of their desires.</note> perhaps never coincide. Now, it is one of the unavoidable limitations of man and his (perhaps also all other worldly beings') power of **practical reason** <term>praktische Vernunft</term> <note>The capacity of a person to decide how to act based on moral principles.</note> to look around for the result of all actions, in order to find something in this result that could serve as a purpose for him and also prove the purity of his intention. Even though this result is the last thing in the actual execution (the <term>effective connection</term> <note>original: *nexu effectivo*; the chain of cause and effect in the physical world</note>), it is the first thing in his mental representation and intention (the <term>final connection</term> <note>original: *nexu finali*; the chain of purpose or ends</note>).

In this purpose—even if it is presented to him by mere reason—man seeks something he can love. Therefore, the **law** (which merely inspires respect), even though it does not recognize that "love" as a need <sup>a</sup>), nevertheless expands itself for the sake of man's need. It does this by including the moral **final end** <term>Endzweck</term> of reason among its determining grounds. That is, the principle: "make the highest possible good in the world your final end," is a **synthetic proposition a priori** <term>synthetischer Satz a priori</term> <note>A statement where the conclusion is not already contained within the definition of the subject, but is known to be true through reason alone rather than through experience.</note>.

This principle is introduced by the moral law itself. Through it, practical reason extends itself further, which is possible because the law is connected to a natural human quality: the need to think of a purpose for every action in addition to the law itself (a quality which makes man an object of experience). This extension (much like theoretical and synthetic propositions <margin>XIII</margin> *a priori*) is only possible because it contains the principle for knowing the grounds of a free choice in experience. This choice, by displaying the effects of morality in its purposes, gives the concept of morality an objective—though only practical—reality as a form of causality in the world. 

If, however, the strictest observation of moral laws is to be thought of as the cause for bringing about the **highest good** (as an end), then we must assume an **omnipotent moral being** as the ruler of the world. This is necessary because human power is not sufficient to ensure that happiness in the world is in harmony with the worthiness to be happy. Under the care of such a ruler, this harmony occurs. That is to say: **Morality leads inevitably to religion.**

Regarding the title of this work (for doubts have also been raised concerning the intention hidden beneath it), I note the following: Since revelation <note>The idea of truths communicated to humanity by God, rather than discovered by human reason.</note> can at least include pure rational religion <note>A system of belief based entirely on what human reason can conclude about morality and God, independent of scripture.</note> within itself, but rational religion cannot conversely include the historical <margin>XXII</margin> elements of the former, I will be able to consider revelation as a wider sphere of faith that contains the latter as a narrower one within it (viewing them not as two separate circles, but as concentric circles). <margin>20</margin> **shaken together** to be joined for a short time. However, like oil and water, they would soon separate from one another, and the purely moral (the religion of reason) would have to be left floating on top.

For in his judgment, it is nothing other than an answer to the question I posed to myself: “How is the ecclesiastical system of dogmatics, in its concepts and doctrines, possible according to pure (theoretical and practical) reason?” — “This attempt, therefore, does not concern those who neither know nor understand his (Kant’s) system, nor desire to be able to do so; for them, it should be regarded as non-existent.” — To this I reply: in order to understand the essential content of this work, one only needs common morality, without having to involve oneself in the *Critique of Practical Reason*, and even less so in the theoretical one. And if, for example, virtue as a skill in duty-bound actions (according to their outward legality) is called **phenomenal virtue** <term>virtus phaenomenon</term> <note>original: "virtus phaenomenon"; virtue as it appears to observers through outward behavior or habit.</note>, while the same virtue as a steadfast disposition to perform such actions out of duty (for the sake of their inner morality) is called **noumenal virtue** <term>virtus noumenon</term> <note>original: "virtus noumenon"; virtue as it exists in the realm of the mind and intent, or the "thing-in-itself."</note>, these expressions are used only for the sake of the school XXVI <note>i.e., for academic precision.</note>. The matter itself, however, is contained in the most popular children's instruction or sermon—albeit in different words—and is easily understood. If only the same could be said for the "mysteries" regarding the divine nature included in religious doctrine! These are placed in the catechisms as if they were entirely accessible to the people, but later they must first be transformed into moral concepts if they are to become understandable for everyone.

->Königsberg, January 26, 1794.<-

# First Part.

## On the Indwelling of the Evil Principle alongside the Good,

### or

## On the Radical Evil in Human Nature.

<margin>10</margin>
<margin>20</margin>
That the world lies in wickedness <note>original: "im Argen liege." A common biblical and philosophical idiom suggesting the world is in a state of moral ruin.</note> is a complaint that is as old as history—even as old as the even older art of poetry, and indeed just as old as the oldest of all poems: priestly religion. All of them nonetheless let the world begin from a state of good: from a golden age, from life in Paradise, or from an even happier existence in communion with heavenly beings. But they let this happiness vanish soon like a dream; and now they depict the decline into evil (the moral, with which the physical <note>physical: Here referring to suffering, pain, or natural disasters that follow moral failings.</note> | always kept pace) as hurrying toward something [4] worse with an accelerated fall,*) so that we now (but this **N o w** is as old as history) live in the final times; Judgment Day and the end of the world are at the door. In some regions of Hindustan <note>Hindustan: An archaic term for northern India or the Indian subcontinent.</note>, the judge and destroyer of the world, Rudra <note>original: "Ruttren". An older European spelling for Rudra, a Vedic deity often associated with Shiva.</note> (otherwise also called Shiva or Siwen), is already worshiped as the god now in power, after the preserver of the world, Vishnu, became weary of the office he took over from the creator of the world, Brahma, and resigned it centuries ago.

A newer, but far less widespread, is the opposite "heroic" opinion, which has likely found a place only among philosophers and, in our times, primarily among educators <note>Kant likely refers to the "Philanthropinists," a group of Enlightenment educators who believed children were naturally good and could be perfected through education.</note>: that the world progresses incessantly (though barely noticeably) in the opposite direction, namely from bad to better; at least, that the predisposition for this is to be found in human nature. All these predispositions in the human being are not only (negatively) *good* (they do not conflict with the moral law), but are also predispositions toward the good (they promote the *observance* of it). They are *original*; for they belong to the possibility of human nature. <margin>10</margin> A human being can indeed use the first two in a way contrary to their purpose, but can never eradicate them. By the predispositions of a being, we understand both the *constituent parts* required for it, as well as the *forms* of their connection to be such a being. They are *original* if they belong necessarily to the possibility of such a being; they are *accidental*, however, if the being would be possible in itself even without them. It is further to be noted that we are <margin>[20]</margin> speaking here of <margin>20</margin> no other predispositions than those that relate directly to the faculty of desire and the use of the **power of choice** <term>Willkür: the capacity to choose which motives to act upon.</term>.

# Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part I.

in the idea <note>original: "in thesi"; referring to the theoretical or ideal level</note> is an invincible incentive, it is subjectively <note>original: "in hypothesi"; referring to the actual application or specific case</note>, when the **maxim** <term>Maxim: a personal rule of conduct or principle that an individual chooses to follow</term> is to be followed, the weaker one (in comparison with inclination).

Secondly, the **impurity** <note>original: "impuritas, improbitas"</note> of the human heart consists in this: that although the maxim is good in terms of its object (the intended compliance with the law) and perhaps even powerful enough for execution, it is not purely moral. That is, it has not, <margin>10</margin> as it should be, adopted the law alone as its sufficient incentive; instead, it usually (perhaps always) requires other incentives besides the law to determine the **power of choice** <term>Willkür: the capacity to decide between different motives</term> toward what duty requires. In other words, actions consistent with duty are not performed purely out of duty.

<margin>[23]</margin> Thirdly, the **wickedness** <note>original: "vitiositas, pravitas"</note> or, if one prefers, the **corruption** <note>original: "corruptio"</note> of the human heart, is the propensity of the power of choice to <margin>20</margin> prioritize incentives other than the moral law in its maxims. It can also be called the **perversity** <note>original: "perversitas"</note> of the human heart, because it reverses the moral order regarding the incentives of a free power of choice. Although legally good actions can still coexist with this perversity, the **mindset** <term>Denkungsart: the fundamental way one thinks or views the world</term> is thereby corrupted at its root (regarding the moral **disposition** <term>Gesinnung: the underlying moral attitude or orientation of a person's will</term>), and the person is therefore characterized as evil.

It will be noted that the propensity to evil is attributed here <margin>30</margin> to the human being—even the best (according to their actions). This must be done if one is to prove the universality of the propensity to evil among humans, or, what means the same thing here, that it is woven into human nature.

However, regarding the agreement of actions with the law, there is no difference (at least there ought to be none) between a person of **good habits** <note>original: "bene moratus"; someone who behaves well outwardly</note> and a **morally good person** <note>original: "moraliter bonus"</note>. The only difference is that for the one, it is not <margin>[24]</margin> always—perhaps never—the law itself that serves as the incentive, while for the other, it is.

The following explanation is still necessary to define the concept <margin>20</margin> of this *propensity*. Every *propensity* is either *physical*, meaning it belongs to the power of choice of the human being as a natural being; or it is *moral*, meaning it belongs to the power of choice of the same as a moral being. — In the former sense, there is no *propensity* toward *moral evil*; for this must spring from *freedom*; and a *physical* <margin>[25]</margin> *propensity* (which is grounded on sensory impulses) toward any use of *freedom*, be it for good or evil, is a contradiction. Therefore, a *propensity* to *evil* can only attach itself to the moral capacity of the power of choice. Now, however, nothing is ethically (that is, accountably) evil except what is our own *act*. <margin>30</margin> In contrast, one understands by the concept of a *propensity* a subjective determining ground of the power of choice that precedes every *act*, and thus is not yet itself an *act*; for there would be a contradiction in the concept of a mere *propensity to evil* if this expression could not be taken in two different meanings, both of which can nonetheless be reconciled with the concept of *freedom*. Every state, as long as it has a neighbor it hopes to conquer, strives to enlarge itself through such subjugation and thus move toward a **universal monarchy**. This is a constitution in which all freedom—and with it (as a consequence) virtue, taste, and science—must perish. However, this monster (in which laws gradually lose their force), after it has swallowed all its neighbors, eventually dissolves from within. Through rebellion and discord, it splits into many smaller states. These, instead of striving for a union of states (a republic of free, allied peoples), each begin the same game all over again. Thus, they ensure that war (this scourge of the human race) never ceases. Although war is not as incurably evil as the "grave" of universal autocracy (or a league formed to prevent the decline of despotism in any state), it nevertheless, as an ancient said, "makes more evil people than it takes away." <note>Kant refers to a Greek proverb often attributed to various ancients, suggesting war corrupts the living more than it kills the wicked.</note> <gloss>b)</gloss>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of radical evil in human beings. Having previously established that humans are "evil by nature" through historical and social observation, Kant now begins to analyze the philosophical "ground" or origin of this evil, systematically ruling out two common explanations: our physical nature and a totally corrupted reason.</meta>

# Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part I.

The ground of this evil cannot 1) be placed, as is commonly done, in the **sensuality** <term>Sensuality (*Sinnlichkeit*): In this context, it refers to our physical senses, instincts, and desires, which Kant argues are not "evil" in themselves, but simply part of our biological nature.</term> of man and the natural inclinations arising from it. For not only do these have no direct relation to evil (rather, they provide the opportunity for what the **moral disposition** <term>Moral Disposition (*moralische Gesinnung*): The internal, fundamental orientation of a person's will; the "heart" from which moral or immoral choices spring.</term> can prove in its power, namely virtue), but we are also not responsible for their existence—nor can we be, for since they are innate to us, we are not their 
<margin>10</margin> authors. We are, however, responsible for the **propensity to evil**, which, because it concerns the morality of the subject and is therefore found in him as a freely acting being, must be possible to reckon as self-incurred; this is despite the deep rooting of this propensity in the **power of choice** <term>Power of Choice (*Willkür*): The capacity to choose between following one's desires or following the moral law.</term>, due to which one must say that it is found in man by nature. — The ground of this evil can also 2) not be placed in a corruption of the **moral-legislating reason**; as if this reason could **extinguish** 
<margin>[32]</margin> the authority of the law itself within itself and | deny the obligation arising from it; for that is absolutely impossible. To think of oneself as a freely acting being and yet released from the law appropriate to such a being (the moral law) would be the same as thinking of a cause acting without any laws at all (since determination by natural laws is excluded for the sake of freedom); which is a contradiction. — Therefore, to state a ground of the morally-evil in man, **sensuality** contains too little; for by removing the **incentives** <term>Incentive (*Triebfeder*): The subjective motive or "driving force" that determines the will to act in a certain way.</term> 
<margin>30</margin> that can arise from freedom, it turns man into a merely animal being. On the other hand, a reason that releases itself from the moral law—a malicious reason, as it were (an absolutely evil will)—contains too much, because through it, opposition to the law itself would be elevated to an incentive (for without some incentive, the power of choice cannot be determined), and thus the subject would be made into a **devilish being**. — Neither of these, however, is applicable to man.

<header>III. Man is Evil by Nature. 37</header>

<margin>[33], 10</margin>
While the tendency toward evil in human nature can be demonstrated through evidence from experience—specifically, the actual conflict we see in time between the human **power of choice** <term>Power of Choice (*Willkür*): The capacity to choose between different courses of action, specifically between following one's desires or following the moral law.</term> and the moral law—this experience does not teach us the true nature of evil or the underlying ground of this conflict. Instead, because this involves a relationship between the **free power of choice** (a concept that is not derived from experience) and the **moral law** as an **incentive** <term>Incentive (*Triebfeder*): Literally a "driving spring"; the internal motive or force that prompts the will to act.</term> (the concept of which is likewise purely intellectual—see note **a)**), this relationship must be recognized *a priori* <note>original: *a priori*; meaning "from what is before," referring to knowledge that comes from pure reason rather than from sensory observation</note> from the concept of evil, insofar as it is possible according to the laws of **freedom** (which involve obligation and accountability). The following is the development of this concept.

<margin>20, 30, [34]</margin>
A human being (even the worst of us) does not, in whatever **maxims** <term>Maxim (*Maxime*): A personal rule or subjective principle that an individual adopts for their own conduct.</term> they may hold, renounce the moral law in a rebellious manner, as if by a formal withdrawal of obedience. On the contrary, the law forces itself upon the human being irresistibly by virtue of their moral predisposition. If no other incentive worked against it, the human being would adopt the law into their supreme maxim as the sufficient determining ground of their choice; that is, they would be morally good. However, by virtue of their equally blameless natural predisposition, the human being also depends on the incentives of **sensuality** <term>Sensuality (*Sinnlichkeit*): Our physical nature, including instincts, feelings, and desires for happiness.</term> and adopts them into their maxim as well (according to the subjective principle of **self-love**). Yet, if they were to adopt these sensory incentives into their maxim as being sufficient on their own to determine the choice, without concerning themselves with the moral law (which they nonetheless possess within), they would be morally evil. Now, since the human being naturally adopts both incentives into the same maxim, and since they would find each incentive, if it were alone, sufficient to determine the will, it follows that if the distinction between maxims depended merely on the difference between the incentives (the matter of the maxims)—namely, whether the law or the sensory impulse provided the incentive—the human being would be morally good and evil at the same time; which (according to the Introduction) is a contradiction. Therefore, the distinction as to whether a human being is good or evil must lie not in the difference between the incentives that he adopts into...

Now, if a **propensity** <term>Propensity (*Hang*): A natural inclination or predisposition toward something, in this case, a tendency to prioritize oneself over the moral law.</term> for this reversal lies in **human nature**, then there is in man a natural propensity to **evil**; and this propensity itself—because it must ultimately be sought in a free **power of choice**, and can therefore be attributed to us—is **morally evil**. <margin>40</margin>

<summary>Kant argues that evil consists of a "reversal" of moral priorities, where we make our own happiness the condition for following the moral law. Every evil action, when one seeks its rational origin, must be viewed as if the person had fallen into it directly from a state of innocence. For whatever his previous conduct may have been, and whatever natural causes may have influenced him— <margin>10</margin> whether these causes are found within him or outside of him—his action is nevertheless free and determined by none of these causes. It can and must, therefore, always be judged as an original use of his power of choice. He should have refrained from the action, regardless of the temporal circumstances and connections in which he may have been; for through no cause in the world can he cease to be a free-acting being. It is rightly said, to be sure, that the consequences arising from a person's <margin>20</margin> former free but unlawful actions are also attributed <margin>[43]</margin> to him; but by this one only means that it is not necessary to get involved in the excuse of determining whether the latter actions might be free or not, because there is already a sufficient ground for accountability <term>Accountability (*Zurechnung*): The moral or legal assignment of responsibility for an action to a person as its free author.</term> in the admittedly free action that was their cause. ### On the Restoration of the Original
### Predisposition to Good to its Power.

Whatever the human being is or is to become in a moral sense, whether good or evil, they must make or have made themselves into it. Both must be an effect of their free power of choice <term>Willkür: the capacity of the human will to choose between acting on sensory desires or acting according to the moral law</term>; for otherwise, it could not be attributed to them, and consequently, they could be neither morally good nor evil. When it is said, "he is created good," this can mean nothing more than: he is created *for* the good, and the original **predisposition** <note>original: "Anlage" — the inherent potential or capacity within human nature for morality.</note> in the human being is good. <meta>This page continues the "General Remark" regarding the restoration of the human being's original predisposition to good. <header>General Remark: On the Restoration of the Original Predisposition.</header>

The restoration of the original predisposition to [52] good in us is therefore not the acquisition of a lost **incentive** <term>Incentive (Triebfeder): the internal "spring" or motivating force that drives a person to act</term> for the good; for we could never have lost this incentive, which consists in respect for the moral law, and were the latter possible, we would also never be able to reacquire it. It is, therefore, only the restoration of the purity of the law as the supreme ground of all our **maxims** <term>Maxim: a personal rule or principle that a person chooses to follow</term>. According to this purity, the law is not merely connected with other incentives or perhaps even subordinated to them (our inclinations) as conditions, but <margin>10</margin> rather must be adopted in its total purity as a sufficient incentive in itself

be. To adopt the first [natural inclination] into one’s maxim is natural (for who would not want things to go well for them at all times?). However, it is rational only insofar as, on the one hand, regarding the goal, only that which can coexist with the greatest and most lasting well-being is chosen, and on the other hand, the most suitable means are chosen for every component of happiness. Here, reason merely takes the place of a servant to natural inclination; the maxim adopted for this purpose has no relationship at all to morality. However, if this is made into the unconditional principle of the **power of choice** <term>Power of choice (Willkür): the capacity to decide between different courses of action</term>, it becomes the source of an immeasurably great conflict against morality. — A | rational love of satisfaction in oneself [51] can now be understood in two ways: either we are satisfied with ourselves in those aforementioned maxims aimed at the satisfaction of natural inclination (insofar as that goal is achieved through following them); and in that case, it is the same as the love of **benevolence** <note>original: "Wohlwollens"</note> <note>a</note> toward oneself; one is pleased with oneself like a merchant whose business speculations turn out well, and who rejoices in his good insight regarding the maxims he employed. However, the maxim of self-love of unconditional satisfaction in oneself (not depending on gain or loss as the consequences of the action) would be the internal principle of a contentment possible for us only under the condition of the subordination of our maxims to the moral law. No human being to whom morality is not a matter of indifference can have satisfaction in themselves—indeed, they cannot even be without a bitter dissatisfaction with themselves—if they are conscious of such maxims that do not agree with the moral law within them. One could call this <note>b</note> the rational love of oneself, which prevents any mixing of other causes of contentment from the consequences of one’s actions

General Remark: On the Restoration of the Original Predisposition. 51

But if a person is corrupt in the very ground of their maxims, how is it possible that they could bring about this revolution through their own powers and become a good person on their own? And yet, duty commands us to be so; but duty commands nothing of us except what is feasible for us. This can only be reconciled by 30 saying that the revolution is necessary for the **mode of thought** (<note>original: *Denkungsart*</note>), while gradual reform is necessary for the **mode of sense** (<note>original: *Sinnesart*</note>) (which presents obstacles to the former); and therefore, both must be possible for the human being. That is: if a person reverses the supreme ground of their maxims, through which they were a bad person, by a single unchangeable decision (and <margin>[55]</margin> thereby "puts on the new man"), then in that respect, according to their principle and mode of thought, they are a subject receptive to the good. # General Remark: On the Restoration of the Original Predisposition. 53

To teach people to admire virtuous deeds, whatever they may have cost, is not yet the right mood that should sustain the apprentice’s mind for the **morally good**. For no matter how virtuous someone may be, everything they can ever do that is good is merely **duty** <term>Duty (Pflicht): the necessity of an action done out of respect for the moral law</term>; but doing one's duty is nothing more than doing what is in the ordinary **moral order**, and thus does not deserve to be <margin>[57]</margin> admired. Rather, this admiration is a lowering of our feeling for duty, as if it were something extraordinary and meritorious to obey it. <margin>10</margin>

But there is one thing in our soul which, when we properly consider it, we cannot cease to view with the highest wonder, and where admiration is legitimate and at the same time soul-elevating; and that is: the **original moral predisposition** <term>Moral Predisposition (moralische Anlage): the inherent human capacity to recognize and be moved by the moral law</term> in us generally. — What is this (one can ask oneself) in us, through which we—beings who are constantly dependent on nature through so many needs—are yet at the same time elevated so far above nature in the idea of an original predisposition (in us) <margin>20</margin> that we consider all these needs together as nothing, and ourselves unworthy of existence, if we were to indulge in their enjoyment (which alone can make life desirable to us) in opposition to a law through which our **reason** <term>Reason (Vernunft): the faculty that provides the principles of logic and morality</term> powerfully commands, without yet promising or threatening anything? The weight of this question must be felt most inwardly by every human being of the most common capacity, who has previously been taught of the holiness that lies in the idea of duty, but who does not venture so far as to investigate the concept of **freedom** <term>Freedom (Freiheit): for Kant, the ability to act according to laws we give ourselves, independent of physical urges</term>, which only first arises from this law; <margin>30</margin> and even the incomprehensibility of this [predisposition] announcing a divine origin <margin>[58]</margin> <margin>[59]</margin> must feel...

### Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part I.

The predisposition <term>Predisposition (Anlage): the inherent potential or capacity within human nature</term> must work upon the mind until it reaches the point of enthusiasm, strengthening it for those sacrifices which respect for duty may impose. To frequently activate this feeling of the sublimity of one's moral destiny is to be highly recommended as a means of awakening moral dispositions. This is because it directly counteracts the innate leaning toward reversing the incentives within the maxims of our power of choice <term>Power of Choice (Willkür): the capacity to act according to one's own decisions, rather than by mere instinct</term>, in order

to be able to overcome [temptation] through a firm resolve, even if <note>original Latin: "admoto dictet perjuria tauro"</note> a tyrant dictates perjury with the bronze bull brought near.<a> Everyone must admit that they do not know whether, if such a case occurred, they would not waver in their resolve. Nevertheless, duty commands unconditionally: one *should* remain faithful to it. From this, one rightly concludes: they *must* also be able to do it, and their power of choice is therefore free. Those who pretend that this unfathomable property is entirely understandable create an illusion through the word **Determinism** (the principle that the power of choice is determined by internal sufficient reasons). They act as if the difficulty consisted in reconciling this with freedom—which no one actually disputes. Rather, the real question is how **Predeterminism** can coexist with freedom. According to predeterminism, voluntary actions, as events, have their determining causes in a preceding time (which, along with what it contains, is no longer in our power). Yet, according to freedom, the action, as well as its opposite, must be in the subject's power at the moment of its occurrence. This is what one wishes to understand, and never will understand.

<margin>[59]</margin> There is no difficulty at all in reconciling the concept of freedom with the idea of God as a necessary being. This is because freedom does not consist in the randomness of an action (that it is not determined by reasons at all)—that is, not in **Indeterminism** (the idea that it must be equally possible for God to do good or evil for his action to be called free). Instead, freedom consists in **absolute spontaneity**. This spontaneity only faces danger with Predeterminism, where the determining cause of the action is in the past. In such a case, the action is no longer in my power but in the hands of nature, which determines me irresistibly. However, since no sequence of time can be conceived in God, this difficulty disappears.<b>

<header>General Remark: On the Restoration of the Original Predisposition. 55</header>

...in unconditional respect for the law, as the highest condition of all maxims to be adopted, to restore the original moral order among the incentives <term>Incentives (Triebfedern): the internal motivations or "springs of action" that drive a person to act</term> and hereby the predisposition to good in the human heart in its purity.

<margin>10, 20, 30, 40</margin>
But does not the proposition of the innate depravity of man for all that is good directly oppose this restoration through one's own application of power? Certainly, as far as comprehensibility—that is, our <gloss>| insight [60]</gloss> into its possibility—is concerned, as with everything that is to be represented as an occurrence in time (change) and thus necessary according to laws of nature, yet whose opposite is simultaneously to be represented as possible through freedom under moral laws; but it is not opposed to the possibility of this restoration itself. For if the moral law commands that we *ought* now to be better humans, it follows unavoidably that we *must* also be able to be so. The proposition of innate evil is of no use at all in moral dogmatics <term>Moral Dogmatics: the theoretical study of moral principles and duties</term>; for its prescriptions contain exactly the same duties and remain in the same force, whether or not there is an innate leaning toward transgression within us. In moral ascetics <term>Moral Ascetics: the practical discipline and "exercise" of the soul to attain virtue</term>, however, this proposition means more, yet says nothing more than this: in the moral cultivation of the created moral predisposition to good, we cannot begin from a state of natural innocence. Instead, we must start from the presupposition of a malevolence of the power of choice <term>Power of Choice (Willkür): the capacity to decide which motives to act upon</term> in adopting its maxims contrary to the original moral predisposition and—since the leaning toward this is inextinguishable—with incessant counteraction against it. Since this leads only to a progression from bad to better that extends into infinity, it follows: that the transformation of the disposition of the evil <gloss>| into that of a good person in the change [61]</gloss> of the supreme inner ground for the adoption of all his maxims must be situated in accordance with the moral law, insofar as this new ground (the new heart) is now itself unchangeable. However, a person cannot naturally arrive at a conviction of this, neither through immediate consciousness nor through the proof of the conduct of his life led up to that point; because
