### Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part I.

...the depths of the heart (the subjective first ground of his maxims) is unfathomable to him; but he must be able to hope to reach the path that leads there—a path indicated to him by a fundamentally improved disposition <term>Disposition (Gesinnung): the fundamental internal orientation or "heart" from which a person’s moral choices flow</term>—through his own application of power; because he *ought* to become a good person, but he is only to be judged as *morally good* according to that which can be credited to him as having been done by himself.

Against this demand for *self-improvement*, reason—which by its *nature* is reluctant <margin>10</margin> toward *moral labor*—brings up all kinds of impure religious ideas under the pretext of natural inability (which includes: imagining that *God* himself makes the *principle of happiness* the supreme condition of His commands). One can, however, divide all religions into those of *currying favor* (of mere *cultic worship*) and *moral* religion, that is, the *religion of a good* <margin>[62]</margin> *way of life*. According to the former, the *human being* either flatters himself that *God* can make him eternally happy without him needing to become a better <margin>20</margin> *human being* (through the *remission of his debts* <note>In this context, "debts" refers to sins or moral failings</note>), or—if this does not seem possible to him—that *God* can surely *make* him a *better human* without him having to do anything more than ask for it; which, since asking before an *all-seeing Being* is nothing more than wishing, would actually amount to nothing being done; for if it could be accomplished with a *mere wish*, every person would be good. According to *moral religion*, however (of which the *Christian* is the <margin>30</margin> only one among all the public religions that have ever existed), it is a *fundamental principle*: that everyone must do as much as is in their power to become a better person; and only then—if he has not buried his innate *pledge* <note>original: "Pfand"; a reference to the "talents" or "minas" in the biblical parable</note> (Luke XIX, 12–16), and if he has used the original predisposition to good in order to become a better person—can he hope that what is not in his power will be supplemented through *higher cooperation* <term>Higher Cooperation (höhere Mitwirkung): divine assistance or "grace" that completes what human effort cannot achieve on its own</term>. It is also *not absolutely necessary* for the person to know what this assistance consists of; it may even be <margin>40</margin> unavoidable that, if the way it occurs was *revealed* at a certain time, different people at <margin>[63]</margin> another time will form different concepts of it, and indeed...

<summary>Kant distinguishes between "moral religion," which requires personal effort toward self-improvement, and religions of "currying favor," which rely on divine flattery or ritual to avoid the hard work of character building. He argues that divine grace (higher cooperation) is only available to those who first exert their own maximum effort.</summary>

<header>General Remark: On the Restoration of the Original Capacity. 57</header>

...with all sincerity, would make of it. But then the principle also applies: “It is not essential, and thus not necessary for everyone to know what God does or has done for his salvation”; but it is certainly necessary to know what he himself must do to become worthy of this assistance. *)

*) This general remark is the first of the four, [63] one of which is appended to each part of this work, and which could bear the headings: 1) of works of grace, 2) miracles, 3) mysteries, 4) means of grace. — These are, as it were, **parerga** <note>original: *Parerga*; a Greek term referring to "side-works" or "supplementary items" that are outside the main subject but attached to it</note> of religion within the boundaries of pure reason; they do not belong within it, but they do border upon it. Reason, conscious of its inability to satisfy its moral need, extends itself to extravagant ideas that could supplement that deficiency, without however appropriating them as an expanded possession. It does not contest the possibility or reality of their objects, but it simply cannot include them in its maxims for thinking and acting. It even counts on the fact that if, in the inscrutable field of the supernatural, there is something more than it can make intelligible to itself—which would nonetheless be necessary to supplement its moral inability—this will be available to its good will even if unrecognized. This involves a faith that one might call "reflecting" (on the possibility of such help), because "dogmatic" faith, which announces itself as knowledge, appears to it insincere or presumptuous. For to clear away difficulties against what stands firm for itself (practically) is, when they concern transcendent questions, only a side-business (parergon). 

As for the disadvantage arising from these ideas—which are also morally-transcendent—if we wanted to | introduce them into religion, [64] the effect of this, according to the order of the four aforementioned classes, is: 
1) regarding supposed inner experience (effects of grace), **fanaticism** <note>original: *Schwärmerei*; a term Kant uses for the delusion of believing one can feel or perceive the supernatural</note>; 
2) regarding alleged outer experience (miracles), **superstition**; 
3) regarding the imagined enlightenment of the understanding in view of the supernatural (mysteries), **illuminatism** <note>A belief in having special, secret divine light or knowledge</note>, or the **delusion of the initiates**; 
4) regarding the daring attempts to act upon the supernatural (means of grace), **thaumaturgy** <note>original: *Thaumaturgie*; the practice of "wonder-working" or trying to manipulate the divine through ritual</note>: 

These are nothing but aberrations of a reason exceeding its boundaries, and done so with a supposedly moral (God-pleasing) intention. — But as for what specifically concerns this general remark for the first part of the present treatise, the summoning of the effects of grace is of the latter kind and cannot be included in the maxims of reason if the latter keeps within its boundaries; just as, in general, nothing supernatural can be included, because it is precisely at this point that all use of reason ceases.

<summary>Kant introduces the concept of "parerga" (supplementary ideas) to religion, arguing that while we may hope for divine grace to assist our moral efforts, we cannot incorporate supernatural phenomena like miracles or fanaticism into a rational moral system.</summary>

# Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part I.

— For making them theoretically identifiable (meaning, to recognize that they are effects of grace and not internal natural effects) is impossible, because our application of the concept of *cause and effect* cannot be extended beyond *objects of experience*, and thus not beyond the laws of *nature*. However, the presupposition of a practical application of this idea is entirely self-contradictory. For to "apply" it would presuppose a rule regarding what we ourselves must do (with a certain intent) to achieve something *good* <note>In Kantian ethics, "good" refers specifically to the moral worth of an action</note>; but to expect an *effect of grace* <note>original: *Gnadenwirkung*; the theological concept that God provides supernatural assistance to help a person become morally better</note> means the exact opposite: namely, that the good (the *moral* good) would not be our own deed, but the *deed of another being*. This implies we could acquire it through *inactivity* alone, which is a contradiction. Therefore, we can admit such things as *incomprehensible*, but we can include them in our *maxims* <note>original: *Maxime*; the personal rules or principles that guide an individual's choices</note> for neither *theoretical* nor *practical* use. a))

## **the dominion over man.**

To become a morally good person, it is not enough to simply allow the seed of the good <note>original: "Keim des Guten"; Kant suggests humans have an inherent "seed" or predisposition toward moral goodness that must be cultivated</note> inherent in our species to develop unhindered. One must also combat an opposing cause of evil found within us. Among all the ancient moralists, it was primarily the **Stoics** <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that taught the development of self-control and fortitude as a means of overcoming destructive emotions</note> who made this known through their watchword **Virtue**. This term—in both Greek and Latin <note>In Greek, *arete*; in Latin, *virtus*. Both terms historically linked moral excellence with "manliness" or "valor" in battle</note>—signifies courage and bravery, and thus presupposes the existence of an enemy. <margin>10</margin> In this regard, the name "Virtue" is a magnificent name, and it cannot be harmed by the fact that it has often been boastfully misused or (like the word **Enlightenment** <note>original: "Aufklärung"; the 18th-century intellectual movement emphasizing reason and individual autonomy over tradition and dogma</note> recently) ridiculed. — For to summon courage <margin>[68]</margin> is already halfway toward instilling it; conversely, a lazy, small-minded <term>way of thinking</term> <note>original: "Denkungsart"; a central Kantian term referring to one's fundamental internal mindset or moral orientation</note> (in morality and religion) that entirely distrusts itself and waits for external help saps <margin>20</margin> all of a person’s powers and makes them unworthy of that very help.

However, those brave men nonetheless misidentified their enemy. This enemy is not to be sought in the natural <note>original: "natürlichen Neigungen"; our biological impulses or "inclinations," such as hunger or the desire for comfort, which Kant argues are not "evil" in themselves</note> inclinations, which are merely undisciplined and reveal themselves openly to everyone’s consciousness. Rather, it is an invisible enemy, as it were, hiding behind **Reason**, and is therefore all the more dangerous. They summoned **Wisdom** against **Folly**, <margin>30</margin> which merely allows itself to be carelessly deceived by inclinations, instead of calling it up against the **Malice** (of the human heart), which with...

The inclinations are only opponents of principles in general (be they good or evil), and to that extent, that noble principle of morality is advantageous as a preliminary exercise (discipline of the inclinations) for the susceptibility of the subject to be guided by principles. But insofar as there are to be specific principles of the **morally good**, and yet they are not such as maxims, another opponent of these principles must be presupposed in the subject, with whom virtue must do battle. Without this struggle, all virtues would be—not as that Church Father<gloss>d</gloss> <note>d) Referring to St. Augustine, though the exact wording is not found in his extant works</note> claims, "splendid vices" <note>original: "glänzende Laster"; often attributed to Augustine as *splendida vitia*, referring to the virtues of those without faith</note>, but rather "splendid miseries"; for while the rebellion is often quelled by this means, the rebel himself is never defeated and uprooted.

# First Section.

## On the Rightful Claim of the Good Principle to Sovereignty over Humanity.

### a) The Personified Idea of the Good Principle.

That which alone can make a world the object of a divine decree <note>original: "Ratschluss"; refers to God’s plan or intended purpose for the universe.</note> and the goal of creation is humanity (the rational being of the world in general) in its complete moral perfection. From this perfection, as its supreme condition, happiness <note>Kant distinguishes between "happiness" (well-being) and "worthiness to be happy" (morality), arguing here that God intends the latter to lead to the former.</note> is the immediate consequence in the will of the Highest Being. — This human being, who alone is pleasing to God, "is in Him from all eternity"; the idea of this person proceeds from God's own essence. In this respect, he is not a created thing, but His only-begotten son; "the Word (the *Let there be!* <note>original: "das Werde!"; the creative command of God, as in "Let there be light."</note>), through which all other things exist, and without which nothing exists that was made"; (for it is for his sake—that is, for the sake of the rational being in the
<margin>[74]</margin> world, as it can be conceived according to its moral destination—that everything was made.) — "He
<margin>20</margin> is the reflection of His glory." — "In Him, God has loved the world," and only in Him and through the adoption of His mental dispositions can we hope "to become children of God," and so forth.

To elevate ourselves to this ideal of moral perfection—that is, the archetype <note>original: "Urbild"; the perfect original model or pattern of which humans are imperfect copies.</note> of the moral disposition in all its purity—is a universal human duty. The power to do this can be given to us by this very idea, which is presented to us by reason for our pursuit. However, precisely because we are not its
<margin>30</margin> authors, but rather because it has taken its place in humanity without our understanding how human nature could even be receptive to it, one can better say: that this archetype has [descended from...] <note>The text cuts off as Kant begins to explain that the ideal of moral perfection feels like a gift from heaven rather than a human invention.</note>

<summary>Kant explains that the purpose of creation is "perfected humanity," an ideal he identifies philosophically with the "Son of God." He argues that every person has a moral duty to strive toward this perfect archetype, which is present in our reason.</summary>

For a human can form no concept of the degree and strength of a force, such as that of a moral disposition, except by imagining it struggling with obstacles and yet conquering under the greatest possible temptations.

# Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part II.

...a person can hope to become well-pleasing to God (and thereby also blessed); that is, the person who is aware of such a **moral disposition** <note>original: "moralische Gesinnung"; refers to the underlying attitude or "heart" that directs one's actions.</note> that he can believe and place a grounded trust in himself that, under similar temptations and sufferings (insofar as these serve as the touchstone <note>A "touchstone" is a metaphorical test of quality or genuineness.</note> of that idea), he would remain unchangeably attached to the **archetype of humanity** and remain similar to his example in faithful succession. Such a person, and only such a person, is entitled <margin>10</margin> to consider himself as one who is an object not unworthy of divine approval.

### b) Objective reality of this idea.

This idea has its reality, in a practical sense, entirely within itself. For it resides in our morally legislative **reason**. We ought to conform to it, and therefore we must be able to do so. If we had to prove beforehand the possibility of being a human who conforms to this archetype—as is unavoidably necessary with concepts of nature (so that we do not <margin>20</margin> run the risk of being misled by empty concepts)—we would likewise have to hesitate to grant the moral law the authority <margin>[77]</margin> to be the unconditional and yet sufficient determining ground of our **choice** <term>Willkür: the capacity for choosing between different possible courses of action.</term>. For how it is possible that the mere idea of lawfulness in general could be a more powerful **incentive** <term>Triebfeder: the subjective ground or "driving spring" that moves a person to act.</term> for the will than any imaginable advantage, can neither be understood through reason nor illustrated by examples from experience. Regarding the <margin>30</margin> first point, the law commands unconditionally; regarding the second, even if there had never been a person who rendered unconditional obedience to this law, the objective necessity of being such a person remains undiminished and is self-evident. Therefore, we require no example from experience to make the idea of a person morally well-pleasing to God our model; as such, it already resides in our reason. — However, if someone requires more than what he sees—that is, more than a completely blameless <margin>40</margin> [conduct]—in order to recognize a human being as an example for imitation that agrees with that idea...

<margin>10</margin> "Which among you can convict me of sin?" <note>A reference to John 8:46, used here to illustrate the teacher's moral integrity as a visible example.</note> It is, however, consistent with fairness to credit the blameless example of a teacher to his own purest disposition—especially when what he teaches is already a duty for everyone—unless one has evidence to the contrary. ...to **schematize** <note>to make an abstract concept understandable by comparing it to something we can perceive with our senses</note> (making a concept graspable through analogy with something sensible), but absolutely not to conclude—based on the analogy of what belongs to the former—that it must also be attributed to the latter (and thus expand one's concept of it). This is for the very simple reason that such a conclusion would run contrary to all analogy; it would be like saying that because we necessarily need a schema for a concept to make it understandable to ourselves (to illustrate it with an example), it must also necessarily belong to the object itself as a characteristic. For I cannot say: just as I can only make the cause of a plant (or any organic creature, and indeed the purposeful world in general) graspable through the analogy of a craftsman in relation to his work (a watch)—namely, by attributing intelligence to him—so too must the cause itself (of the plant, or the world in general) have intelligence. That is to say, attributing intelligence to it is not merely a condition of my own comprehension, but a condition of the possibility of it being a cause at all. Between the relationship of a schema to its concept and the relationship [83] of this very schema | of the concept to the thing itself, there is no analogy at all, but rather a violent leap (**transition to another genus** <note>original Greek: "μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος"</note>), which leads directly into **anthropomorphism** <note>the error of attributing human traits or limitations to God or non-human entities</note>, for which I have given proofs elsewhere.

### e) Difficulties regarding the reality of this idea and their resolution.
<margin>10</margin>
The first difficulty that makes us doubt whether we can reach that idea of a humanity pleasing to God—especially considering the holiness of the Lawgiver <note>God as the source of moral law</note> and our own lack of righteousness—is as follows. The law says: “Be holy (in your conduct of life), as your Father in heaven is holy!”; for that is the ideal of the Son of God which is set before us as a model. However, the distance between the good that we are supposed to bring about in ourselves and the <margin>20</margin> evil from which we start is infinite. Insofar as it concerns the **deed**—that is, the conformity of one's conduct to the holiness of the law—this distance can never be bridged at any point in time. Nevertheless, the moral character of a human being is supposed to harmonize with it. Therefore, this character must be placed in the **disposition**—in the universal and pure **maxim** <note>a personal rule or principle of action</note> of making one's behavior agree with that law. This serves as the "seed" from which all good is to be developed, proceeding from a holy principle that the human being has adopted into their supreme maxim. [85] A **change of heart** <note>a fundamental shift in one's moral orientation; "Sinnesänderung"</note> must also be possible, because it is a duty. Now, the difficulty lies in this: how the disposition can count as the deed, given that the deed is always (not just generally, but at every single moment) deficient. The resolution of this difficulty, however, rests on the fact that the latter [the deed] is viewed as a continuous progress from a deficient good toward something better, extending into infinity. This is according to our own estimation, as we are inevitably [bound] by the concepts of the relationship between **cause** <note>original: "Ursache". A note by K.V. asks if it should be "Ursachen" (causes).</note> and effect...

However, because of the **disposition** <note>original: "Gesinnung"; this refers to one's fundamental moral orientation or inner attitude</note> from which it is derived, which is *supersensible* <note>existing beyond the reach of our physical senses and the flow of time</note>, its progress toward conformity with that law into infinity can be judged as a completed whole. The second difficulty that arises when one considers a person striving for the good in relation to divine goodness—specifically regarding this moral good itself—concerns *moral happiness*. ->The proverb: *All’s well that ends well* <note>original: "Ende gut, alles gut."</note> can indeed be applied to moral cases, but only if by a "good end" one understands that point where a person becomes a truly good person.<- 

But by what means shall he recognize himself as such, since he can only infer this from a subsequent, persistent good course of life, and at the end of life there is no longer any time for this? This proverb can more easily be granted regarding *happiness* <note>original: "Glückseligkeit."</note>, but even then only in relation to the standpoint from which a person views his life—not from the beginning, but from the end, looking back. Endured sufferings leave no agonizing memory behind when one sees oneself already safe, but rather a sense of joy, which only makes the enjoyment of the happiness now beginning all the more delicious. This is because pleasure or pain (as belonging to our **sensibility** <term>sensibility: "Sinnlichkeit," the faculty through which we receive sensations and feelings</term>), being contained within the series of time, vanish along with it; they do not form a single whole with the currently existing enjoyment of life, but are instead displaced by it as the successor. 

However, if one applies the same proposition to the judgment of the *moral worth* of the life led up to that point, a person may be very much in the wrong to judge it so, even if he has concluded it with an entirely good conduct. For <margin>[92]</margin> the moral-subjective principle of the **disposition** <term>disposition: "Gesinnung," the underlying moral orientation or attitude of the heart that governs a person's choices</term>, according to which his life must be judged, is (as something **supersensible** <term>supersensible: "Übersinnliches," that which exists beyond physical perception or the limits of time and space</term>) not of the kind that its existence is divisible into segments of time; rather, it can only be thought of as an absolute unity. And since we can only infer the *disposition* from actions (as the appearances of that disposition), for the purpose of this estimation, life will only be considered as a unit of time—that is, as a whole. In that case, the reproaches from the first part of life (before the improvement) speak just as loudly as the approval in the latter part, and they might very much dampen the triumphant tone of: *All’s well that ends well.* 

— Finally, another teaching is closely related to that doctrine of the duration of punishments in another world, although it is not identical to it: namely, "that all sins must be forgiven here [on earth]"; that the account must be fully closed by the end of life, and no one can hope to make up there for what was neglected here. # Section 1: On the Legal Claim of the Good Principle.

The resolution of this difficulty rests on the following. The judicial verdict of a **Searcher of Hearts** <term>Searcher of Hearts: "Herzenskündiger," a biblical and philosophical term for a judge (God) who knows the innermost secrets and true motives of the soul</term> <gloss>[96]</gloss> must be conceived as one drawn from the general **disposition** <term>disposition: "Gesinnung," the fundamental moral orientation or "spirit" of a person</term> of the accused, and not from the appearances of that disposition—that is, the actions which either deviate from or harmonize with the law. 

Now, however, we are assuming here that the human being possesses a good disposition which has gained the upper hand over the evil principle that was previously powerful within him. The question then is: can the moral consequence of the former state, namely **punishment** <margin>10</margin> (in other words, the effect of God’s displeasure with the subject), also be applied to his state in the improved disposition, in which he is already an object of divine favor? 

Since the question here is not whether the punishment decreed over him *before* the change of heart would harmonize with divine justice (a point which no one doubts), this punishment shall not (in this investigation) be thought of as having been carried out on him before his improvement. Yet, it can also not be viewed as appropriate to his new quality (as a person pleasing to God) *after* the change, since the human being <margin>20</margin> is already walking in a new life and is morally a different person. Nevertheless, satisfaction must be given to supreme justice, before which a person deserving of punishment can never go unpunished. Since a punishment is necessary and yet, according to divine wisdom, fits neither before nor after the change of heart, it would have to be thought of as appropriate to and carried out in the state of the **change of heart** <term>change of heart: "Sinnesänderung," a total transformation of one's fundamental moral outlook</term> itself <gloss>[97]</gloss>. 

We must therefore see whether, in this latter state, <margin>30</margin> the concept of a moral change of heart can already be thought to contain those evils which the new, well-disposed person can view as being deserved by him (in another respect) and as being such punishments*) through which divine justice is satisfied <gloss>[98]</gloss>

### Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part II.

...now considered in a different light. — This **change of heart** <term>change of heart: "Sinnesänderung," a total transformation of one's fundamental moral orientation, similar to a religious conversion</term> is, namely, a departure from evil and an entrance into the good; it is the "putting off of the old man" and the "putting on of the new," <note>These phrases are allusions to the New Testament, specifically Ephesians 4:22–24 and Colossians 3:9–10, describing the transformation of the self through faith and moral resolve.</note> because the subject of sin (and thus all inclinations that lead toward it) dies away so that he may live for righteousness. In this change, regarded as an intellectual determination, there are not <margin>10</margin> two separate moral acts divided by an interval of time. Instead, it is only a single act, because the abandonment of evil is only possible through the good **disposition** <term>disposition: "Gesinnung," the underlying spirit or motive behind all of a person's actions</term> which effects the entrance into the good, and vice versa. The good principle is therefore contained both in the leaving of the evil and in the adoption of the good disposition; and the pain that rightfully accompanies the former arises entirely from the latter. This exit from a corrupted disposition into a good one is (as <insert>a</insert> "the dying to the old man, the crucifixion of the flesh") in itself a sacrifice and the start of a long series of life’s evils, which the new man accepts in the spirit of the **Son of God**—namely, <margin>20</margin> purely for the sake of the good. These evils, however, were actually owed to another as a **punishment**, namely the "old man" (for the old man is morally a different person). — Thus, although the human being is physically (when viewed according to his empirical character <margin>[99]</margin> | as a being of the senses) the very same punishable...

---

...subject, and must as such still be judged as such before a moral tribunal and hence be punished; yet, in his new spirit (as an intellectual being), he is in the eyes of a divine judge—for whom this disposition takes the place of action—morally a different person. <note>Kant is struggling with a paradox: how can God justly punish a person who is now good for what they did when they were bad? He suggests that the "suffering" of moral transformation serves as the punishment.</note>

This way of thinking allows us to connect the concept of suffering with morality, naturally producing the thought that we must first seek to become better people before we can expect to be freed from the evils of **life** or to have them compensated by a greater well-being. — For this reason, the first man (in Holy Scripture) is represented as being condemned to labor if he wished to eat, his wife to bear children in pain, and both to death because of their transgression. Yet it is not clear how, even if these transgressions had not been committed, animal creatures equipped with such limbs and organs could have expected any other destiny. Among the **Hindus**, humans are nothing other than spirits (called *Dewas* <gloss>Devas: divine beings or spirits in Indian religions</gloss>) imprisoned in animal bodies as punishment for former crimes. Even one philosopher (**Malebranche**) <note>Nicolas Malebranche (1638–1715) was a French priest and philosopher who famously argued that animals were "machines" without souls, partly to avoid the theological problem of why they suffer if they cannot sin.</note> preferred to grant no souls—and thus no feelings—to irrational animals at all, rather than <margin>[98]</margin> admit that | horses should have to endure so many plagues "without having ever eaten of the forbidden hay." <note>original: "ohne doch vom verbotenen Heu gefressen zu haben." This is a witty play on the "forbidden fruit" of Eden.</note>

*) Even the purest moral disposition in a human being as a world-being produces nothing more than a **continuous becoming** <term>continuous becoming: "kontinuierliches Werden," the idea that moral character is a lifelong process of growth rather than a finished product</term> [99] of a subject pleasing to God in terms of deeds (which are found in the world of the senses). It is not immediately obvious what positive use can be made of this concept for religion and one's conduct in life; for this investigation assumes that the person it concerns has already actually achieved the required good **disposition** <term>disposition: "Gesinnung," the fundamental moral orientation or "spirit" of a person's heart</term>. It is for the sake of developing and advancing this very disposition that all practical use of moral concepts is intended. As far as **comfort** is concerned, such a disposition already carries it within itself for the person who is conscious of it—though it carries it as comfort and hope, not as absolute certainty.

In this respect, then, the deduction is merely the answer to a speculative question. However, it cannot be passed over in silence, because otherwise reason could be accused of being utterly incapable of reconciling the hope for a person's **acquittal** <note>original: "Lossprechung," a legal term for being declared free from guilt</note> from their guilt with divine justice. <margin>20</margin> Nevertheless, the **negative** benefit that can be drawn from this for religion and morals for the sake of every human being extends very far. For one sees from the aforementioned deduction that acquittal before heavenly justice can only be conceived for a person burdened with guilt under the condition of a total **change of heart** <term>change of heart: "Herzensänderung," a complete internal moral transformation from evil to good</term>. For this ideal must be adopted into our own disposition in order to count in the place of the deed.ᵃ⁾

Another matter is contained in the question: what a person has to promise themselves, or what they have to fear, at the end of their life based on the conduct they have led. ### On the Legal Claim of the Evil Principle to Sovereignty over Mankind, and the Struggle Between the Two Principles.

<margin>10</margin>
Holy Scripture (specifically the Christian portion) presents this **intelligible** <term>intelligible: "intelligibel," a term used to describe things that exist in the realm of thought or reason rather than the physical world of the senses</term> moral relationship in the form of a narrative. It depicts two principles, as opposite as heaven and hell, existing within man but represented as persons outside of him. They do not merely test their power against one another, but also (one part acting as the accuser, the other as the advocate for mankind) seek to assert their claims through law, as if before a supreme judge.

<margin>20</margin>
<margin>[107]</margin>
<margin>30</margin>
Mankind was originally appointed as the owner of all the goods of the earth (Genesis 1:28), yet with the condition that he should possess these only as a **subordinate owner** (*useful ownership* <note>original: "dominium utile," a legal term for the right to use and benefit from property while someone else holds the ultimate title</note>), under his Creator and Lord as the **supreme owner** (*direct ownership* <note>original: "dominus directus," the ultimate legal owner or feudal lord who holds the title to the land</note>). At the same time, an evil being is introduced (how it became so evil as to turn unfaithful to its Lord, despite being originally good, is unknown). This being, having lost through its rebellion all the property it might have possessed in heaven, now seeks to acquire new property on earth. Since, as a being of a higher kind—as a spirit—earthly and bodily objects can provide him no enjoyment, he seeks to acquire sovereignty over human minds by making the first ancestors of all mankind desert their Sovereign and become dependent on him. In this way, he succeeds in establishing himself as the supreme owner of all the goods of the earth, that is, as the **Prince of this World**. Here, then, in defiance of the good principle, a kingdom of evil was established, to which all humans naturally descending from Adam became subject—and indeed with their own consent, because the **illusion** <insert>[108]</insert> of the goods of this world drew their gaze away from the abyss of ruin for which they were being reserved.

To be sure, the good principle protected its legal claim to sovereignty over mankind by <margin>[102]</margin> establishing a form of government purely arranged for the public, exclusive worship of its name (in the **Jewish theocracy** <note>Theocracy: a system of government in which priests rule in the name of God; here, Kant refers to the ancient Israelite state.</note>). These were thus merely **civil laws**, where the internal **moral disposition** <term>moral disposition: "moralische Gesinnung," the internal motivation or "heart" behind an action, which Kant distinguishes from mere outward obedience to law</term> was not taken into consideration at all. Consequently, this arrangement did no essential damage to the kingdom of darkness, but served only to keep the inextinguishable right of the first owner always in remembrance.

# Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part II.

<margin>[109]</margin>
The world-wise <note>original: "Weltweisen"; Kant uses this term for philosophers who seek practical wisdom for life.</note>, who had gradually gained influence over this state of affairs and brought a great part of the world to reflection—and who were thus ripe for a **revolution**—suddenly saw a person appear. This person’s wisdom was even purer than that of previous philosophers, appearing as if it had come down from heaven. He announced himself, through his teachings and his example, as a true human being, but also as a messenger of such a heavenly origin that he was not included in the contract\*) which the rest of the human race (through their representative, the first **forefather**) had entered into with the evil principle.

<margin>[109]</margin>
\*) To conceive of a person free from the innate tendency toward evil as being born of a **virgin mother** is an idea of reason that accommodates an intuitive moral instinct—one that is difficult to explain and yet impossible to deny. This is because we view natural procreation as something we should *be ashamed of*, since it cannot happen without the sensory lust of both parties. To us, this seems to bring the dignity of humanity into far too close a kinship with the common animal species—a view which was certainly the true cause of the supposed holiness of the **monastic state**. It strikes us as something immoral, incompatible with the perfection of a human being, yet grafted into his nature and thus inherited by his descendants as an evil disposition. To this dark (on one side merely sensory, but on the other moral and thus intellectual) conception, the idea of a (virgin) birth—independent of sexual union and producing a child afflicted by no

moral fault—is quite appropriate. However, this is not without theoretical difficulty (though it is not at all necessary to determine anything about this for practical moral purposes). Therefore, to avoid this consequence, one would have to adopt the system of the **pre-existence of germs** in the parents. Furthermore, one could not use the theory of **involvement**<sup>a)</sup> <note>original: "Einwickelung", also known as "encapsulation" or "preformationism"—the theory that all future generations are folded inside the first ancestor.</note> in the female part (because that would not avoid the consequence), but only in the male part—specifically, not that of the *eggs* <note>original: "ovulorum"</note> but of the *spermatozoa* <note>original: "animalculorum spermaticorum", or "spermatic animalcules".</note>. ### **General Remark.**

If a moral religion (which is to be established not in statutes and observances, but in the **disposition of the heart** <term>disposition: "Gesinnung," the internal orientation of the will toward moral duty</term> toward the observation of all human duties as divine commands) is to be founded, then all miracles that history links with its introduction must eventually make belief in miracles themselves dispensable; for it reveals a blameworthy degree of moral unbelief when one refuses to grant sufficient authority to the commands of duty, as they are originally written into the human heart <margin>10</margin> through **reason**, unless they are further authenticated by miracles: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you will not believe” <note>original: "wenn ihr nicht Zeichen und Wunder seht, so glaubt ihr nicht"; a reference to the Gospel of John 4:48</note>. Now, it is quite consistent with the common way of human thinking that when a religion of mere cult and observances reaches its end, and in its place one founded *in spirit and in truth* (the moral disposition) is to be introduced, the introduction of the latter—even though it | does not strictly need it—is [117] still accompanied and, as it were, adorned in history with miracles. This serves to announce the termination of the former religion, which would have had no authority at all without miracles. Indeed, it may even be that in order to win over the followers of the former for the new **revolution** a) to gain them, the new is interpreted as the fulfillment of an older prototype of that which was the ultimate purpose of **providence** <term>providence: "Vorsehung," the idea of divine guidance in history</term> in the latter. Under such circumstances, it can be of no use to contest those stories or interpretations now, once the true religion is established <margin>30</margin> and can henceforth maintain itself through grounds of reason, even if it required such means to be introduced in its own time. One would have to assume that mere belief and the repeating of incomprehensible things (which anyone can do without becoming a better person or ever becoming one through it) is a way, or even the *only* way, to please God—a claim against which one must fight with all one's might. It may therefore be that the—

The latter, however, excites **concern** that one might lose confidence in those laws already assumed to be known. For if reason is deprived of the laws of experience, it is of no use at all in such an enchanted world—not even for the moral use of reason within it for the fulfillment of one's duty. **Section 2: On the Legal Claim of the Evil Principle. 101**

...no one can distinguish whether they should attribute these changes to themselves or to some other inscrutable cause. — Those whose power of judgment <note>German: "Urteilskraft," a central term in Kant's philosophy referring to the ability to think the particular as contained under the universal</note> is so tuned in this matter that they believe they cannot manage without miracles, think they can soften the offense that reason takes at them by assuming they only occur rarely. If they mean to say that this rarity is already contained in the concept of a miracle (because if such an event occurred commonly, it would not be declared a miracle at all), then one can at best grant them this sophistry—changing an objective question about what the thing *is* into a subjective one about what the *word* we use to denote it means—and ask again: how rarely? Perhaps once in a hundred years, or in ancient times, but now | <insert>[124]</insert> no longer at all? Here there is nothing determinable for us from the knowledge of the object (for that, by our own confession, is transcendent <note>German: "überschwenglich," meaning it goes beyond the limits of all possible human experience</note> for us), but only from the necessary maxims <note>A "maxim" is a personal rule or principle for acting or thinking</note> of the use of our reason: either to admit miracles as occurring daily (though hidden under the appearance of natural events) or never. In the latter case, we must use them as the basis for neither our rational explanations nor the measures of our actions. And since the former is not compatible with reason at all, nothing remains but to adopt the latter maxim; for this principle always remains merely a maxim of judgment, not a theoretical assertion.

No one can push the conceit of their insight so high as to want to declare decisively: that, for example, the most admirable preservation of species in the plant and animal kingdoms—since every new generation represents its original again every spring with all the internal perfection of its mechanism and (as in the plant kingdom) even all the otherwise so delicate beauty of color, without the otherwise destructive forces of inorganic nature in bad autumn and winter weather being able to harm its seeds in this regard—that, I say, this is a mere consequence of laws of nature, or whether instead a direct influence of the Creator is required for it every time. — But these are experiences; for us, they are therefore nothing other than effects of nature and should never be judged otherwise. For that is what the modesty of reason requires in its claims; to go beyond these boundaries, however, is presumption and immodesty in one's claims; although for the most part, in asserting miracles, one pretends to prove a humble <gloss>a)</gloss>, self-renouncing way of thinking.

---

a) Thus in Kant's manuscript (cf. Arnoldt, loc. cit., p. 387). The printing error of the 1st edition: "humiliating" <note>original: "demütigende"</note> has been carried over into all previous editions.

<summary>Kant argues that while we cannot prove miracles never happen, reason requires us to adopt a "maxim" of never relying on them for explanations or actions, as nature's regularities (like the preservation of species) must be treated as natural effects.</summary>

## The Victory of the Good Principle over the Evil

## Founding of a Kingdom of God on Earth.

The struggle that every morally well-disposed person must endure in this life—under the leadership of the good principle—against the temptations of the evil principle can, no matter how much they strive, grant them no greater advantage than liberation from the sovereignty of the latter. <margin>10</margin>That they are free, that they "are released from bondage under the law of sin, so as to live for righteousness," <note>original: "der Knechtschaft unter dem Sündengesetz entschlagen wird, um der Gerechtigkeit zu leben." # On the Victory of the Good Principle over the Evil.

...principle is, however, only to be achieved in this way: that he can <note>This completes the thought from the previous page regarding the individual's struggle.</note> only then get the upper hand over the evil that restlessly assails him.

One can call a union of human beings under mere laws of virtue, following the prescription of this idea, an **ethical** [130] and—insofar as these laws are public—an **ethic-civil** society (in contrast to a **juridico-civil** <note>Also known as a legal-civil society or a political state.</note> society), or an **ethical commonwealth**. This can exist in the midst of a political commonwealth and even consist of <margin>10</margin> all its members (indeed, without the political commonwealth as a foundation, it could not be brought about by humans at all). However, the former has a special and distinct principle of union (the <term>virtue<note>German: "Tugend." For Kant, virtue is the moral strength of a human being's will in obeying duty.</note></term>) and therefore also a form and constitution that differs essentially from that of the latter. Nevertheless, there is a certain analogy between the two, viewed as two types of commonwealths in general; in view of this, the former can also be called an **ethical state**—that is, a **kingdom of virtue** (of the good principle). <margin>20</margin> The idea of such a state has its well-founded **objective reality** in human reason (as a duty to unite into such a state), even if it could never be subjectively hoped from the good will of humans that they would ever<insert>a)</insert> decide to work together in concord toward this goal.

## Division One.

### Philosophical Representation of the Victory of the Good Principle under the Founding of a Kingdom of God on Earth.

->I.<-

->**Of the Ethical State of Nature.**<-

A legal-civil (political) state is the relationship of human beings to one another insofar as they stand together under public <term>laws of right<note>German: "Rechtsgesetze." These are laws governing external behavior and can be enforced by the state.</note></term> (which are, in their entirety, **coercive laws**).
An ethical-civil state is one in which they are united under similar non-coercive laws—that is, mere **laws of virtue**.
Just as the former is contrasted with the legal (though not always lawful), i.e., the juridical **state of nature**, the latter is distinguished from the **ethical state of nature**. In both, each individual gives themselves the law, and there is no external law to which they, along with all others, would recognize themselves as being subject.
<margin>20</margin> In both, each person is their own judge, and there is no public authority possessing the power to determine with legal force, according to laws, what each person's duty is in occurring cases, and to bring those duties into general practice.

<margin>[132]</margin> In an already existing political commonwealth, all political citizens, as such, nonetheless find themselves in the **ethical state of nature** and are entitled to remain within it; for that the former [the political state] should compel its citizens to enter into an ethical commonwealth would be a contradiction in terms <note>original: "in adjecto." A contradiction in the very definition of the words used, because one cannot be "forced" into a state defined by "freedom from force."</note>; because the latter already carries within its very concept freedom from coercion. It may well be the wish of every political...

<summary>Kant distinguishes between the political state (governed by enforceable laws) and the ethical state (governed by voluntary laws of virtue). He explains that even within a legal government, individuals remain in an "ethical state of nature" because the state cannot—and should not—force people to be virtuous.</summary>

### III.

## **The concept of an ethical commonwealth is the concept of a *people of God* under ethical *laws*.**

If an ethical commonwealth <term>ethisches gemeines Wesen: A community organized not by political force or legal threats, but by shared moral principles and internal virtue</term> is to come into being, then all individuals <margin>10</margin> must be subjected to a public legislation, and all laws that bind them must be capable of being viewed as commands of a common lawgiver. If the commonwealth to be founded were a *juridical* <note>In this context, "juridical" refers to a political or legal state (a "Rechtsstaat") where laws govern outward behavior rather than inner conviction.</note> one, then the multitude uniting into a whole would have to be the lawgiver (of the *constitutional laws*) itself, because legislation proceeds from the principle: to restrict the freedom of each to the conditions under which it can coexist with <margin>20</margin> everyone else’s freedom according to a universal law\*), and where the general will thus establishes a legal external compulsion. However, if the commonwealth is to be an ethical one, the people as such cannot be regarded as the lawgiver. For in such a commonwealth, all laws are essentially designed to promote the *morality* of actions (which is something <margin>[138]</margin> *internal*, and therefore cannot fall under public human laws), whereas the latter, which would constitute a juridical commonwealth, <margin>30</margin> are only designed for the *legality* of actions—the part that is visible to the eye—and not for the (internal) *morality*, which is the sole subject of discussion here. Therefore, it must be someone other than the people who could be named as the public lawgiver for an ethical commonwealth. Nevertheless, ethical laws cannot be regarded as originating merely from the will of this *superior being* <note>Referring to God as the moral legislator.</note> (as statutes which, perhaps, without

---

\*) This is the principle of all external right. <note>original: "Prinzip alles äußeren Rechts." This is a foundational concept in Kant's legal philosophy, emphasizing that laws exist to ensure the maximum amount of freedom for everyone simultaneously.</note>

<summary>Kant argues that while a political state is governed by the people's collective will to ensure external freedom, an ethical commonwealth (a "People of God") requires a divine lawgiver because its laws govern internal morality, which no human authority can judge or enforce.</summary>

We could also conceive of a People of God according to **statutory** laws—those, namely,
<margin>20</margin>in whose observance the focus is not on **morality**, but merely on the **legality** of actions. This would be a **juridical commonwealth**, of which God would indeed be the legislator (consequently, the **constitution** of the same would be a **theocracy**), but in which men, acting as **priests** who receive his commands directly from him, would lead an **aristocratic government**. ---

\*) As soon as something is recognized as a duty, even if it were [138] a duty imposed through the mere arbitrary will of a human legislator, it is nonetheless at the same time a divine command to obey it. One cannot, of course, call statutory civil laws "divine commands," but if they are legitimate, then the observation of them is at the same time a divine command. The sentence: <note>original: "man muß Gott mehr gehorchen als den Menschen"</note> "**one must obey God more than men**" means only that if the latter command something that is evil in itself (directly contrary to the moral law), they may not and should not be | obeyed. Conversely, however, if [139] a supposedly divine statutory law is set in opposition to a political civil law that is not in itself immoral, there is reason to regard the former as spurious, because it contradicts a clear duty; moreover, that it is truly a divine command can never be sufficiently authenticated through empirical markers to justify transgressing an otherwise existing duty on its account.

->Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part III.<-

But such a <term>constitution: The foundational structure or system of laws for a community.</term>, the existence and form of which rest entirely on historical grounds, is not the one which constitutes the task of pure <term>moral-legislative reason: The human capacity to determine universal moral laws through logic and ethics alone, independent of historical tradition.</term>, the solution to which is our sole concern here. In the historical section, it will be considered as an institution based on political-civil laws whose legislator, although God, is nonetheless external; here, however, we are concerned only with a constitution whose legislation is purely internal—a **republic under laws of virtue**, that is, a **People of God** who are "zealous for good works." <note>original: "das fleißig wäre zu guten Werken" – A reference to the New Testament, Titus 2:14.</note>

To such a People of God, one can oppose the idea of a **horde of the evil principle**, as a union of those who take its side for the spread of evil. This principle is intent on preventing that former moral union from coming to pass; although here, too, the principle that attacks our virtuous dispositions actually lies within ourselves and is only figuratively represented as an external power.

## IV.
### The Idea of a People of God can (under human arrangement) only be carried out in the form of a Church.

<margin>[141]</margin> The sublime, never fully attainable idea of an <term>ethical commonwealth: A moral community where everyone acts out of duty and virtue rather than being forced by laws or police.</term> is greatly diminished under human hands. It becomes an institution which, at most, is capable only of representing the pure form of such a commonwealth, but which is very limited in the means of establishing such a whole, due to the conditions of <gloss>sensory</gloss> a) human nature. For how can one expect that something perfectly straight be fashioned from such **crooked timber**? <note>Kant’s famous metaphor "crooked timber of humanity" (aus so krummem Holze) suggests that human nature is fundamentally flawed and imperfect, making perfect justice or morality impossible to achieve in practice.</note>

To establish a moral People of God is therefore a work whose execution cannot be expected from humans, but only from God himself. Yet, for this reason, the human being is not permitted to remain idle in this undertaking; and providence—

### Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part III. ###

<margin>[143]</margin>
1. **Universality**, and consequently its numerical **unity**. The church must contain the inherent capacity for this: though it may be divided by differing opinions on minor matters, it must be built upon principles that necessarily lead to a universal union into a single church (and thus, avoid sectarian schism).

2. Its **quality**; that is,
<margin>10</margin>
**purity**. The union must be formed under no other than **moral motives**. (It must be purified from the absurdity of superstition and the madness of <term>religious fanaticism: Kant uses the word "Schwärmerei," referring to a state of delusional religious ecstasy or a claim to private, mystical "inner light" that ignores reason.</term>).

3. The **relation** under the principle of **freedom**. This applies to both the internal relationship of its members to one another and the external relationship of the church to political power; both must exist within a **free state**. (Thus, it is neither a hierarchy nor "illuminatism"—a kind of democracy based on private inspirations, which can differ from person to person according to their own whims).

<margin>[144]</margin>
4. Its **modality**, specifically the **unchangeability** of its constitution. This includes the provision that while administrative arrangements may be changed according to time and circumstances, the constitution itself must contain secure principles <term>a priori: Knowledge that is independent of experience; here, it refers to principles that are logically necessary and universal.</term> (grounded in the very idea of its purpose).
<margin>30</margin>
(Thus, it exists under original laws, publicly established as a code of conduct, rather than under arbitrary <gloss>creeds or symbols</gloss> which, lacking authenticity, are merely accidental, subject to contradiction, and changeable.)

An ethical commonwealth viewed as a Church—that is, as a mere representative of a **Kingdom of God**—does not actually have a constitution similar to a political one. Its structure is neither monarchical (under a Pope or Patriarch), nor aristocratic (under bishops and prelates),
<margin>40</margin>
nor democratic (as seen with sectarian "illuminati"). It could best be compared to a household (family) under a common, although...

For statutory legislation (which presupposes a revelation) can only be regarded as contingent—something that has not reached, or cannot reach, every human being—and therefore as not <margin>30</margin> binding upon humanity in general. # Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part III.

However, if we consider ourselves bound to act not simply as human beings, but also as **citizens** in a divine state on earth, and to work toward the existence of such a union under the name of a Church, then the question of how God wishes to be honored in a Church (as a congregation of God) does not seem answerable through mere reason alone. Instead, it seems to require a <term>statutory legislation</term> <note>laws established by decree or tradition rather than discovered by reason</note> made known to us only through revelation; it requires, therefore, a historical faith which, <margin>10</margin> in contrast to pure religious faith, may be called <term>ecclesiastical faith</term>. For in the case of the former <note>pure religious faith</note>, what matters is simply the substance of the worship of God—namely, the observation of all duties as His commands, performed with a moral disposition. A Church, however, as a union of many people under such dispositions into a moral commonwealth, requires a public obligation—a certain ecclesiastical form based on empirical conditions. This form is <margin>20</margin> inherently contingent and diverse, and therefore cannot be recognized as a duty without divine **statutory laws**. <margin>[150]</margin> | But the task of determining this form must not immediately be regarded as the business of the Divine Legislator. Rather, one may reasonably assume that the divine will is this: that we ourselves carry out the <term>idea of reason</term> <note>a concept produced by the mind that serves as a goal or standard, even if it cannot be fully realized in experience</note> of such a commonwealth. And though humans may have attempted many forms of a Church with unsuccessful results, they should nonetheless never cease to strive toward this goal, making new attempts where necessary and avoiding the mistakes of previous ones as much as possible. This task, which is simultaneously a duty for them, is left entirely to them. There is, therefore, no reason to regard the laws for the foundation and form of any Church as directly **divine and statutory**. On the contrary, it is a presumption to pass them off as such in order to exempt oneself from the effort of further improving the church's form; or it is even a <term>usurpation</term> <note>the wrongful taking of someone else's power</note> of higher authority,<sup>a)</sup> used to impose a yoke upon the multitude through ecclesiastical ordinances under the pretext of divine <margin>40</margin> **authority**.

Now, a few more things that attach to this concept of a faith based on revelation.
There is only **one** (true) religion; but there can be many kinds of **faith**. — One can add that in the many various churches, separated from one another because of the diversity of their kinds of faith, one and the same true religion can nevertheless be <margin>20</margin> found.
It is therefore more proper (as it is also more common in actual usage) to say: this person is of this or that (**Jewish, Mohammedan, Christian, Catholic, Lutheran**) faith, rather than: he is of this or that religion. The latter expression should properly not even be used in addressing the general public (in catechisms and sermons); for it is too learned and unintelligible for them<gloss>b)</gloss>, just as modern languages provide no <margin>30</margin> synonymous word for it. The common man always understands it to mean his **church faith**, which is perceptible to his senses, whereas **religion** is hidden within and depends on **moral dispositions**. [155]

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the end of the previous section where the author distinguished between a single "true religion" and the various "kinds of faith" (churches) that act as its vehicle. Here, the author examines how institutionalized "church faith" leads to labels like "heretic" and "unbeliever."</meta>

### Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Piece III.

One grants most people too much honor by saying of them that they profess this or that religion; for they know none and desire none. A **statutory church faith** <note>original: "statutarische Kirchenglaube"; this refers to a faith based on the specific rules, rituals, and historical traditions of an institution rather than universal moral principles</note> is all they understand by this word. Furthermore, the so-called religious disputes, which have so often shaken the world and spattered it with blood, have never been anything other than bickering over church faith. The oppressed person did not actually complain that he was being hindered from adhering to his **religion** <margin>10</margin> (for no external force can do that), but rather that he was not permitted to follow his **church faith** publicly.

Now, when a church presents itself—as usually happens—as the only universal one (even though it is based on a particular **faith of revelation** <note>original: "Offenbarungsglaube"</note>, which, being historical, can never be required of everyone), then anyone who does not recognize its (particular) church faith is called an **unbeliever** <term>unbeliever: "Ungläubiger", usually referring to someone completely outside the faith tradition</term> and is hated with all one's heart. One who deviates from it only in part (in non-essentials) is called <margin>20</margin> **heterodox** <note>original: "Irrgläubiger"</note> and is avoided as if they were contagious. ### VI.

### **Church faith has pure religious faith as its highest interpreter.**

We have noted that a church lacks the most important hallmark of its truth—namely, a legitimate claim to universality—if it founds itself upon a <margin>20</margin> **faith of revelation** <term>faith of revelation: "Offenbarungsglaube"; a belief system based on historical events or scriptures revealed at a specific time, rather than on universal logic</term>. Nevertheless, because of the natural human need to demand something sensory and tangible—some confirmation from experience and the like—for the highest concepts and grounds of reason <margin>30</margin> (which must indeed be taken into account when one intends to introduce a faith universally), some historical church faith, which one usually finds already at hand, must be utilized.

# Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part III.

<margin>[167]</margin>
### VII.

### **The gradual transition of ecclesiastical faith to the exclusive sovereignty of pure religious faith is the approach of the Kingdom of God.**

The hallmark of the true church is its **universality**; the characteristic of this universality, in turn, is its **necessity** and its **determinability** in only a single possible way. Now, historical faith (which is grounded on revelation as an experience) has only <margin>10</margin> particular validity—namely, for those who have been reached by the history upon which it rests. Like all empirical knowledge, it does not contain within itself the consciousness that the object believed in *must* be so and not otherwise, but only that it *is* so; consequently, it simultaneously contains the consciousness of its own contingency <note>In philosophy, "contingency" refers to something that happens to be true but could have been otherwise, unlike "necessity," which must be true.</note>. Thus, while historical faith may suffice for an ecclesiastical faith <term>ecclesiastical faith (Kirchenglaube): the specific beliefs, scriptures, and rituals of a particular religious institution</term> (of which there can be several), only a) pure religious faith, which is grounded entirely on reason, can be recognized as necessary, and therefore as the only one that distinguishes the <margin>20</margin> true church. — Therefore, even if (in accordance with the unavoidable limitation of human reason) a historical faith affects pure religion as a guiding means, it must do so with the consciousness that it is merely such b) a means. If this ecclesiastical faith carries with it a principle of continually approaching <margin>[168]</margin> pure religious faith, in order finally to be able to dispense with | that guiding means, then such a church can always be called the true one. However, since conflict over historical dogmas can never be avoided, it can only be called the **church militant** <note>original: "streitende Kirche" (ecclesia militans); a traditional term for the church on earth still struggling against sin and disagreement.</note>; <margin>30</margin> yet it remains with the prospect of finally developing into the unchangeable and all-unifying **church triumphant** <note>original: "triumphierende Kirche" (ecclesia triumphans); the theological state of the church when it has achieved final victory and peace.</note>! The faith of every individual who possesses the moral receptivity (**worthiness**) to be eternally blessed is called **saving** faith. This faith can also only be one; despite all the diversity of ecclesiastical faiths, it can be found in each one in which, by relating itself to its goal—pure religious faith—it [is] practical...

Saving faith contains two conditions for its hope of salvation: the first concerns what man himself *cannot* do—namely, to legally undo his past actions (before a divine judge) [169]; the second concerns what he himself *can and should* do—namely, to walk in a new life consistent with his duty. <margin>20</margin> The first is the faith in a satisfaction <term>satisfaction (Genugtuung): the theological idea that a debt or sin must be "paid for" to restore a relationship with God</term> (payment for one's guilt, redemption, reconciliation with God); the second is the faith that one can become well-pleasing to God through a future good <gloss>b) "good" is missing in the 1st edition.</gloss> conduct of life.

— These two conditions constitute only one faith and necessarily belong together. However, one cannot perceive the necessity of this connection unless one assumes that one can be <margin>(171)</margin> derived from the other. This means either that the faith in the acquittal from the guilt resting upon us produces the good conduct of life, or that the truthful and active <margin>30</margin> disposition of a good conduct of life, to be led at all times, produces the faith in that acquittal according to the law of morally effective causes.

Here, a remarkable antinomy <term>antinomy: a contradiction between two principles that both seem equally logical or necessary</term> of human reason with itself reveals itself. The resolution of this antinomy—or if that should not be possible, at least its settlement—is the only way to determine whether a historical (ecclesiastical) faith must always be added to pure religious faith as an essential part of saving faith.

<summary>Kant distinguishes between a "servile" faith based on ritual and a "saving" faith based on moral disposition, identifying a tension between the need for atonement for past sins and the requirement for future moral improvement.</summary>
<keywords>saving faith, moral disposition, satisfaction, atonement, conduct of life, antinomy of reason, ecclesiastical faith</keywords>

**Necessity of the second principle b) practically and specifically purely moral;** we certainly cannot hope to share in the appropriation of even a **foreign, satisfying merit** <note>original: "fremden genugtuenden Verdienstes"—referring to the merit of Christ which "satisfies" the debt of sin</note> and thus share in salvation, in any other way than by qualifying ourselves for it through our own striving to fulfill every human duty. For since the latter command <note>the moral duty</note> is unconditional, it is also necessary that man should make it the **maxim** <term>maxim (Maxime): a subjective principle of action; a rule a person sets for themselves</term> of his faith—namely, that he begins with the improvement of his life as the supreme condition under which alone a saving faith can exist.
Ecclesiastical faith, as a historical faith, rightly begins with the former <note>faith in atonement</note>; but since it only contains the **vehicle** for pure religious faith (in which the actual purpose lies), then that which is the condition in the latter as a practical faith—namely, the maxim of action—must make the beginning. The maxim of knowledge or theoretical faith should only effect the strengthening and completion of the former.
Here it can also be noted that according to the
<margin>[174]</margin> first principle, faith (namely, faith in a **vicarious satisfaction** <term>vicarious satisfaction (stellvertretende Genugtuung): the doctrine that Christ’s suffering pays the penalty for human sin</term>) would be reckoned to man as a duty, whereas the faith of a good life-path, as worked through a higher influence, would be reckoned to him as **grace** <term>grace (Gnade): divine assistance given to humans that they have not earned</term>. — According to the second principle, however, it is the other way around. For according to this, the good life-path, as the supreme condition of grace, is an unconditional duty, whereas the higher satisfaction is a mere matter of grace. — The former is often (and not without reason) accused of **religious superstition**, which knows how to reconcile a punishable life-path with religion; the latter is accused of **naturalistic unbelief**, which combines an otherwise perhaps even exemplary life-path with indifference or even opposition toward all revelation. — That would be to **cut the knot** <note>a reference to the Gordian Knot; solving a complex problem by a single bold action</note> (through a practical maxim) instead of untying it (theoretically)—

### Philosophical Representation of the Founding of a Kingdom of God. VII. 137

By contrast, 
<margin>10</margin>
faith in the very same archetype in its appearance (in the **God-man**), as an **empirical (historical) faith**, is not the same as the principle of a good way of life (which must be entirely rational), and it would be something quite different to want to start from such a faith*) and derive a good way of life from it. To this extent, there would indeed be a conflict between the two aforementioned propositions. But in the appearance of the God-man, it is not that which is perceptible to the senses or can be known through experience, but rather 
<margin>20</margin>
the **archetype** residing in our reason—which we attribute to the appearance (because, as far as can be perceived from his example, he is found to be in accordance with it)—that is actually the object of **saving faith**; and such a faith is one and the same as the principle of a way of life pleasing to God. — Therefore, we do not have here two inherently different principles where choosing one or the other would require taking opposite paths. Rather, it is only one and the same **practical idea** from which we proceed: once, insofar as it 
<margin>30</margin>
represents the archetype as residing in God and proceeding from Him; another time, as residing in us; but in both cases, insofar as it represents the archetype as the **standard** for our way of life. Thus, the **antinomy** <term>antinomy (Antinomie): a logical contradiction between two principles that both seem equally valid</term> is only apparent; because, through a misunderstanding, it regards the very same practical idea—just taken in different relations—as two different principles. — If, however,

It is here as it is with the political idea of **constitutional law**, insofar as it is simultaneously meant to be related to a universal and powerful **international law** (the law of nations). Experience denies us all hope for this. <margin>[183]</margin> There seems to be a tendency | placed within the human race (perhaps intentionally) that every single state, when things go according to its wishes, strives to subject every other and to establish a **universal monarchy**; yet when it has reached a certain size, it eventually splits apart of its own accord into smaller states. Likewise, every church harbors the proud claim of becoming universal; but as soon as it has spread and becomes dominant, a principle of dissolution and separation into various sects soon appears.

The premature—and therefore harmful (because it arrives before humans have become morally better)—melting together of states is prevented primarily by two powerfully acting causes, namely: differences of **languages** and differences of **religions**. This is the case if we are permitted to assume an intention of **Providence** <note>Kant views "Providence" as a guiding force in history that uses human conflict or natural differences to achieve progress toward a higher moral goal.</note> here. <gloss>d) The last paragraph is an addition of the 2nd edition.</gloss>

### Historical Presentation of the Gradual Establishment of the Rule of the Good Principle on Earth.

Regarding religion on earth (in the narrowest sense of the word), one cannot demand a **universal history** <meta>[184]</meta> of the human race; for religion, being grounded in pure **moral faith** <term>moral faith (moralischer Glaube): a belief in God and immortality based on our internal moral needs and the requirements of duty, rather than external evidence</term>, is not a public state of affairs. Rather, each individual can only be aware for themselves of the progress they have made in it. 
<margin>10</margin> It is therefore **ecclesiastical faith** <term>ecclesiastical faith (Kirchenglaube): the specific dogmas, rituals, and organizational structures of an institutional church</term> alone from which one can expect a general historical presentation. This is done by comparing its various and changing forms with the one, unchangeable, pure **religious faith**. From the moment the former publicly acknowledges its dependence on the restrictive conditions of the latter and the necessity of harmonizing with it, the universal Church begins to form itself into an **ethical state of God** <term>ethical state of God (ethischer Staat Gottes): a "Kingdom of God" on earth where people are united under moral laws rather than through political coercion</term>. It then begins to progress toward its completion according to a fixed principle that is 
<margin>20</margin> one and the same for all people and all times. — One can foresee that this history will be nothing but the narrative of the constant struggle between the **faith of divine service** <note>original: "gottesdienstlichen... Humans are constantly inclined to place the former—as a **historical faith**—at the top, whereas the latter has never given up its claim to the priority it deserves as the only faith that truly improves the soul, and it will certainly assert that claim in the end.

...because the distinction between rational faith <term>rational faith (Vernunftglauben): a belief based on universal moral principles that any person can arrive at through their own reason</term> and historical faith <term>historical faith (Geschichtsglauben): a belief based on specific historical revelations, scriptures, or traditions unique to a particular group</term> has already been publicly established and its resolution has been **made** the greatest moral concern; for otherwise, the history of the statutes<sup>a)</sup> of various peoples—whose faiths have no connection with one another—provides no unity for the Church. <margin>10</margin> people that differed significantly from the previously dominant one, even if the latter carried within itself the inducing causes for the generation of the new one. # Historical Representation of the Foundation of a Kingdom of God.

...had given an example conforming to the **archetype** <term>Urbild: an original model or ideal pattern of moral perfection</term> of a humanity alone pleasing to God, he is represented [192] as returning [193] again to the heaven from which he had come. However, since this teaching belongs merely to a moral, soul-improving faith, it can dispense with all such proofs of its truth. Nevertheless, in a holy book, this teaching is still accompanied by miracles and mysteries, the announcement of which is itself again a miracle and requires a historical faith, which can only be documented through **scholarship** <term>Gelehrsamkeit: formal academic learning or erudition</term> and secured in its meaning and sense.

Now, at the time of that **revolution** <note>Kant uses "revolution" here to describe the profound shift from traditional Jewish law to the moral teachings of Christianity.</note> among the people who ruled the Jews and were widespread even in their very seat (the Roman people), there was already a **learned public** <term>gelehrtes Publikum: a literate, critical community of scholars, historians, and thinkers</term>. From this public, the history of that time—at least regarding political events—has been handed down to us through an uninterrupted series of writers. Furthermore, this Roman people, even if they cared little about the religious beliefs of their <margin>[195]</margin> non-Roman subjects <note>original: "ihrer."
