<margin>20</margin> Yet, as contemporaries, these writers mentioned nothing of these miracles, nor of the revolution that nonetheless took place publicly and which the Christians brought about (in respect to religion) in the people subjected to Rome. Only late, after more than a generation, did they conduct any inquiry into the nature of this change in faith, which had remained unknown to them until then (even though it had not occurred without public commotion). However, they conducted no investigation into the history of its | first beginning in order to seek it out in their own annals. 

From that point until the time when Christianity itself constituted a learned public, its history is therefore obscure. Thus, it remains unknown to us what effect its teaching had on the **morality** of its fellow believers—whether the first Christians were truly morally improved people or merely people of the ordinary sort. 

<margin>30</margin> But since the time Christianity itself became a learned public, or at least entered into the general one, its history—regarding the beneficial effect one can rightly expect from a **moral religion**—by no means serves as a recommendation for it.

<header>Historical Presentation of the Founding of a Kingdom of God. 151</header>

...a hierarchy forced upon free men, the terrible voice of **orthodoxy** <term>Rechtgläubigkeit: strict adherence to established church dogmas</term> rose from the mouths of arrogant, self-appointed **interpreters of Scripture** and split the Christian world into embittered factions over religious opinions (about which, unless one declares pure reason to be the interpreter, no universal agreement can ever be achieved); ᵃ) how both Christian parts of the world— <margin>20</margin> much like plants and animals which, nearing their dissolution through disease, attract destructive insects to finish them off—were attacked by barbarians; how in the latter [the West], that spiritual head ruled and disciplined kings like children with the magic wand of his threatened excommunication, inciting them to foreign wars that depopulated another part of the world (the **Crusades**), to feuds among one another, to the rebellion of subjects against their authorities, and to bloodthirsty hatred against fellow members of one and the same general <margin>30</margin> so-called Christianity who held different views; how the root of this discord, which even now is only kept from violent outbreaks by political interest, lies hidden in the principle of a despotically commanding **church faith** <insert>[197]</insert> and still gives cause to fear scenes similar to those:—this history of Christianity (which, insofar as it was to be built upon a historical faith, could not have turned out otherwise), if one grasps it as a single picture at a glance, might well justify the exclamation: *so great is the evil that religion could prompt!* <margin>40</margin> <note>original: "tantum religio [potuit suadere malorum]" — a famous line from the Roman poet Lucretius criticizing the cruelties committed in the name of religion.</note>

<header>Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part III. 152</header>

*...could religion prompt such great evils!* <note>original Latin: *potuit suadere malorum!* from Lucretius, *De rerum natura* I, 101</note> [to so much mischief could religion give occasion] <margin>a)</margin>, if it were not clearly enough apparent from the founding of the same that its true, first intention was none other than to introduce a **pure religious faith**, about which there can be no conflicting opinions; all that turmoil, however, by which the human race was disrupted and is still divided, arises solely from a tendency of human nature:

...it is remarkable that the worshippers of the former (the Jews) have still preserved themselves as such, although scattered throughout the world, whereas the faith of other religious associates usually melted away into the faith of the people among whom they were scattered. This phenomenon seems so wondrous to many that they judge it as not being possible according to the course of nature, but as an extraordinary arrangement for a special divine purpose. — But a people who have a written religion (holy books) never melt away into a faith with those who (like the Roman Empire — which was then the entire civilized world) have no such thing, but merely customs; rather, sooner or later, they make proselytes <term>Proselyte: a person who has converted from one religion or belief to another</term>. Thus the Parsis, followers of the religion of Zoroaster, have preserved their faith until now, despite their dispersion; because their **Desturs** <gloss>b)</gloss> <note>original: "Desturs"; high-ranking Zoroastrian priests</note> had the **Zendavesta** <note>original: "Zendavesta"; the primary collection of religious texts of Zoroastrianism</note>. What the Jews alone would nevertheless not have achieved, the Christian and later the Mohammedan religion did, especially the former; because they presuppose the Jewish faith and the holy books belonging to it (even though the latter [Islam] declares them to be corrupted). For the Jews could always find their old documents again among the Christians who had branched out from them, whenever, during their wanderings, the skill to read them and therefore the desire to [possess them]...

But <margin>20</margin> this very freedom is also the only thing which, when applied to the ultimate object of practical reason—the realization of the idea of the moral end-goal <note>original: "Endzweck"; the final purpose or highest good</note>—inevitably leads us to holy mysteries.*)

But it is nonetheless no mystery; rather, it can be made manifest to everyone because its **law** is sufficiently known. If Newton represents it as if it were the divine omnipresence in appearance <note>original: "omnipraesentia phaenomenon"</note>, this is not an attempt to explain it (for <margin>[210]</margin> the existence of God in space contains a contradiction), but rather a sublime analogy in which the focus is merely on the union of bodily beings into a world-whole, by placing an incorporeal cause beneath it; and so it would also fare with the attempt to understand the independent principle of the union of rational world-beings in an ethical state <note>original: "ethischen Staat"; a moral community or "Kingdom of Virtue" where members are governed by laws of virtue rather than legal coercion</note> and to explain the latter from it. <meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of "mysteries" within religion. Following the discussion on how freedom itself is a mystery of the human will, Kant now examines the "holy mysteries" regarding God’s role in human morality and the "highest good."</meta>

# General Note (the “Mysteries”).

Because a human being cannot, by his own power, realize the idea of the **highest good** <note>original: "höchsten Gutes"; the Kantian ideal where human virtue and happiness are perfectly joined</note>—which is inseparably bound to a pure **moral disposition** <note>original: "moralische Gesinnung"; one's inner moral attitude or orientation</note> (not only in terms of the happiness belonging to it, but also the necessary union of all people toward that total end)—and yet he finds within himself the duty to work toward it, he finds himself drawn to believe in the cooperation or arrangement of a **moral ruler of the world**, through whom alone this end is possible. And now, there opens before him the abyss of a **mystery** <meta>line 10</meta> regarding what God does in this matter: whether anything at all is to be attributed to Him, [211] and what | specifically is to be attributed to Him (God); meanwhile, the human being recognizes nothing else in every duty than what he himself must do in order to be worthy of that supplementation which is unknown, or at least incomprehensible, to him.

This idea of a moral ruler of the world is a task for our **practical reason** <note>the capacity of a rational being to act according to moral principles rather than just instincts</note>. It is not so much a matter for us to know what God is in himself (**his nature**)<sup>a)</sup>, but rather what he is for us as **moral** <meta>line 20</meta> **beings**; although for the sake of this relationship, we must think and assume the divine nature to be of such a kind as is required, in all the perfection necessary for this relationship, for the execution of his will.

---

# Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part III.

...is necessary (for example, as an unchangeable, omniscient, omnipotent, etc., being) and without this relationship we can recognize nothing in him.

According to this need of **practical reason** <note>the capacity of a rational being to act according to moral principles rather than just instincts</note>, the universal true **religious faith** is the belief in God: 
1) as the **omnipotent creator** of heaven and earth—that is, morally as a **holy legislator**; 
2) as the **preserver** of the human race, its **benevolent ruler** and **moral provider**; 
<margin>10</margin> 3) as the **administrator** of his own holy laws—that is, as a **just judge**.

This faith actually contains no mystery, because it merely expresses the moral relationship of God to the human race; it also offers itself to all human reason of its own accord and is therefore found in the religion of most civilized peoples.*)
<margin>[212]</margin> It lies | in the concept of a people as a **commonwealth** <note>original: "gemeinen Wesen"; a community of people organized under shared laws</note>, in which such a **threefold supreme power** (**authority** <note>original: "pouvoir"</note>) must always be thought of, only that this 
<margin>20</margin> is here presented as **ethical**; hence this threefold quality of the moral head of the human race...

This seems to indicate that humanity itself, conscious of its own limitation and frailty, will pronounce the verdict in this selection; which is a **goodness** <note>original: "Gütigkeit"; or benevolence/mercy</note> that nevertheless does not detract from **justice**. — On the other hand, the judge of men in his **divinity**—that is, as <gloss>a)</gloss> he speaks to our conscience according to the holy law recognized by us and our own accountability—can be presented <gloss>b)</gloss> (the **Holy Spirit**), and thought of only as judging according to the rigor of the law. *) One cannot easily state the reason why so many [212] ancient peoples agreed on this idea <note>the idea of a Trinity or divine triad</note>, if it is not that it lies within universal human reason whenever one wishes to conceive of the governance of a people and (by analogy) the governance of the world. # Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part III.

...gracious, and thus indulgent <note>original: "nachsichtlich (indulgent)"</note> toward human weakness, nor as a despot who commands solely by his own unlimited right. We must not imagine his laws as **arbitrary** ones—having no connection to our own concepts of morality—but rather as laws directed toward the **holiness** of the human being. Second, his goodness must not be placed in an unconditional benevolence toward his creatures; instead, we must understand that he looks first to their moral character <note>the inner state by which they can be pleasing to him</note> and only then completes what is lacking in their own ability to satisfy this condition. Third, his justice cannot be imagined as "kind" or "placable" <note>original: "abbittlich"; the idea that God can be talked out of justice through prayer</note> (which would be a contradiction). Even less can it be seen as the exercise of the Lawgiver's absolute holiness (in the face of which no human is righteous). Rather, justice must be seen as the limitation of his goodness; it is the requirement that humans must live in harmony with the holy law as far as they, as "children of men," are able to meet its demands.

In a word: God wishes to be served in a threefold, specifically distinct moral quality. To describe these as the different **personalities** (not physical, but moral) of one and the same Being is a fitting expression. This symbol of faith <note>the Trinity</note> simultaneously expresses the whole of pure moral religion. Without this distinction, human nature tends to imagine the Godhead as if it were a human ruler (because in human government, these three qualities are usually not separated, but often mixed or confused). Without this moral framework, faith risks degenerating into an **anthropomorphic faith of servitude** <note>original: "anthropomorphistischen Fronglauben"; a "Fronglaube" is a religion based on fear or forced labor, like a serf's duty to a lord</note>.

<margin>[215], 40</margin>

As such, it would be beyond the capacity of human understanding to grasp, even through revelation. To believe in it as an expansion of our theoretical knowledge of the divine nature would only be the profession of a...

# General Note (The "Mysteries")

...be an entirely unintelligible and—if people believe they understand it—an anthropomorphic <term>Anthropomorphism: the habit of imagining God as having human form or human emotions</term> symbol of a church faith. From such a symbol, not the slightest bit of moral improvement would be achieved. — Only that which can be understood and seen quite well in a **practical** <term>Practical: in philosophy, this refers to action and ethics—what we *ought* to do—rather than just abstract theory</term> sense, but which (in terms of defining the nature of the object in itself) exceeds all our theoretical concepts, is a **mystery** (in one sense) and yet can (in another sense) be **revealed**. Of this latter kind is the mystery mentioned above, which can be divided into three mysteries revealed to us through our own reason:

1. The mystery of the **call** (of human beings as citizens of an **ethical state** <note>Often translated as "ethical commonwealth," this refers to a society governed by moral laws rather than just legal ones</note>). — We cannot imagine the universal, unconditional submission of a human being to divine legislation except insofar as we see ourselves, at the same time, as His creatures; just as God can only be seen as the author of all laws of nature because He is the creator of all things in nature. However, it is absolutely inconceivable to our reason how beings should be **created** for the **free use** of their powers. This is because, according to the principle of **causality** <note>The rule that every effect must have a prior cause</note>, we cannot assign any other inner ground for the actions of a being that is "produced" other than the ground placed in it by its cause. In that case, every action would be determined by an external cause | (the Creator), and the <insert>[216]</insert> being itself would therefore not be free. 

Thus, the divine, holy legislation—which concerns only free beings—cannot be reconciled by our reason with the concept of those beings having been "created." Instead, one must regard these beings as already <gloss>a) Kant: "already as"; corrected by Vorländer</gloss> **existing** free beings, who are determined not by a dependence on nature through their creation, but through a purely moral necessity possible only under laws of freedom—that is, a **call** to citizenship <gloss>b) 1st Edition: "guarantee"; Manuscript: "to [be] citizens"</gloss> in the divine state. Thus, the "call" to this purpose is morally quite clear, but for theoretical speculation, the possibility of such called beings remains an impenetrable mystery.

---

b) <note>A note on a printing variation: the first edition used a word meaning "guarantee," while the original manuscript used "citizens."</note>

Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part III.

**2. The Mystery of Satisfaction.** <term>Satisfaction: in a theological context, this refers to making amends or "atonement" for sins to satisfy divine justice</term> The human being, as we know him, is corrupt and by no means naturally in harmony with that holy law. Nevertheless, if the goodness of God has, as it were, called him into being—that is, invited him to a particular way of existing (as a member of the Kingdom of Heaven)—then he must also have a means to replace the lack of his own required fitness for this from the fullness of [God’s] own holiness. This, however, is contrary to **spontaneity** <term>Spontaneity: the capacity for an agent to act independently and initiate a sequence of events from themselves, rather than being moved by external causes</term> (which is presupposed in every moral <margin>10</margin> good or evil that a person may possess), according to which such a good must not originate from another, but from himself, if it is to be credited to him. — Therefore, as far as reason can see, no other person can represent him through the excess of their own good conduct and through their merit; or, if this is accepted, it can only be necessary to accept it for a **moral** <margin>[217]</margin> purpose; for theoretical reasoning <note>original: "Vernünfteln" – a term Kant uses for intellectual hair-splitting or "empty reasoning" that attempts to go beyond the limits of human understanding</note> it is an unreachable mystery.

<margin>20</margin> **3. The Mystery of Election.** <term>Election: the theological concept of predestination, where God chooses certain individuals for salvation</term> Even if that vicarious satisfaction is granted as possible, the moral-believing acceptance of it is a determination of the will toward the good, which already presupposes a God-pleasing disposition in the human being. However, due to his natural corruption, he cannot produce this disposition in himself. But the idea that a heavenly grace should work within him, granting this assistance <note>original: "diesen Beistand" – addition to the 2nd edition</note> not according to the merit of works, but through an unconditional decree to one human being <margin>30</margin> while denying it to another, and that one part of our race is chosen for salvation and the other for eternal rejection, again yields no concept of a divine justice. Instead, it would at best have to be attributed to a wisdom whose rule is absolutely a mystery to us.

Concerning these mysteries, insofar as they affect the moral life-history of every human being—namely, how it happens that a moral good or evil exists at all in the world, and (if the latter exists in everyone and at every <margin>40</margin> time) how the former can nonetheless arise from the latter...

<summary>Kant examines the "mysteries" of Atonement and Predestination, arguing that while they are incomprehensible to theoretical reason, they must be interpreted through a moral lens to be meaningful. He highlights the tension between the need for divine grace and the requirement that moral worth must come from an individual's own free choice.</summary>

An umpire or judge of a competition who awards the prize.</note>) <gloss>a)</gloss> who judges, the judgment of choice falls between **two** persons (or parties) competing for the prize (of salvation); but the one in the second quality (the actual judge) delivers the sentence **upon one and the same person** before a court of law (the **conscience**), which pronounces the legal verdict between the accuser and the advocate. <gloss>b)</gloss> — If it is now assumed that all humans indeed stand under the debt of sin, but that merit may nevertheless be credited to some of them, then the pronouncement of the **Judge out of love** <note>Kant distinguishes between a judge acting from pure legal justice and one acting from a disposition of love/mercy.</note> takes place; the lack of this merit would merely entail a **judgment of rejection**, from which the **judgment of condemnation** (insofar as the human then falls to the **Judge out of justice**) would be the inevitable consequence. — In such a way, in my opinion, the seemingly conflicting propositions can be reconciled: "The Son will come to judge the living and the dead," <note>A phrase from the Apostles' Creed.</note> and on the other hand: "God did not send him into the world that he should judge the world, but that the world through him might be saved" (Gospel of John 3:17). These can then stand in agreement with what is said elsewhere: "He who does not believe in the Son is **already judged**" 
<margin>[222]</margin> (verse 18), namely by that Spirit of whom it is said: "He will judge the world for the sake of sin and for the sake of righteousness." — The anxious care of such distinctions in the field of bare reason, for which they are actually employed here, could easily be regarded as useless and burdensome subtlety; and so it would be, if it were intended for the investigation of the divine nature. However, since humans in their religious affairs are constantly inclined to turn to divine goodness regarding their debts, yet at the same time cannot bypass His justice—and since a "kind judge" in one and the same person is a contradiction—one sees quite clearly that, even from a practical perspective, their concepts on this matter must be very wavering and inconsistent. Therefore, the correction and precise definition of these concepts is of great practical importance.

However, since we nonetheless stand at all times in the **service of God** while respecting all our duties (which we must collectively regard as divine commands), the pure religion of reason will have all well-meaning people as its servants (though without them being officials); they simply cannot be called servants of a *church* (specifically a visible one, which is the only thing being discussed here).

Meanwhile, because every church erected on statutory laws <note>Laws based on specific historical revelations or human decrees rather than universal reason.</note> can be the true one only insofar as it contains within itself a principle of constantly approaching pure rational faith (as that which, when practical, actually constitutes religion in every faith) and being able, in time, to dispense with the church-faith (according to what is historical in it), we can nonetheless posit a **service** (*cultus* <note>original: "cultus" – worship or ritual practice</note>) of the church in these laws and in the officials of the church founded upon them, insofar as these officials direct their teachings and arrangements at all times toward that ultimate end (a public religious faith).

If this person denies the
<margin>10</margin> reality of all supernatural divine revelation, he is called a **Naturalist**; if he admits its possibility but asserts that knowing it and accepting it as real is not a requirement for religion, [232] then he could be called a **pure Rationalist**; but if he considers faith in such revelation to be necessary for a universal religion, he could be called a **pure Supernaturalist** in matters of faith.

The Rationalist, by virtue of this title, must inherently remain within the limits of human insight. Therefore, he will never speak as a Naturalist would and deny either the internal possibility of a revelation in general, or the necessity of a revelation as a divine means for the introduction of the

For that which is permitted and commanded by the latter is certainly a duty; but whether something that is permitted in itself, yet recognizable to us only through divine revelation, is *actually* commanded by God, is (at least for the most part) highly uncertain.

# Part I: Concerning the Service of God in a Religion in General.

...the dispute only concerns the mutual claims of the pure **rationalist** and the **supernaturalist** in matters of faith, or what one or the other assumes as necessary and sufficient for the only true religion, or merely as incidental to it.

If religion is divided not according to its first origin and its internal possibility (since it is divided into **natural** and **revealed**), but merely according to its <gloss>a)</gloss> constitution, which makes it capable of outward communication, then it can be <margin>10</margin> of two kinds: either the **natural religion**, of which (once it exists) everyone can be convinced through their own reason, or a **learned religion**, [233] of which others can be convinced only by means of scholarship <note>In this context, "scholarship" refers to the specialized study of historical texts and traditions</note> (in and through which they must be guided). — This distinction is very important; for from the origin of a religion alone, one can infer nothing regarding its fitness or unfitness to be a universal religion for humanity, but one can certainly do so from its constitution—whether it is generally communicable or <margin>20</margin> not. The former quality, however, constitutes the essential character of that religion which is intended to bind every human being.

Accordingly, a religion can be natural and yet also revealed, if it is so constituted that human beings could and should have arrived at it themselves through the mere use of their **reason**, even though they might not have arrived at it so early or in such wide expansion as is required. Consequently, a revelation of it <margin>30</margin> at a certain time and at a certain place could be wise and very beneficial for the human race—provided that, once the religion introduced by this means is there and has been made publicly known, henceforth everyone can convince themselves of this truth by themselves and their own reason. In this case, the religion is **objectively** a natural one, although **subjectively** a revealed one; which is why the former name is actually more appropriate to it. For in the future | at any rate, it could be entirely [234]

I. Part, 1st Section: The Christian Religion as Natural Religion: 183

## Section I of the First Part.
### The Christian Religion as Natural Religion.

Natural religion—viewed as morality (in relation to the freedom of the individual), combined with the concept of that which can bring about its ultimate purpose (the *concept of God as the moral author of the world*), and related to a human existence long enough to fulfill this entire purpose (to immortality)—is a pure concept of practical reason. Despite its infinite depth, it <margin>30</margin> requires so little theoretical intellectual ability that every person can be practically convinced of it. At the very least, its *effect* can be expected of everyone as a duty. ## Section Two.

# The Christian Religion as a Learned Religion.

Insofar as a religion presents dogmas as necessary which cannot be recognized by reason alone, but which must nevertheless be communicated unadulterated (in their essential content) to all people for all future times, it must be viewed as a sacred treasure entrusted to the care of the learned—unless one wishes to assume a continuous miracle of revelation. For although such a religion may have been accompanied by miracles and deeds at its beginning, allowing it to find entry everywhere even in matters <margin>30</note> not confirmed by reason, the very report of these miracles, along with the teachings that required confirmation through them, will in the course of time require a written, documentary, and unchangeable instruction for future generations.

The acceptance of the principles of a religion is called, preeminently, faith (<note>original Latin: *fides sacra*, or "sacred faith"</note>). We shall...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into how the Christian religion functions as a "learned religion." It builds on the previous discussion of how universal moral truths were historicaly packaged in specific cultural forms, now moving into the distinction between faith based on reason and faith based on established tradition or revelation.</meta>

Part I, Section 2: The Christian Religion as a Learned Religion. 191

...we must therefore consider the Christian faith on the one hand as a pure **faith of reason**, and on the other hand as a **faith of revelation** (<term>statutory faith</term> <note>original Latin: "fides statutaria"; a faith based on established laws and doctrines rather than inner moral logic</note>). The former can be viewed as a faith freely adopted by everyone (<term>elicited faith</term> <note>original Latin: "fides elicita"; faith that is drawn out from within the individual</note>), while the latter is a commanded faith (<term>enjoined faith</term> [248] <note>original Latin: "fides imperata"; faith that is required by an outside authority</note>). Every person can be convinced by their own reason of several things: the evil that lies in the human heart and from which no one is free; the impossibility of ever considering oneself justified before God through one's own conduct; yet the simultaneous necessity of such a <margin>10</margin> **righteousness** that is valid before Him; the futility of substituting church observances and pious "forced labor" <note>original: "Frondienste"; originally referring to feudal labor, here meaning religious rituals performed out of obligation rather than love</note> for a lack of true integrity; and, in contrast, the indispensable obligation to become a new person. It is an essential part of religion to convince oneself of these truths.

From that point on, however, since Christian doctrine is built upon facts and not merely upon concepts of reason, it is no longer called simply the Christian religion, but the Christian **faith**, which has been laid down as the <margin>20</margin> foundation of a church. The service of a church dedicated to such a faith is therefore two-sided: on the one hand, that which must be performed according to historical faith; and on the other, that which is due according to practical and moral faith of reason. Neither of these can exist on its own within the Christian church or be separated from the other. The latter (faith of reason) cannot be separated from the former because the Christian faith is a religious faith; the former (historical faith) cannot be separated from the latter because it is a learned faith. <margin>30</margin>

Christian faith as a learned faith [249] relies on history and, insofar as it is based on scholarship (objectively), it is not a faith that is inherently free or derived from theoretical grounds of insight (<term>elicited faith</term> <note>original Latin: "fides elicita"</note>). If it were a pure faith of reason, it would have to be regarded as a free faith—as was presented in the first section—even though the moral laws upon which it is founded (as faith in a divine lawgiver) command unconditionally. Indeed, <margin>40</margin> even as a historical faith, it could be a theoretically free faith, provided that believing was not made a duty.

<summary>Kant distinguishes between faith based on universal moral reason and faith based on historical revelation and scholarship, arguing that the Christian church requires both to function as a "learned religion." He emphasizes that while moral duties are clear to all, the historical and scholarly elements of faith create a complex structure where belief is often treated as a commanded duty.</summary>

# Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part IV.

...if everyone were a scholar. But if it is to be valid for everyone, including the unlearned, then it is not merely a commanded faith, but one that obeys the command blindly—that is, without investigating whether it is truly a divine command—a **servile faith** <note>original Latin: "fides servilis"</note>.

In the Christian doctrine of revelation, however, one can by no means start with an **unconditional faith** in revealed propositions (which are hidden from reason on its own) and let scholarly knowledge follow merely as a defense against <margin>10</margin> an enemy attacking the rear guard; for otherwise the Christian faith would be not just an **enjoined faith** <note>original Latin: "fides imperata"; a faith required by an authority</note>, but actually a **servile** one. It must therefore always be taught at least as a **historically elicited faith** <note>original Latin: "fides historice elicita"; a faith drawn out from historical records and testimony</note>; that is, 

<margin>[250]</margin> **Scholarship** in this revealed doctrine of faith must not form the rear guard, but the vanguard. The small number of scripture scholars (the clergy), who also cannot do without secular learning, would drag behind them the long train of the unlearned (the laity), who are themselves ignorant of the scriptures <margin>20</margin> (among whom even world-governing rulers belong). — If this is not to happen, then universal human reason must be recognized and honored as the highest commanding principle within a natural religion within Christian doctrine. The doctrine of revelation, upon which a church is founded and which requires scholars as interpreters and preservers, must be loved and cultivated as a mere, yet highly valuable, means to provide the former with clarity even for the ignorant, as well as with expansion and permanence. <margin>30</margin> 

This is the true **service** of the church under the dominion of the good principle. However, where faith in revelation is intended to precede religion, it becomes **counterfeit service** <note>original German: "Afterdienst"; a "pseudo-service" or "mock-worship" where the outward form is mistaken for the inner moral purpose</note>, whereby the moral order is completely reversed and that which is only a means is commanded unconditionally (as if it were the end itself). The faith in propositions which the unlearned person cannot verify either through reason or scripture (insofar as the latter would first have to be authenticated) would be made into an absolute duty <margin>[251]</margin> (**enjoined faith**) and so, along with other associated observances, would be elevated to the rank of a "forced labor" <note>original: "Frondienst"; religious rituals performed as a mandatory feudal-like obligation to God</note> which is supposedly soul-saving even without moral motives for one's actions—

<summary>Kant argues that if religious revelation is placed above human reason, faith becomes a "servile" and "counterfeit" service. He asserts that scholarly interpretation of scripture should only serve as a tool to help spread universal moral truths that reason can discover on its own.</summary>

### Part 1, Section 2: The Christian Religion as a Learned Religion. 193

### Part 1, Section 2: The Christian religion as a learned religion. 195

The Christian religion, to be sure, has a similar fate in that, although its sacred events occurred publicly under the eyes of a learned people, its history was nevertheless delayed by more than a human generation before it entered the learned <margin>10</margin> public; consequently, its authenticity <term>Authenticity: Here referring to the historical reliability and verifiable origin of the New Testament texts</term> must lack confirmation by contemporaries. It has, however, a great advantage over Judaism in that it is presented as having emerged from the mouth of its first teacher not as a statutory <term>Statutory religion: A religion based on revealed laws, rituals, and external commands rather than internal moral principles</term>, but as a moral religion. In this way, entering into the closest connection with reason, it could be spread by reason itself with the greatest certainty among all times and peoples, even without historical scholarship. But the first founders <margin>20</margin> of the congregations nevertheless found it necessary to intertwine the history of Judaism with it, which was done wisely according to their situation at the time—but perhaps only for that specific situation—and so it has come down to us in their sacred legacy. The founders of the church, however, took these episodic means of recommendation as essential articles of faith and increased them either with tradition or interpretations that received legal force from councils <gloss>a)</gloss>, or <margin>[255]</margin> were documented through scholarship. Regarding the latter, or its opposite, the "inner light" <note>The "inner light" refers to a mystical or direct spiritual intuition, often contrasted by Kant with the rational or scholarly study of religion</note> which any layman can also claim <margin>30</margin> for himself, it cannot yet be foreseen how many changes still await faith; this cannot be avoided as long as we seek religion not within ourselves, but outside of ourselves.

# Part Two.

## Concerning the Pseudo-Service of God in a Statutory Religion.

The true and only religion contains nothing but laws—that is, those practical principles of whose absolute necessity we can become conscious, and which we therefore recognize as revealed through **pure reason** <term>Pure reason: The capacity of the human mind to arrive at truths and moral laws independently of sensory experience or divine revelation</term> (rather than empirically). It is only for the sake of a **church**—of which there can be various equally good forms—that there can be
<margin>10</margin>
**statutes**: ordinances held to be divine, which for our pure moral judgment are arbitrary and incidental. To consider this statutory faith (which is at most restricted to a single people and cannot contain the universal world religion) as essential to the service of God in general, and to make it the
<margin>[256]</margin>
supreme condition of God’s favor toward humanity, is a **religious delusion** <note>original: *Religionswahn*</note>, the

---

<margin>[256]</margin>
*) **Delusion** <note>original: *Wahn*</note> is the deception of treating the mere representation of a thing as being equivalent to the thing itself. For example, a miserly rich man suffers from a "greedy delusion" in that he believes the mere *idea* of being able to use his riches whenever he wished is a sufficient substitute for actually using them. The **delusion of honor** <note>original: *Ehrenwahn*</note> places value on the praise of others—which is fundamentally only the external representation of their respect (which they may not even internally harbor)—rather than on the value he should only attribute to the respect itself. This also includes the **craving for titles and medals**, as these are merely external representations of an advantage over others. Even **madness** <note>original: *Wahnsinn*; literally "delusion-sense"</note> takes its name from this, because it is the habit of taking a mere representation (of the imagination) for the presence of the thing itself and valuing it as such. — Now, the awareness of possessing a *means* to an end (before one has actually used that means) is the possession of the end only in one’s imagination; therefore, to be satisfied with the former as if it could serve in place of the possession of the latter is a **practical delusion**; and it is this kind of delusion that is the sole subject of our discussion here.

<summary>Kant distinguishes between "true religion" based on universal moral reason and "statutory religion" based on arbitrary church laws. He defines religious delusion as the error of mistaking external rituals or means for the actual moral end of pleasing God.</summary>

**Anthropomorphism** <term>Anthropomorphism: The tendency to attribute human characteristics, emotions, or intentions to God</term>, which is almost unavoidable for humans in our theoretical conception of God and His nature, is otherwise harmless enough (provided it does not influence our concepts of duty). However, it is highly dangerous in regard to our practical relationship to His will and for our **morality** itself. ---

<margin>[257]</margin>
*) It sounds questionable, but it is by no means reprehensible to say: that every human being creates a God for themselves. Indeed, according to moral concepts (accompanied by the infinitely great attributes necessary to represent an object in the world adequate to those concepts), one must create such a Being for oneself in order to honor, in Him, the One who created us. For in whatever way a Being might be made known and described as God by another—or even if such a Being should appear to him personally (if that were possible)—he must still first compare this representation with his own ideal to judge whether he is authorized to consider it and worship it as a Divinity. <margin>30, 40</margin>

<meta>This page continues Kant’s exploration of the "pseudo-service" of God. ## II. Part. Concerning the Pseudo-Service of God. § 2.

But is there not also, perhaps, | a dizzying **delusion of virtue** rising above the limits [266] of human capacity, which might well be counted among the general class of self-deceptions along with cringing **religious delusion**? No, the **disposition of virtue** <term>Tugendgesinnung: The internal moral orientation and commitment to doing one's duty</term> occupies itself with something real, which is in itself pleasing to God and harmonizes with the highest good of the world. To be sure, a delusion of self-conceit may accompany it—the belief that one is adequate to the idea of one's holy duty—but that is only accidental. However, to place the highest value in virtue is not a delusion, like that found in church devotional exercises, but a pure contribution working toward the best for the world.

Moreover, it is a custom (at least a churchly one) to call that which can be done by humans by virtue of the principle of virtue **nature**, but to call that which serves only to supplement the deficiency of all our moral capacity **grace**. Because achieving moral sufficiency is our duty, grace can only be wished for, or hoped and prayed for. Both together are seen as the efficient causes 20 of a disposition sufficient for a life-conduct pleasing to God; but they are not merely distinguished from one another, but even set in opposition to one another.

### Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part IV.

To wish to **perceive** heavenly influences within oneself is a kind of madness, in which there may even be a "method" <note>An allusion to Shakespeare’s *Hamlet*: "Though this be madness, yet there is method in 't." Kant suggests that while these inner "revelations" are delusions, they often align themselves with moral principles to seem logical.</note> (since those supposed inner revelations must always connect to moral, and thus rational, ideas), but which nonetheless remains a self-deception detrimental to religion. To believe that there can be effects of grace—and perhaps even must be, to supplement the incompleteness of our struggle for virtue—is everything that we can say about them;
<margin>10</margin> moreover, we are incapable of determining anything regarding their characteristics, and even less capable of doing anything to produce them.

The delusion that one can achieve something regarding justification before God through religious acts of worship is religious **superstition** <term>Aberglaube: The belief that ritualistic or mechanical actions—rather than moral improvement—can win God's favor</term>; just as the delusion of wanting to bring this about through the endeavor for a supposed communion with God is religious **fanaticism** <term>Schwärmerei: Often translated as 'enthusiasm' or 'delusion'; the belief that one can experience a direct, sensible connection or communication with the Divine</term>. —
<margin>[268]</margin> It is a superstitious delusion | to want to become pleasing to God through actions that any person can do without having to be a good
<margin>20</margin> person (e.g., through the profession of statutory articles of faith, through the observation of church ritual and discipline, and the like). But it is called superstitious for this reason: because it chooses mere natural means (not moral ones) which, in themselves, can effect absolutely nothing toward that which is not nature (namely, the morally good). — A delusion, however, is called fanatical when even the imagined means, being supersensible, are not within the human capacity, without even looking at the unreachability of the
<margin>30</margin> supersensible purpose intended by them; for this feeling of the immediate presence of the Supreme Being and the distinguishing of it from every other feeling, even the moral feeling, would be a receptivity to an intuition for which there is no sense in human nature. — Superstitious delusion—because it contains a means that is in itself suitable for some subjects and at the same time possible for them, at least to counteract the obstacles to a disposition pleasing to God—is nonetheless related to reason in so far as it only
<margin>40</margin> becomes reprehensible by chance, through the fact that it makes that which can only be a means into an object immediately pleasing to God; on the other hand, fanatical religious delusion

<meta>This page continues Kant's analysis of "counterfeit service" to God. He moves from distinguishing between free moral service and mercenary service to defining the psychological delusion of thinking one can influence the divine through ritual acts without moral worth.</meta>

### Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part IV.

The art of attempting to bring about a supernatural effect through entirely natural means is what we usually call **magic**. However, we will instead use the term **fetish-making** for such attempts. We choose this word because "magic" carries the secondary connotation of a partnership with the evil principle <note>meaning a pact with the devil or dark forces</note>, whereas these attempts might simply be misunderstandings by someone who actually has a good moral intention. A supernatural effect produced by a human being would <margin>10</margin> be one that exists only in his imagination, because he believes he can act upon God and use Him as a tool to bring about a result in the world. To do this, his own powers—and even his own insight into whether such an act would be pleasing to God—are insufficient; such a concept already contains a logical absurdity.

However, a person may realize that besides what directly makes him an object of divine favor (the active disposition <note>German: *Gesinnung*. This refers to the inner moral attitude or "heart" behind one's actions.</note> of a <margin>20 [274]</margin> good life-conduct), he also needs to make himself worthy of supernatural assistance to supplement his own weaknesses. If, with this intention, he practices certain formalities—which have no intrinsic value but serve as a means to encourage that moral disposition—and thinks of himself as merely becoming **receptive** to the achievement of his good moral wishes, then he is indeed counting on something **supernatural** to help his natural inability. Yet, he does not view this as something <margin>30</margin> **wrought by the human being** (by influencing the divine will), but rather as something **received**, which he can hope for but cannot force to happen.

On the other hand, a person might believe that certain actions—which, as far as we can see, contain nothing moral or pleasing to God in themselves—should serve as a means or even a condition for expecting the fulfillment of his wishes directly from God. In this case, he must be under the delusion that even though he possesses neither the physical power nor the moral <margin>40</margin> **receptivity** for this **supernatural** aid, he can nonetheless achieve it through natural actions which are not related to **morality** at all (actions which require no disposition pleasing to God)...

<summary>Kant defines "fetish-making" as the superstitious attempt to influence God through non-moral rituals. He distinguishes between hoping for divine aid through a moral life and the delusion of "magic," where one tries to use God as a tool for personal ends.</summary>

### Part II. On the Counterfeit Service of God. § 3.

<margin>10</margin>
...needs a disposition <note>German: *Gesinnung*; the internal moral orientation of the heart.</note>, which the worst of men can exercise just as well as the best), [believing] one can bring about and, as it were, conjure up the assistance of the Godhead through formulas of invocation, through confessions of a faith based on reward, through church observances, and the like. For there is no connection whatsoever—according to any law that reason can conceive—between merely physical [275] means and a morally acting cause, whereby the latter could be represented as determinable to certain effects by the former <note>Kant refers here to the physical means, such as rituals.</note>.

<margin>20</margin>
Whoever, therefore, gives precedence to the observation of statutory laws—laws that require a revelation—as being necessary to religion, and treats them not merely as a means for the moral disposition but as the objective condition for becoming immediately pleasing to God, and subordinates the effort toward a good life-conduct to this historical faith (instead of ensuring that the former, which can only be pleasing to God conditionally, conforms to the latter, which alone pleases Him absolutely)—that person transforms the service of God into mere **fetish-making**. They practice a **counterfeit service** <term>Afterdienst: A "pseudo-service" or "counterfeit" worship where external rituals are mistaken for true moral devotion.</term> that reverses all the progress made toward true religion. When one wishes to combine two good things, so much depends on the order in which they are combined!

<margin>30</margin>
— In this distinction, however, lies true **Enlightenment**; only through this does the service of God first become a free, and therefore moral, service. But if one departs from this path, then instead of the freedom of the children of God, a yoke of a law (the statutory law) is imposed upon man. This yoke—because it is presented as an unconditional necessity to believe something that can only be known historically [276] and thus cannot be convincing to everyone—is for conscientious people a far heavier yoke *) than the entire heap of imposed pious practices.

<margin>[277]</margin> **Priestcraft** <term>Pfaffentum: A term used by Kant to describe a religious system where a clergy rules through rituals and "magic" rather than moral instruction; often translated as "clericalism."</term> is, therefore, the constitution of a church insofar as a **fetish-service** <margin>10</margin> governs it. This is always to be found wherever the foundation and the essentials of the church do not consist of principles of morality, but rather of statutory commands, rules of faith, and observances a). Now, there are indeed many forms of church in which the "fetish-making" is so manifold and so mechanical that it seems to displace almost all *morality*, and thus *religion* itself, appearing to take their place; such forms border very closely on **paganism**. However, it is not a matter of "more or less" here <margin>20</margin> where the value or lack of value depends on the nature of the highest binding principle. If this principle imposes obedient submission to a decree as a form of **slavish service** <note>original: "Frondienst," referring to the compulsory labor a peasant owed a lord.</note>, rather than the free homage that should be paid primarily to the moral law, then it does not matter how few the imposed observances may be. It is enough that they are declared absolutely necessary; if so, this is always a **fetish-faith** through which the masses are governed and, through obedience to a *church* (*rather than to religion*), are robbed of their moral freedom. <margin>30</margin> The constitution of such a church (**hierarchy**) may be monarchical, aristocratic, or democratic; that concerns only its organization. Its underlying nature is and [remains despotic].

### Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part IV.

**Historical faith** <note>original: "Geschichtsglaube" — faith based on historical accounts and scriptures rather than pure reason.</note>, especially when the concepts it requires to grasp its reports are entirely **anthropological** <note>conceived in human terms</note> and highly adapted to **sensibility** <note>original: "Sinnlichkeit" — the faculty of sensory perception</note>, is exactly of this kind.<sup>b)</sup> For what is easier than to grasp such a sensory and simple narrative and to share it with one another, or to repeat the words of "mysteries" without it being at all necessary to attach a meaning to them? How easily does such a thing—especially when a great promised interest is at stake—find 
<margin>10</margin> general acceptance? And how deeply rooted does a belief in the truth of such a narrative become, which moreover is based on a **document** <note>original: "Urkunde" — a reference to the Bible or sacred texts</note> that has been recognized as authentic for a long time? Thus, such a faith is indeed suited to the most common human capacities.
However, although the proclamation of such an event, as well as the belief in rules of conduct based upon it, must not be given solely or primarily for **scholars** or **philosophers** <note>original: "Weltweise" — literally "the world-wise," an 18th-century term for philosophers</note>, these thinkers are nevertheless not excluded from it. And there 
<margin>20 [280]</margin> | now arise so many doubts, partly regarding its truth and partly regarding the sense in which its presentation should be taken, that to accept such a faith—which is subject to so many disputes (even those intended sincerely)—as the supreme condition of a universal and **only-saving faith**, is the most **absurd** <note>original: "Widersinnigste"</note> thing one can imagine. — Now, however, there exists a **practical knowledge** which, although it rests solely on reason and requires no historical teaching, is yet so 
<margin>30</margin> close to every human being, even the simplest, as if it were literally **written in his heart**: a law which one only needs to name to immediately reach an agreement with everyone regarding its authority, and which carries with it unconditional obligation in everyone’s consciousness—namely, that of **morality**. And what is more, this knowledge either leads on its own to a belief in God, or at least alone defines His concept as that of a **moral lawgiver**; consequently, it leads to a **pure religious faith** <note>original: "reinen Religionsglauben"</note> that is not only comprehensible to every human being 
<margin>40</margin> but also venerable in the highest degree; indeed, it<sup>a)</sup>

---

a) namely the knowledge; <note>Kant used the masculine pronoun "he" (er) and the editor Wobbermin used the neuter "it" (es) to refer back to "Erkenntnis" (knowledge).</note>

<summary>Kant argues that while historical faith is popular because it uses simple stories, it is too prone to dispute to be the foundation of a universal religion. Instead, he points to the universal moral law "written in the heart" as the true basis for a pure religious faith.</summary>

Thus, the doctrine of godliness cannot itself constitute the final purpose of moral striving; it can only serve as a means to strengthen that which constitutes a better person in himself—the **virtuous disposition**. It does this by promising and securing for that disposition (as a striving toward the good, and even toward holiness) the expectation of the final purpose, for which the disposition itself is insufficient. 
<margin>30</margin> On the other hand, the **concept of virtue** is drawn from the human soul. A person already possesses it entirely within themselves, though undeveloped; it does not need to be "reasoned out" through logical conclusions like the concept of religion. <margin>40</margin> leading toward the **Godhead** itself (who is only worthy of adoration through His holiness and as a lawgiver for virtue), that even if a man is still far from...

### Philosophical Theory of Religion. Part IV.

the highest danger and uncertainty in this supposed means of prudence—the attempt to cunningly evade the disadvantageous consequences that might arise from not confessing, only to hold with both parties and thereby perish with both. —

### General Remark.

<margin>[296]</margin>
Whatever good a person can do for themselves according to the laws of freedom, in comparison to the power that is only possible through supernatural assistance, can be called **nature** to distinguish it from **grace**. We do not use the term "nature" here to imply a physical quality distinct from freedom. Rather, we use it because we can at least recognize the laws (of virtue) governing this human power; <margin>10</margin> therefore, reason has a visible and comprehensible guide, treating it as an **analogue** <note>In Kant's philosophy, an "analogue" is a way of understanding something we cannot directly experience by comparing its structure to something we can experience—in this case, comparing the laws of freedom to the laws of nature.</note> of nature. In contrast, whether, when, and what—or how much—**grace** will work within us remains entirely hidden. In this realm, as with the supernatural in general (to which morality as **holiness** <note>original: "Heiligkeit" — a state of perfect moral purity that human beings strive for but cannot fully achieve on their own.</note> belongs), reason is left without any knowledge of the laws according to which it might occur.
The concept of a supernatural contribution to our—

---

—downward? I can certainly admit—though it is much to be regretted—that **candor** <note>original: "Offenherzigkeit" — the willingness to tell the whole truth that one knows.</note> is not found in human nature. However, **sincerity** <note>original: "Aufrichtigkeit" — the requirement that everything one *does* say must be spoken with total truthfulness.</note> must be something we can demand from every human being. Even if there were no natural predisposition for it in our nature, and its cultivation were merely neglected, the human race would have to be an object of the deepest contempt in its own eyes. — But this required quality of mind is one that is exposed to many temptations and costs many a sacrifice; therefore, it also requires moral strength, that is, **virtue** (which must be acquired) <margin>[296]</margin> and must be guarded and cultivated earlier than any other. This is because the opposite inclination, once allowed to take root, is the most difficult to eradicate. — Now, compare this with our method of education, especially in matters of religion or, better yet, doctrines of faith. There, the accuracy of memory in answering questions concerning these doctrines is accepted as sufficient to make a "believer," without any regard for the sincerity of the confession (about which no examination is ever made). Thus, we create a person who does not even understand that which he solemnly professes. One should no longer wonder at the lack of sincerity, which produces nothing but internal hypocrites.*)

<header>Philosophical Religious Theory. Part IV.</header>

moral ability, although a deficient one, and even to our not fully purified—or at least weak—**disposition** <term>original: "Gesinnung" — the underlying moral orientation or "spirit" behind an action, rather than just the outward act.</term> to satisfy all our duty, is **transcendent** and a mere **idea**, of whose reality no experience can assure us. — But even to assume it as an idea for a merely practical purpose is very risky and hardly compatible with reason; because what is to be credited to us as good moral behavior must not happen through foreign influence, but only through the
<margin>10</margin>best possible use of our own powers. Yet, the impossibility of this (that both—human effort and divine influence—happen side-by-side) cannot be proven either, because freedom itself, although it contains nothing supernatural in its concept, nevertheless remains just as incomprehensible to us in its possibility as the supernatural, which one might want to assume as a substitute for the self-active but deficient determination of that freedom.

Since we do at least know the laws according to which freedom is to be determined (the
<margin>20</margin>**moral laws**), but cannot recognize even the slightest bit regarding a supernatural assistance—whether a certain moral strength perceived in us really stems from it, or in what cases and under what conditions it is to be expected—we will be unable to make any further use of this idea beyond the general assumption that what nature cannot accomplish in us, **grace** will effect, provided we have used the former (that is, our own powers) as much as possible. We cannot determine how we might draw its cooperation upon ourselves (beyond the a) steady
<margin>30</margin>effort toward a good life), nor how we could determine in which cases we are to expect it. — This idea

In Kant's technical sense, it refers to ideas that exceed the limits of all possible experience.</note>, and it is moreover beneficial to keep one's distance from it as if from a sanctuary, with respectful distance, so that we do not—in the delusion of performing miracles ourselves or perceiving miracles within us—render ourselves unfit for any use of reason, or b) also allow ourselves to be invited into laziness, expecting from above in passive leisure
<margin>40</margin>that which we should seek within ourselves.

# General Remark (the "Means of Grace")

<margin>10</margin>
<margin>20</margin>
Now, "means" are all those intermediate causes that a human being has within their power to achieve a specific purpose. To become worthy of heavenly assistance, there is nothing else—nor can there be anything else—than the earnest endeavor to improve one’s moral condition <term>original: "sittliche Beschaffenheit" — the state of one's character and ethical makeup</term> to the greatest extent possible. By doing so, a person makes themselves receptive to that perfection which fits them for divine approval—a perfection which is not within their power. This is because the very divine assistance they expect actually has nothing else as its goal but their own morality. It was to be expected from the outset <note>original: *a priori* — reasoning based on theoretical deduction rather than observation</note> that the impure person would not seek grace in this way, but would instead prefer to find it in certain sensory arrangements. These rituals are, of course, within their power, but in themselves they cannot make a person any better <gloss>a) The word "can" is missing in the 1st edition.</gloss>—even though they are supposed to bring this about in a supernatural way. Indeed, this is exactly what we find in practice. The concept of a so-called **means of grace** <term>original: *Gnadenmittel* — religious rites or tools, like sacraments, believed to convey God's favor</term>, although it is self-contradictory (according to what has just been said), serves here as a tool for self-deception, which is as common as it is damaging to true religion.

<margin>30</margin>
The true (moral) service of God is something that believers must perform as subjects belonging to His kingdom, but also (under laws of freedom) as citizens of that kingdom. This service is, like the kingdom itself, invisible; that is, it is a service of the heart (in spirit and in truth) <gloss>b) "(in spirit and in truth)" was an addition in the 2nd edition.</gloss>. It consists only in the disposition <term>original: *Gesinnung* — the fundamental moral attitude or "spirit" of the heart</term> of observing all true duties as if they were divine commands; it does not consist in actions directed exclusively toward God. However, for a human being, the invisible must be represented by something visible (sensory). Even more, for the sake of practical application, the invisible must be accompanied by the visible so that, although it is intellectual, it can be made intuitive (through a certain analogy). This is a means that is not easily dispensed with, yet it is at the same time very much subject to the danger of misinterpretation. It is intended only to make our duty in the service of God present to our minds; however, through a **delusion** <term>original: *Wahn* — a false belief or illusory religious zeal</term> that creeps up on us...

### Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part IV.

...yet <gloss>a) 1st Edition: "but"</gloss> is easily mistaken for the *service of God* itself and is also commonly named as such.

When this alleged service of God is traced back to its spirit and true meaning—namely, a disposition <term>original: *Gesinnung* — the underlying moral attitude or "heart" from which one acts</term> dedicated to the Kingdom of God within and around us—it can be divided by *reason* into four *observances of duty*. Certain formalities, which have no necessary connection to these duties, have been assigned to them as counterparts. 
<margin>10</margin> These rituals have been found since ancient times to be good sensory means, serving as a *schema* <term>original: *Schema* — in Kant's philosophy, a "bridge" or mental image that helps us apply abstract concepts to our sensory experiences</term> for those duties; they aim to awaken and sustain our attention on the true service of God. They are all based on the intention of promoting the moral good: 1) To establish it firmly within ourselves and repeatedly awaken this disposition in the mind (the *private*
<margin>[300]</margin> *prayer*). 2) The external *spreading* of this good through public assembly on days consecrated for that purpose, in order to voice religious doctrines and wishes (and thus such
<margin>20</margin> dispositions) and to share them universally (the *attending of church*). 3) The *propagation* of the moral good to the next generation by accepting new members into the community of faith, as a duty to instruct them in it (in the Christian religion, *baptism*). 4) The *maintenance* of this community through a repeated public formality, which makes the union of these members into an ethical body permanent, specifically according to the principle of equality regarding their rights and
<margin>30</margin> their share in the fruits of the morally good (the *communion*).

Any undertaking in religious matters—if it is not taken purely morally but is instead adopted as a means that is supposedly pleasing to God in itself, and thus a way to satisfy all our wishes through Him—is a *fetish-faith* <term>original: *Fetischglaube* — the belief that God can be influenced through ritual acts rather than through moral improvement</term>. This is a persuasion that what can have no effect according to either the laws of nature or the moral laws of reason will nevertheless produce the desired result on its own, provided one only firmly believes

## Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part IV.

...mystery is, namely, the ability to bring about the influence of God on our
<margin>[302]</margin> **morality** (belief in the **means of grace**). — Of the first two artificial <term>original: *erkünstelten* — meaning contrived or man-made rituals intended to bypass moral duty</term> types of faith, we have dealt with in the general remarks of the two preceding parts of this work. It remains for us now to deal with the **means of grace** ᵃ) (which are still distinguished from **effects of grace**, *) i.e., supernatural moral influences, in which we remain merely passive, but whose supposed experience is a fanatical delusion that belongs purely to the realm of feeling).

1. **Praying**, conceived as an internal, formal divine service and therefore as a means of grace, is a superstitious delusion (a **fetish-making** <note>Kant uses this term to describe the attempt to influence a supernatural being through rituals or charms, rather than through moral character</note>); for it is a mere expressed wishing toward a Being who needs no explanation of the inner disposition <term>original: *Gesinnung* — the core moral attitude or "heart" from which a person acts</term> of the one wishing. Thus, nothing is actually done through it, and none of the duties incumbent upon us as commands of God are exercised; therefore, God is not truly served. A heartfelt wish to be pleasing to God in all our "doing and letting" <note>a German idiom meaning all our actions and omissions</note>—that is, the disposition accompanying all our actions to perform them as if they occurred in the service of God—is the **spirit of prayer**, which can and should occur within us "without ceasing" <note>original: *ohne Unterlaß* — a reference to the New Testament exhortation to pray continually</note>. <margin>[303]</margin> of a means for the repeated awakening of that disposition...

### General Remark (the "Means of Grace").

...carry within ourselves, but have no immediate relation to divine favor, and for that very reason cannot be a duty for everyone; because a means <margin>[304]</margin> [is only for the] mere spirit of the same). — The truth of this latter observation will be confirmed by anyone who imagines a pious and well-meaning person—who is otherwise limited in regard to such purified religious concepts—being surprised by another person; I will not say while praying aloud, but even just in the gestures that indicate it. One will naturally expect, without my saying so, that the person will fall into confusion or embarrassment, as if in a state for which they ought to feel ashamed. But why is that? That a person caught talking aloud to themselves is immediately suspected of having a slight fit of madness; and one judges them (not entirely unjustly) in the same way if they are caught, while alone, in an occupation or gesture that can only belong to someone who has another person before their eyes—which is not the case in the assumed example. — **The Teacher of the Gospel** <note>A reference to Jesus Christ</note> has, however, expressed the spirit of prayer quite excellently in a formula that makes this formula—and thus also itself (as a literal letter)—at the same time dispensable. In it, one finds nothing but the resolution for a good conduct of life, which, combined with the consciousness of our frailty, contains a constant wish to be a worthy member in the Kingdom of God; thus, it is not an actual petition for something that God, in His wisdom, might well refuse us, but a wish which, when it is earnest (active), brings about its own object (becoming a person pleasing to God). Even the wish for the means of sustaining our existence (bread) for one day—since it<sup>a)</sup> is explicitly not directed toward its long-term continuation, but is rather the effect of a merely animal felt need—is more a confession of what nature in us wants, than a specific deliberate petition for what the human being wants: such as a request for bread for the next day; which is clearly enough excluded here <note>Kant is likely referencing the phrase "daily bread" from the Lord's Prayer, interpreting the Greek term *epiousios* as bread for the immediate day, rather than accumulating wealth for the future</note>. — A prayer of this kind, which occurs in a moral <term>original: *moralisch* — relating to the internal law of duty</term> (enlivened only by the idea of God) disposition, because as the moral spirit of prayer it produces its own object (being pleasing to God), can alone occur in faith; the latter meaning as much as keeping oneself assured that it will be heard; but of this kind, nothing but the **morality** within us can be. For even if the petition were only for bread for today, no one can keep themselves assured of its being heard, i.e., that it is necessarily connected with the wisdom of God...

# Philosophical Theory of Religion. Part IV.

<margin>[305]</margin>
...can only be prescribed to someone who **requires it for certain purposes**, but it is by no means necessary for everyone to use this means (**of talking to oneself, ostensibly but more understandably talking to God**),

<margin>[305], [306]</margin>
to grant it to him; it might perhaps harmonize better with that wisdom to let him die today from this deficiency. It is also an absurd and at the same time arrogant delusion to try, through the insistent pestering <note>original: "pochende Zudringlichkeit"</note> of our begging, to see if God might be diverted from the plan of His wisdom (for some temporary benefit to us). Thus, we cannot consider any prayer that does not have a moral object as being certain to be heard; that is, we cannot pray for such a thing **in faith**. Indeed, even if the object were moral, but only possible through supernatural influence (or at least we expected it from there because we do not want to trouble ourselves to achieve it—such as the "change of heart," the "putting on of the new man," or what is called "rebirth" <note>Kant is referencing common theological terms for a person's moral and spiritual transformation</note>), it is so very uncertain whether God would find it in accordance with His wisdom to supplement our (self-inflicted) deficiency in a supernatural way that one has more reason to expect the opposite. Therefore, a person cannot pray "in faith" even for this. — From this, we can explain the true nature of a **miracle-working faith** (which would always be combined with an inner prayer). Since God cannot grant a human being the power to act supernaturally (because that is a contradiction), and since a human being—based on the concepts they form of good ends possible in the world—cannot determine what divine wisdom judges on the matter, and thus cannot use divine power for their own purposes through a wish they have generated themselves; a **gift of miracles**, understood literally as something a person can choose to have or not have ("**if you had faith as a grain of mustard seed**" <note>A reference to Matthew 17:20</note> and so on), is quite unthinkable. Such a faith, if it is to mean anything at all, is a mere idea of the overwhelming importance of a person's moral character. If a person possessed this character in its full perfection, pleasing to God (which they never actually reach), it would outweigh all other motives God might have in His supreme wisdom. It is therefore a reason to trust that if we were **entirely** what we ought to be and (in constant progression) could be, nature would have to obey our **wishes**, which in that state would never be unwise.

Regarding the edification <note>In this context, "edification" refers to the process of being morally or spiritually "built up" or improved</note> intended through church-going, public prayer is likewise not a means of grace, but rather an ethical ceremony, whether it be...

<summary>Kant argues that petitionary prayer is often an arrogant attempt to change God's wise and fixed plan, asserting that even prayers for moral improvement cannot be expected to trigger supernatural intervention. He interprets the biblical "faith that moves mountains" not as a literal power, but as a symbol of the supreme value of a perfect moral character.</summary>

<keywords>petitionary prayer, divine wisdom, miracle-working faith, moral character, means of grace, edification, rebirth, mustard seed faith</keywords>

# General Note (the “Means of Grace”).

...rather, through the continued purification and elevation of the
moral disposition, work must be done toward <margin>[306]</margin>
this spirit of prayer alone being sufficiently<sup>a)</sup>
enlivened within us, so that the letter of it (at least
for our own benefit) may finally fall away. For
the letter rather weakens—as does everything directed
indirectly toward a certain goal—the effect of the
moral idea (which, viewed subjectively, is called **devotion** <note>original: "Andacht"</note> <margin>[307]</margin>).
Thus, the contemplation of the deep wisdom of
divine creation in the smallest things, and its majesty in the great—
just as it has always been recognizable by humans,
but in recent times has been expanded to the highest point of admiration—has 
such power not only to transport the mind into that
sinking mood, which as it were annihilates a person in their 
own **eyes** <note>Kant describes the feeling of being "nothing" compared to the vastness of the universe</note>, a mood called **adoration** <note>original: "Anbetung"</note>, but it is also, with regard to

through the united singing of the hymn of faith, or also
through the formal **address** <note>original: "Anrede"</note> directed to God by the mouth of the 
clergyman in the name of the entire congregation, encompassing
all the moral concerns of humanity. This address, by presenting
these concerns as a public matter—where the wish of each individual
is represented as united with<sup>b)</sup> the wishes of all toward one and the 
same goal (the bringing about of the Kingdom of God)—can not 
only elevate the emotions toward moral **enthusiasm** (whereas
private prayers, because they are offered without this sublime idea, 
gradually lose their influence on the mind through habit), but 
also has more rational basis <margin>[307]</margin> for clothing the 
**moral wish**, which constitutes the spirit of prayer, in 
a formal address. Yet, in doing so, one should not think of 
the actual presence of the Supreme Being or of any special **power** 
within this rhetorical figure as a "means of grace." 
For there is a specific purpose here: namely, through an 
external ceremony representing the union of all people in<sup>c)</sup> the 
common wish for the Kingdom of God, to set the moral incentive 
of each individual even more into motion. This cannot happen 
more appropriately than by addressing the Sovereign of that 
Kingdom, just as if He were particularly present in that place.

a) “sufficiently” is missing in the 1st edition.
b) Kant: “itself with”; corrected by Vorländer <note>Hans Vorländer was a prominent 19th-century editor of Kant’s works</note>.
c) 1st ed.: “toward”.

<summary>Kant argues that prayer should evolve from an external ritual (the "letter") into an internal moral disposition (the "spirit"), viewing public prayer primarily as a tool for communal moral inspiration rather than a way to influence God.</summary>

This delusion indeed accords well enough with the **way of thinking** <note>original: "Denkungsart"</note> of a good citizen in a political commonwealth and with outward decency, but it contributes nothing at all to one’s quality as a citizen in the **Kingdom of God**; rather, it falsifies the latter and serves to hide the poor moral content of one’s disposition from the eyes of others, and even from one’s own, through a deceptive varnish.

However, people believe themselves to be very much **edified** <note>Kant is punning on the word "Erbauung" (edification), which literally means "building up." <summary>Kant critiques the view of religious rituals like church attendance and baptism as "means of grace" that please God independently of moral conduct, warning that such ceremonies are merely symbolic and should not be treated as "edification" without actual moral improvement.</summary>
