->### General Note (The “Means of Grace”).<-

...to be a good servant (one hears only of duties mentioned there); he would therefore rather be a **favorite**, where much is overlooked or, if a duty has been too grossly violated, everything is made right again through the mediation of someone favored in the highest degree, while he remains the same idle servant he was. But in order to satisfy himself with some appearance of the feasibility of this intention, he carries over his concept of a human being (together with its faults) as is usual to the Godhead <margin>[312]</margin>; and, just as even with the best superiors of our own species, legislative severity, beneficent grace, and punctilious justice do not (as they should) <margin>10</margin> each work separately and for themselves toward the moral effect of the subject's actions, but instead mix together in the mindset of the human sovereign when forming his decrees—so that one need only seek to reach one of these qualities, the frail <gloss>a)</gloss> wisdom of the human will, in order to determine the other two toward indulgence—so <margin>20</margin> he hopes to achieve this also with God by turning merely to His **grace**. (Hence, the separation of the aforementioned attributes—or rather, God’s relations to man—through the idea of a triple personality <note>original: "dreifachen Persönlichkeit" — Kant is referring to the Trinity here as a philosophical model for God’s roles as Legislator, Governor, and Judge</note>, in analogy to which they should be conceived, was an important distinction for religion, making each particularly recognizable.) To this end, he applies himself to all conceivable formalities, which are intended to indicate how much he honors the divine commands, so as not to have to observe them; and <margin>30</margin> so that his deedless wishes may also serve as compensation for his transgression of those commands, he cries: "Lord! Lord!", merely so as not to have to "do the will of the heavenly Father" <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 7:21</note>. Thus, regarding the ceremonies intended for the use of certain means to enliven truly practical dispositions, he forms the concept of them as means of grace in themselves; he even passes off the belief that they are such as an essential piece of religion (the common man even taking them for the whole of it) and leaves it to all-bountiful Providence to make out of him <margin>[313]</margin>

---

a) 1st Edition: "frailty of the".

<summary>Kant argues that humans prefer the status of a "favorite" over a "servant" of God, using religious rituals as "means of grace" to bypass moral duty. He critiques the human tendency to anthropomorphize God as an indulgent ruler who can be swayed by formalities rather than moral conduct.</summary>

# Philosophical Doctrine of Religion. Part IV.

...to make him a better person, in that he applies himself to **piety** (a passive veneration of the divine law) instead of **virtue** (the application of one's own powers to the fulfillment <gloss>a)</gloss> of the duty he venerates). This latter quality, only when combined with the former, can constitute the idea understood by the word **godliness** (true religious disposition). — When the delusion of this supposed favorite of heaven rises to the level of a fanatical <margin>10</margin> imagination of feeling special effects of grace within himself (even to the point of an assumed intimacy in a supposed hidden communion with God), then virtue finally begins to disgust him and becomes an object of contempt. It is therefore no wonder that there are public complaints that religion still contributes so little to the improvement of human beings, and that the "inner light" (kept "under a bushel" <note>A reference to Matthew 5:15, suggesting these "favored" people hide their lack of actual good works behind a veil of private spirituality.</note>) of these favored ones does not also wish to shine outwardly through good works. One might especially demand this (given their claims) <margin>20</margin> over and above other naturally honest people, who embrace religion not as a substitute for, but as a promotion of, a virtuous disposition that manifests itself actively in a good way of life. The teacher of the Gospel <note>Jesus</note> nevertheless provided these external proofs of outward experience as a touchstone, as "fruits" by which one can recognize them and by which everyone can know themselves. Yet, it has not yet been seen that those who consider themselves extraordinarily favored (the elect) <margin>30</margin> surpass in the slightest the naturally honest man who can be trusted in social intercourse, in business, and in times of need. <margin>[314]</margin> On the contrary, taken as a whole, they can hardly withstand a comparison with him. This proves that the right path is not to proceed from grace to virtue, but rather from virtue to grace.

---

<margin>a)</margin> "to the fulfillment" <note>original: "zur Beobachtung"</note> is missing in the 2nd edition.

<summary>Kant distinguishes between passive piety and active virtue, arguing that true godliness must include the latter. He critques those who claim "special grace" or mystical experiences but fail to demonstrate superior moral conduct in their daily lives.</summary>
<keywords>piety, virtue, godliness, grace, moral improvement, religious delusion, Gospel, ethics, fruits of faith</keywords>
